20334-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London Charivari, volume one hundred and fifty-nine, is dated December 29, 1920. A joke notes fines for speeding, yet no official joke was made. It asks why Mr. Justice Darling never gets a case like this. Another item tells of a New York policeman caught moving a safe.

Caught in the act, he offered to run and fetch a burglar. Such brief gags fill Punch's famous short paragraphs each week. The 1920 volume shows Britain joking again after the Great War. Readers get a year-end slice of Punch wit, light and sharp.
20392-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London humor magazine, filled its pages with jokes, cartoons, and light verse on the news of the week. This issue, dated November 24, 1920, belongs to volume 159. Its writers poked fun at politics, fashion, and foreign affairs alike.

One joke takes up a claim from the United States Bureau of Standards. The bureau said the jaw's pressure while chewing reaches eleven tons to the square inch. Punch wonders if this is crude propaganda work on behalf of the American bacon trade. The quip shows the magazine's dry way with official news.
20779-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
A sailor fined twenty shillings opens the October 27, 1920 Punch in a droll court tale. He had refused to join his ship, blaming a rat as big as a cat in his cabin. The court replied that only officers may claim rats in the cabin.

Punch in 1920 kept its old trade of jokes, verse, and cartoons on public life. The war was past, but its shadow still touched the fun. This single weekly issue holds one slice of British humor at a set date. Readers can track how the famed magazine met a changed world with its wit intact.
21002-the-writings-of-thomas-jefferson-l:
Clear thought, tact, and force of appeal win respect in all ages, this Jefferson volume notes. Yet many able men lack balance and fall prey to their feelings, it warns. Volume six of the Library Edition of Jefferson's writings holds such musings.

Letters and papers from Jefferson's rich middle years fill this sixth of twenty volumes. The Thomas Jefferson Memorial Association issued the set in 1903-04. Statecraft, farming, books, and friendship share his tireless pen here. Readers meet Jefferson whole, not just the sage of set phrases, in the daily grain of his own words.
22957-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Tipping trouble leads Punch's issue of April 14, 1920, from volume 158. An American journal with a wonderful title, the Commercial Bribery and Tipping Review, offers a prize for essays against tipping barbers. The barbers reply that their coins are no tip at all. They call them payment for keeping secrets.

Peace had returned, and the magazine's jokes turned back to waiters, barbers, trains, and prices. Cartoons and short paragraphs in this number catch Britain adjusting to 1920, glad of quiet and cross about costs. Single issues of Punch reward browsing exactly as they did on publication day. This one also preserves the transatlantic joke trade, American habits supplying British punch lines as reliably as ever.
23200-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
Volume 5 of The Journal of Negro History, issued in 1920, gathers scholarly studies of Black history. One study takes up how enslaved people were taught, and how that teaching varied between empires. In Spanish districts, it notes, Latin custom around mixed unions softened objections to instructing enslaved readers.

The passage sets that practice beside teaching tied to the Bible in other colonies. Such comparisons are the journal's method: careful, source-based history of Black life under slavery and after. Readers get early academic history writing that treated Black education, faith, and custom as serious subjects of study.
aitareya-brahmana-keith-1920:
Arthur Berriedale Keith translated the Aitareya Brahmana for the Harvard Oriental Series in 1920. The Aitareya is the old ritual manual of the Rigveda's priests. Keith's volume also includes the Kausitaki Brahmana, a sister text.

The manual walks priests through the great soma rites, chant by chant. Myths appear strung through the rules, explaining why each rite matters. The Kausitaki covers similar ground from a related priestly school. Together they show how India's earliest grand rites were actually performed. Keith was among the leading Sanskritists of his generation. His translation remains the standard English access to these difficult prose texts.
alchemy-a-symphonic-poem-1920: Alchemy: A Symphonic Poem, published in 1920, is a long poem by Robert Hillyer, the American poet. A symphonic poem is properly a piece of orchestral music built on a poetic idea, and Hillyer borrows that musical form for verse. Alchemy, the old art of transformation, supplies his theme: base matter striving toward gold, read as a figure for the spirit's own refining. The poem stands among his early books, from the years when he was making his name in American lyric poetry.
alexander-space-time-deity-vol-1-1920:
Samuel Alexander published Space, Time, and Deity, Volume 1, in 1920, from his Gifford Lectures. Alexander builds a metaphysics on the idea of emergent evolution. Space-time itself is the basic stuff of the universe. From it emerge matter, life, and mind, each a new level with new qualities.

Deity, in his striking phrase, is the universe's nisus, its drive toward a higher level not yet reached. This volume treats space-time, categories, and matter in detail. Alexander writes as a naturalist who still finds room for religion. The lectures drew wide attention in Britain and America. They remain a key work of emergent thought.
alexander-space-time-deity-vol-2-1920:
Samuel Alexander completed Space, Time, and Deity with Volume 2 in 1920. This volume rises through life and mind to value and deity. Mind emerges from living bodies, and values emerge with mind. Truth, goodness, and beauty are treated as features of the world, not mere feelings.

Alexander argues that the universe strains toward deity as its next emergent level. God, in this scheme, is both ideal and growing with the world. The view influenced Whitehead and later process thinkers. The style is systematic yet often vivid. Together the volumes state emergent evolution as a full metaphysics. They are a high point of British philosophy after the war.
anderson-poor-white-1920:
Sherwood Anderson published Poor White in 1920, the year after Winesburg, Ohio made his name. Anderson set the novel in Bidwell, Ohio, a farming town about to be remade by factories. He drew on the Midwest he had traveled as a paint salesman and advertising writer.

Hugh McVey, a dreamy telegraph operator raised in poverty, teaches himself to invent farm machines. His corn-picker and other devices bring factories, money, and strangers flooding into Bidwell. The town grows rich and frantic while Hugh, the cause of it all, feels the human price mounting. Anderson treats the industrial revolution as a spiritual event, not just an economic one. Poor White is his fullest novel of that change.
arxiv-2510-00220:
Daniel Brandon and nine colleagues published this 2025 physics paper on switching magnetism in four-layer graphene. In stacked two-dimensional materials, how the sheets slide against each other can change their behavior entirely. Rhombohedral stacking in graphene hosts exotic electronic phases that ordinary Bernal stacking lacks. The team asked whether an electric gate could slide the layers between these two arrangements.

Transport measurements show the gate does drive a sharp structural switch in tetralayer graphene. The device flips between a Bernal-rich state and a mixed stacking state, and the change sticks without power. Magnetism flips with it, from nonmagnetic to ferromagnetic, complete with an anomalous Hall signal. Reversing the field direction reverses that signal's sign as well. The authors see a route to on-demand toggling of quantum phases in layered materials.
arxiv-2510-00320:
K. Albert and eleven colleagues published this 2025 solar physics paper on faculae, the bright magnetic patches on the Sun. Faculae drive much of the Sun's brightness variation, yet they are hardest to read near the solar limb, the visible edge. Solar Orbiter gave the team a second vantage point in space. Earth-based instruments watched the same region at the same time.

One region sat near disc center for Solar Orbiter while Earth saw it near the limb. The team measured each facula's magnetic strength from the clear view, then its brightness from the edge view. Two viewpoints consistently yielded higher limb contrast than one viewpoint alone. Magnetic fields read at the limb proved unreliable against the disc-center values. The authors show dual-viewpoint data give a more consistent picture of the Sun's magnetic landscape near the edge.
arxiv-2510-00620:
Vasu and six co-authors present HARPA in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI tools for scientific ideation. Language models can brainstorm research hypotheses, but their ideas often prove untestable or drift from the published literature. HARPA mimics how human researchers work, first mining the literature for emerging trends, then mapping the space of possible hypotheses. Finally it narrows to precise, testable proposals and justifies each design choice against known gaps.

Expert judges rated HARPA proposals about level with a strong AI-researcher baseline on novelty and overall quality. On feasibility and groundedness, HARPA scored clearly higher on a ten-point scale. When an automated discovery agent ran the proposals, HARPA ideas produced twenty successful executions against eleven for the baseline. A learned reward scorer, trained on past experimental outcomes, improved hypothesis ranking by roughly twenty-eight points over the untrained version.
arxiv-2510-01120:
Ghose proposes a contextual seven-valued logic for quantum mechanics in this 2025 arXiv paper on the philosophy and foundations of physics. The measurement problem pits smooth unitary evolution against abrupt collapse, and Ghose, following Wittgenstein and Bohr, calls that clash a grammatical illusion. Statements about quantum systems borrow their meaning from experimental contexts, so mixing contexts manufactures paradox. His remedy borrows the ancient Jaina doctrine of sevenfold predication, saptabhanginaya.

He gives two formulations of the resulting logic. One assigns each proposition a triplet marking it true, false, or unsayable within a context, with paraconsistent rules that block logical explosion. The other builds context directly into quantified conditional statements. Applied to Schrödinger's cat and Wigner's friend, both versions dissolve the paradoxes once context is explicit. Ghose presents the framework as a coherent semantics for quantum discourse.
arxiv-2510-01720:
Sarkar constructs special Boolean functions for cryptography in this 2025 paper. A Boolean function turns a string of bits into a single bit, and ciphers rely on such functions. Three traits make them resist known attacks: resiliency, nonlinearity, and algebraic immunity. Functions that maximize one trait usually score poorly on the others. Designers therefore need provable trade-offs among all three.

Sarkar gives several families of functions with guarantees on every trait at once. Given target levels for each trait, his recipe builds a function that meets them all. The number of variables grows only in step with those targets. Each function also needs just a linear number of two-input gates, which is essentially optimal. Two families extend bent functions with strong algebraic immunity. Two more revive and complete an older sketch, giving the first such constructions for higher resiliency levels.
arxiv-2510-01820:
Nandi, Ghosh, Mohapatra, and Das report an optical cousin of the Hall effect in this 2025 physics paper. In electronics, the topological Hall effect bends charge flow in materials with twisted spin textures. The team created similar textures with light itself. A structured pump laser beam wrote pseudo-spin patterns into an organic solvent, toluene.

A weaker probe beam passed through the patterned region and picked up the effect. Phase-retrieval methods read the probe's phase profile after transmission. From that profile the authors extracted a topological charge for the texture. The value matched independent estimates of Berry curvature from their paraxial model of the third-order interaction. A synthetic magnetic field from the pump grew stronger at higher pump power. The result shows topological transport ideas working in an all-optical, nonlinear setting.
arxiv-2510-02020:
Zheng, Sze, and Huang pin down two elusive parameters of a family of BCH codes in this 2025 coding theory paper. BCH codes correct multiple errors with clean algebraic structure and efficient decoding. Despite decades of study, their dimension and Bose distance are unknown in general. The authors study narrow-sense codes whose length is a prime-like quotient built from a finite field size.

For codes over the field with q elements and length (q^m minus one) over a divisor of q minus one, they derive explicit formulas. The dimension formula covers designed distances up to a stated bound growing with m. A matching formula gives the Bose distance across nearly the same range. Both results require the exponent m to be at least four. Exact parameters let engineers predict a code's rate and error floor without computer search.
arxiv-2510-02620:
Klazar encodes Cantor's theorem into a single formula over directed graphs. His 2025 mathematics paper blends set theory with graph language. A digraph counts as Cantor when no set inside surjects onto its power set. That mirrors Cantor's classic theorem inside the graph's own logic. Klazar builds one set theory formula of length four hundred ninety four. A digraph satisfies it exactly when the digraph is Cantor. Abbreviation schemes for formulas make that brevity possible. He also defines extensive and strongly extensive digraphs. The standard argument shows both kinds are Cantor.

A countable strongly extensive digraph can have huge finite in-degrees. Open problems ask how short the magic formula could be. Counting the finite digraphs of each kind is also open. Compressing logic into abbreviations is a craft of its own. The paper shows how much meaning fits in few symbols. Graph theorists and logicians share the playground here.
arxiv-2510-02820:
Bernasconi and co-authors study online learning when inputs arrive in random order. An adversary picks the full list of losses in advance. A random shuffle then sets the order the learner sees. Random data is friendly, while ordered attacks are harsh. Random order looks friendly in the long run. Over short spans, though, it can drift and mislead. Some simple methods built for random data fail badly here.

The team offers a general fix called Simulation. It wraps a method built for random data. The wrapped method keeps nearly the same regret promise in random order. The fix yields sharper bounds for several known problems. Those include learning with delays and bandits with switching costs. The authors also settle a theory question for classification. In random order, the VC dimension sets what can be learned. The harsher Littlestone dimension rules the adversarial world instead.
arxiv-2510-03320:
Dankworth and Schwalbe wrote a short 2025 position paper on attacking the logic of vision networks rather than their final answers. Standard attacks flip an output class, for instance turning a stop sign reading into some other class. The authors argue that richer targets exist. A network should also honor concept rules, such as red and eight sided together meaning a stop sign. Breaking those rules exposes faults that class flips can miss.

The team shows how to state concept rules on trained networks using tools from explainable AI. Their math suggests that searching for broken rules needs a smaller search space than classic attacks. The search gap shrinks further as more concepts are added. Standard class attacks turn out to be a special case of the attack family. If the idea holds in practice, rule based attacks could harden networks faster and guide retraining toward behavior people find sensible.
arxiv-2510-03420:
Hoang and Ehrhardt present a 2025 arXiv paper on numerical methods that keep positive quantities positive during simulation. Many models track things like infected people or chemical levels, where negative values make no sense. Standard solvers can dip below zero unless steps stay tiny. Their method belongs to the nonstandard finite difference family, with a new nonlocal way of sampling the model's right hand side. It promises second order accuracy for systems whose rules change over time.

The authors prove the method keeps solutions positive for any step size, with no extra side conditions. That freedom sets it apart from many earlier methods of the same accuracy class. Tests include an improved scheme for the SIR epidemic model, and the method extends to partial differential equations and boundary value problems. Simple code and low cost add to its appeal. Modelers in epidemics, ecology, and chemistry gain a safer everyday solver.
arxiv-2510-03520:
Pandit and colleagues at the New Jersey Institute of Technology present a 2025 arXiv paper on training language models that are safer. Standard safe training juggles a reward and a cost through a multiplier, which is costly to tune and offers no guarantee. Their method, CS-RLHF, replaces the juggling with a fixed penalty drawn from penalty theory. A cost model trained on a jailbreak corpus scores responses for meaning, not keywords, which grounds the safety signal.

With the penalty scaled, the optimizer itself must land inside the safety limits, the authors argue. Tests showed the method beating models on prompt handling, with at least five times the efficiency against jailbreak prompts in their measure. Responses also grew stable during training. No fixed scheme can promise safety forever, and the authors call for adaptive versions as attacks evolve. Still, certifiable training is a step beyond best effort safety claims.
arxiv-2510-03620:
Peng, Kong, and Lu present a 2025 arXiv paper building a compact source of entangled photons at two different wavelengths and using it for quantum teleportation. Quantum networks must link devices that work at mismatched wavelengths, such as telecom fiber. The Sagnac source uses a periodically poled lithium niobate crystal pumped by a laser. It emits pairs at 810 and 1550 nanometers, entangled in polarization. A periscope rotates the polarizations, keeping the interferometer small and stable.

The pairs came out bright, at thirty thousand pairs per second per milliwatt of pump power. Entanglement fidelity reached about ninety eight and a half percent, and a Bell inequality test scored well above the classical limit. The team teleported photon states from the near infrared wavelength to the telecom one. That transfer kept a fidelity of about ninety five and a half percent. Wavelength bridging sources like this are hardware for joining quantum devices into networks.
arxiv-2510-03820:
Fabiano presents this 2025 arXiv paper extending a recent fixed point theorem from metric spaces to the wider world of b-metric spaces. Path-averaged contractions generalize Banach contractions by measuring shrinkage through the average distance along a mapping's orbits. A unique fixed point was known in complete metric spaces. B-metric spaces loosen the triangle inequality by a multiplicative constant, covering more distance-like functions used in applications.

Fabiano proves every continuous path-averaged contraction on a complete b-metric space has a unique fixed point, provided the contraction constant times the b-metric coefficient stays below one. The argument runs on geometric decay of successive distances plus the generalized triangle inequality. Every Banach contraction is a path-averaged contraction, but not conversely, so the generalization is strict. Path-averaged and Kannan contractions, by contrast, are incomparable in general.
arxiv-2510-04020:
Wu and a large team present this 2025 arXiv paper recasting weather-like forecasting as a planning problem. Physical forecasts struggle with rare extremes, scarce data, and quality metrics that cannot be optimized directly. Ordinary deep learning trains on smooth error losses, ignoring the domain scores that scientists actually care about. The authors borrow the machinery of model-based reinforcement learning to close that gap.

Their framework, SFP, first learns a generative world model that can imagine many plausible futures. Beam search planning explores inside the world model, scoring candidates with the true domain metrics as rewards. The best imagined futures become training labels that improve the forecaster in a self-training loop. Experiments cut prediction error sharply on several benchmarks, by up to about two-fifths in mean squared error. The method also captured extreme events and physical consistency better than baselines.
arxiv-2510-04120:
Ye and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper probing how language models understand metaphors, and where that understanding breaks. Metaphor maps one domain onto another, as when falling describes love rather than motion. Models ace many language tasks, but their grip on mapping is poorly understood. The authors attack the question from concept mapping, internal knowledge, and syntax.

Embedding projections showed models producing conceptually irrelevant interpretations in a sizable minority of cases, roughly fifteen to twenty-five percent. Tests suggested models lean on memorized links between metaphorical words and literal counterparts. Shuffling syntax revealed stronger sensitivity to surface than to structural meaning. Together the results depict fluent but shallow metaphor handling driven by training-data indicators. The authors call for methods that align concepts, use context properly, and integrate syntax. These gaps matter wherever figurative language carries real content, from literature to everyday instruction.
arxiv-2510-04520:
Hanyu Wang and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on turning math statements into formal ones a computer can check. Formal libraries like Lean Mathlib grow slowly because translation is slow and expert work. Language models can draft translations, but they hallucinate terms and miss meanings. The team built Aria, an agent that formalizes at the level of conjectures. It mimics how an expert breaks a hard statement down.

Aria first splits a statement into a dependency graph of smaller claims. It then builds the formal text from grounded pieces, starting from the leaves. A checker named AriaScorer fetches definitions from Mathlib to anchor each term. On ProofNet, the system reached about 92 percent compilation success and about 69 percent final accuracy. On a hard algebra suite drawn from research papers, it scored 44 percent against 24 percent for the best rival. On homological conjectures, it reached about 43 percent while all rivals scored zero.
arxiv-2510-04920:
Yury Zabegaev, Inga Berre, and Eirik Keilegavlen tackle a slow step in underground simulations in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their simulations model flow and heat in porous rock for industry-scale problems. Each run must solve huge linear systems again and again. Picking the fastest solver settings by hand is slow, expert work.

Their algorithm picks solver settings on its own while the simulation runs. A classifier first throws out settings that are likely to fail. A second model then predicts run times for the survivors. Feedback from each solved system keeps retraining both models. In tests on flow-heat and fractured-rock problems, picks landed within the best 3 percent of all options. The method matched a reference policy that had seen all past data.
arxiv-2510-05020:
Nada Alghamdi, Paolo de Angelis, Pietro Asinari, and Eliodoro Chiavazzo test an AI force field for battery research in this 2025 arXiv paper. The material is lithium fluoride, a key part of the protective layer inside lithium-ion batteries. How fast lithium ions diffuse through it affects battery life and safety. Simulating that motion needs an accurate atomic force model.

The team benchmarks the MACE foundation model against a well-trained DeePMD potential. Untuned, MACE already matched DeePMD on the main diffusion properties. Its activation energy estimate of 0.22 electron volts sat close to the reference value of 0.24 in their runs. Fine-tuning with only 300 data points nudged the estimate to 0.20 electron volts. DeePMD, by contrast, had needed more than 40,000 training points.
arxiv-2510-05120:
Farjana Yesmin and Nusrat Shirmin build machine learning that explains itself in plain words in this 2025 arXiv paper. Big data models often act as black boxes, which regulators and users distrust. Post-hoc explanation tools like LIME and SHAP patch the problem from outside. Their explanations can cost accuracy and still miss the model's real logic.

The proposed framework combines type-2 fuzzy sets, granular computing, and clustering. Fuzzy rules come out in linguistic form that people can read directly. On the UCI Air Quality dataset, type-2 clustering improved cohesion by about 4 percent over type-1 methods. Fairness entropy improved as well, and the rules covered most cases. Runtime scaled linearly, keeping the approach practical for large, noisy sensor data.
arxiv-2510-05220:
Jack Higginson and ten co-authors hunt fingerprints of the first stars around young galaxies in this 2025 arXiv paper. The EIGER survey uses six bright quasars as background lights. Gas along those sightlines absorbs light when neutral oxygen is present. The team catalogued 40 galaxies near the sightlines at redshift about six.

Five oxygen absorption systems matched five galaxy overdensities within 300 kiloparsecs. The absorbing gas sits beyond typical galaxy halos, tracing the wider overdense environment instead. Its oxygen mass rivals the oxygen inside the galaxies themselves. Abundance patterns in four of the five systems match enrichment by Population III stars, the first generation ever formed. These rare systems open a direct window on how first stars seeded the cosmos with metals.
arxiv-2510-05720:
Esentepe weighs two ideals that measure singular points of a local ring. The cohomology annihilator collects members killing all high Ext modules. A second ideal kills the stable class of maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules. Kimura showed the two agree up to roots; Esentepe seeks a full match.

The paper gives a test that is enough for the ideals to coincide exactly. It then applies the test to rings of dimension one that are almost Gorenstein. For unramified complete local rings of that class, the cohomology annihilator equals the conductor. The conductor is concrete and can be worked out from the ring's integral closure. Such matches turn abstract annihilators into usable tests for singular points. Slopes of the defining equations supply standard annihilator members. The zero set of the ideal already traces the singular locus broadly. Rings of dimension one are the natural first case for exact claims.
arxiv-2510-06620:
Shijie Qin examines turbulence through the equations that govern fluid motion. His 2025 paper uses two-dimensional turbulent flow as a test case. He asks a deep question about chaos in the Navier-Stokes equations. Ordinary chaos means a tiny change alters a system's path. Qin studies a stronger form, called ultra-chaos, where even the statistics shift.

To rule out numerical noise as a false cause, he uses a clean simulation method. That method keeps errors so small that they cannot explain the results. He finds that a tiny change in the starting flow leads to huge differences later. The flow's symmetry and its long-run statistics both change. That means small disturbances matter even at the level of averages. The finding helps explain why turbulence is so hard to predict. It also raises a logical puzzle, since real models must ignore some small disturbances.
arxiv-2510-07220:
Wagner and colleagues use a cosmic lens to probe the jet of a blazar, a galaxy firing a beam toward Earth. Their 2025 paper studies PKS 1830-211, whose light a foreground galaxy splits into two images. The team gathered X-ray and gamma-ray data from three space telescopes. They compared a quiet period in 2016 with a flaring one in 2019. A sharpened timing method extracted the lens delay from the gamma-ray record.

The delay came out near twenty-one days, and it stayed fixed across epochs. The brightness ratio between the images also held steady. X-ray output barely changed between the two periods. Gamma rays, in contrast, swung wildly. The combined spectrum fits a model where electrons radiate directly and also bounce infrared light to gamma energies. Stable lens numbers help separate source behavior from lens effects in future studies.
arxiv-2510-07420:
Cavey, Gorsky, Oblomkov, and Turner compute convex bodies that encode the sections of line bundles on nested Hilbert schemes. Their 2025 paper works in algebraic geometry. A Hilbert scheme parametrizes clusters of points on the plane, and nested versions track clusters inside clusters. Line bundles on these spaces carry spaces of sections with rich structure. Earlier work by Haiman described those sections through special ideals in many variables. The authors analyze trailing terms under a monomial order to extract explicit bases for the section spaces from that description.

From those bases, the Newton-Okounkov bodies follow. These convex bodies summarize a bundle's sections the way a shadow summarizes a shape. Computing them turns asymptotic questions about sections into geometry that can be drawn and measured. The nested setting is substantially harder than the classical one, since two point counts interact.
arxiv-2510-07620:
Usman and Lee present DGTEN in this 2025 computer science paper on trust in changing networks. Online systems must judge which users and nodes deserve trust. Those judgments shift over time, and attackers work to distort them. DGTEN is a graph neural network built to score trust while stating its own uncertainty. It also aims to resist attacks such as reputation laundering and sabotage.

The network treats nodes and edges as probability distributions rather than fixed values. It tracks abrupt shifts and smooth trends in trust over time. A defense step down-weights suspicious interactions before they sway the scores. On two signed Bitcoin trust networks, DGTEN beat the best rival method by clear margins. Its gains were largest in cold-start cases, where little history exists for new users. Trust scores guide decisions in finance, social platforms, and device networks.
arxiv-2510-07720:
Liu, Wang, Cui, and Ye wrote this 2025 information retrieval paper on video search. A short text query rarely captures everything a video contains. Systems that match queries to metadata word by word miss that richness. The authors argue that queries should not stand alone. Related queries carry extra shades of meaning that can widen the match. Their framework builds that idea into the search process.

The framework, called Video-Text Cluster, groups related queries into clusters before matching. A Sweeper module then cleans noise out of each cluster. An attention mechanism weighs the cluster's text features against the actual video frames. That keeps retrieval focused on what the video really shows. Across five public datasets, the model beat existing state-of-the-art systems. The results suggest that borrowing meaning from neighboring queries is a cheap way to sharpen video search without new annotations.
arxiv-2510-07820:
Beckey and four coauthors wrote this 2025 quantum information paper on testing whether a quantum state is a product state. A product state has no entanglement across a split. Testers can measure one copy at a time or many copies jointly. The authors ask how many samples each strategy needs. They study two variants: finding any clean split, and checking that every split is clean.

For the first variant, they prove an exponential lower bound for all single-copy algorithms. Joint multi-copy methods are efficient there, so the gap is exponential. That hardness spreads to related entanglement learning tasks. For the second variant, they prove another lower bound separating the strategies. They also give a single-copy local algorithm for the multipartite task that is optimal for two parties. A technical lemma about overlaps of permutation operators drives the proofs.
arxiv-2510-07920:
Li and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a profit mirage in AI trading agents. Language-model traders post dazzling back-tested returns. Once trading moves past the model's training window, those returns collapse. The cause is information leakage baked into the model itself. It has quietly memorized the future it is supposedly predicting. The authors measure that leakage across four dimensions and build tools to fight it.

They release FinLake-Bench, an evaluation suite designed to resist leakage. Their FactFin framework then attacks the cause. Counterfactual perturbations force the agent to learn what drives prices instead of memorizing outcomes. A strategy generator, retrieval, tree search, and a counterfactual simulator form the pipeline. In out-of-sample tests, FactFin beat every baseline on risk-adjusted performance. The authors argue that honest evaluation must assume leakage until proven otherwise. Their work resets expectations for what AI traders really earn.
arxiv-2510-08020:
Duer-Milner and four coauthors wrote this 2025 planetary science paper seeking one mechanism behind the equatorial jets of all four giant planets. Jupiter and Saturn blow strong eastward jets at their equators. Uranus and Neptune blow strong westward ones. Earlier theories explained the two directions with different mechanisms. The shared planetary parameters made that split unsatisfying. The authors instead test convection-driven columnar structures as a single cause.

Their analysis shows the two jet patterns emerge as two stable branches of one solution, a bifurcation. Eastward superrotation and westward subrotation are both stable outcomes of the same dynamics. The branches even share equatorial wave properties and the same leading momentum balance. One mechanism thus covers gas giants and ice giants alike. The result suggests jet formation follows broader rules than planet-by-planet theories assumed. It also gives modelers a unified target when simulating giant planet weather.
arxiv-2510-08120:
Gajcin and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper extracting readable global policies from language models used as judges of other models' text. Judge models scale evaluation, but their hidden criteria may encode bias. One algorithm generates contrastive, concept-based explanations for individual decisions and verifies each. A second clusters, summarizes, and verifies those local rules into a global policy. The team tested the pipeline on seven harm detection benchmarks.

The extracted policies proved highly faithful to the judge's actual decisions. They also survived robustness checks against perturbations and adversarial attacks. A user study found users understood the judge's policy somewhat better, and perceived usefulness improved significantly. Explanation quality remains limited by the pipeline's own components. Still, the work shows a judge's implicit rules can be surfaced, checked, and debated, which is essential wherever automated judges gatekeep content.
arxiv-2510-08220:
Huang, Fang, Chen, and Wu wrote this 2025 semiconductor physics paper on how electrons move through silicon at cryogenic temperatures, where quantum computer wiring must operate. Using multi-valley Monte Carlo simulations of silicon in the (110) orientation, they found the transport rules change fundamentally when cold. Phonon scattering fades to negligible. Mobility is instead set by a competition: remote Coulomb scattering dominates at low carrier densities, while surface roughness scattering dominates at high densities.

That competition produces a distinct peak in electron mobility at intermediate density. The authors also expose a trade-off with high-permittivity gate oxides such as hafnium oxide. They improve gate control but introduce strong remote phonon scattering that can suppress mobility. Cryogenic transistors run quantum processors' control electronics, so mobility sets real performance limits. The guidance is concrete: choose dielectric and density together, and aim for the mobility peak.
arxiv-2510-08320:
Patryk Lipka-Bartosik and co-authors probe what a reusable quantum helper adds to local operations, in a 2025 arXiv paper. In entanglement theory, two distant parties can transform shared quantum states using local operations and classical messages. Adding a catalyst, a system that helps but stays unchanged, greatly widens what they can do. The open question is how much of that gain comes from the messages alone.

The authors define catalytic local operations, which use a catalyst but no classical communication channel. They compare this class with standard local operations plus classical communication. They also compare it with stochastic versions aided by bounded quantum communication. The classes turn out to be incomparable: each allows transformations the other cannot reach. This shows catalysis and communication are distinct resources, not substitutes for one another.
arxiv-2510-08420:
Rémy Cerda and Alexis Saurin prove a compression property for infinite rewriting systems in a 2025 arXiv paper in logic. Infinitary rewriting handles possibly infinite terms and reduction sequences, modeling programs that run productively forever. Compression says any reduction sequence, however long in ordinal terms, can be shortened. An equivalent sequence of length at most omega, the first infinite ordinal, should always exist.

The authors extend the coinductive presentation of these systems to arbitrary non-wellfounded derivations. They design a generic compression proof that factors out the shared core of earlier arguments. The proof isolates the key property a system must enjoy for compression to hold. Running examples cover first-order rewriting and infinitary lambda calculi, where compression justifies known presentations. A harder application treats cut-elimination in a proof system for linear logic that allows non-wellfounded derivations with fixed points.
arxiv-2510-08520:
Sriram Akella shows that a celebrated toy model of holography fails a three-way entanglement test in a 2025 arXiv paper. Holographic states obey entropy inequalities derived from the Ryu-Takayanagi formula of gravity. Those classic inequalities only involve bipartite entanglement between two regions. A newer GHZ-forbidding inequality uses reflected entropy and tripartite multi-entropy to probe three-way structure.

Akella proves this inequality is either violated or exactly saturated, never strictly satisfied, by stabilizer states. Stabilizer states are a large, tractable class that includes many quantum error-correcting codes. The result therefore shows stabilizer states are not holographic in this stricter sense. As a consequence, tripartite entanglement in the HaPPY code is not holographic. HaPPY is a famous pentagon code often used as a holography toy model. The finding limits how far such toy models mirror real holography.
arxiv-2510-09520:
Ali Javadi-Abhari, Simon Martiel, Alireza Seif, Maika Takita, and Ken Wei report a record in quantum computing in a 2025 arXiv paper. Entanglement links particles so their states must be described together, and faithfully entangling many qubits is a standard benchmark of hardware quality. The test state is the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, also called a cat state, which is easy to verify but very sensitive to noise.

The team prepared the largest such state to date, spanning 120 superconducting qubits. They combined optimised circuit compilation, error detection with low overhead, and temporary uncomputation, with an automated compiler that maximised error detection under each chip's connectivity and error rates. The measured fidelity was about zero point five six, with a post-selection rate of twenty-eight percent. Several certification methods agreed, and the authors discuss the practical trade-offs among them.
arxiv-2510-09820:
Eleonora Parlanti, Giulia Tozzi, and a large team of co-authors dissect a spiral galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young in a 2025 arXiv paper. The galaxy, known as K20-ID7, sits at redshift about two point two, in the cosmic noon era of peak galaxy assembly. It is a large, star-forming spiral with hints of gas flowing inward.

Combining Webb spectroscopy and imaging with a ground-based instrument, the team resolves the galaxy's stars and gas. They find massive star-forming clumps with low dust obscuration and gas density. The central bulge is modest in mass but heavily dust-obscured, and it likely formed most of its stars in the past while still forming some today. The gas shows near-solar metallicity with enhanced nitrogen relative to oxygen.
arxiv-2510-09920:
Gibson and a large team report a TESS discovery around the star RZ Psc in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. TESS, a space telescope that watches starlight for dips, found transiting exocomets, comets passing in front of the star. The system is only the second known with enough events to measure the size distribution of its comets.

RZ Psc hosts an extreme debris disk, a dense ring of rubble left from planet formation. Counting comets by size lets the team compare this system with Beta Pictoris, the first such system, and with the Solar System. Those comparisons test whether comet populations form in similar ways around other stars. The many detected transits make that size census possible.
arxiv-2510-10020:
Smith, Nathaniel L. Diamant, and Brian L. Trippe frame calibration of generative models as optimization in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning. Generative models are often miscalibrated: class probabilities and other statistics of their samples drift away from the values users want. Fixing the drift without wrecking the model is the problem.

The authors pose calibration as a constrained optimization problem. They seek the closest model, measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence, that satisfies the calibration constraints. Closeness matters because a heavy-handed fix could distort everything else the model does well. The framework turns calibration from ad hoc patching into a principled adjustment, with the trade-off between accuracy and fidelity stated in the objective itself.
arxiv-2510-10220:
Keskin, Mehmet Yaşar, and K. Kurt study constant-roll inflation in a modified gravity theory in this 2025 arXiv paper in cosmology. Inflation is the rapid early expansion of the universe. The authors work in f(R, phi, X) gravity, where the gravitational action depends on curvature, a scalar field, and its kinetic energy.

Under a constant-roll condition, which fixes how fast the field's velocity changes, they use a generalized potential raised to a power. They derive formulas for the spectral index, which describes the pattern of primordial fluctuations, and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, which compares gravitational waves to density waves. The dynamics turn out to be governed mainly by the power parameter and the potential's shape, a testable simplification.
arxiv-2510-11120:
When two lead nuclei pass very close without touching, the intense light from one can strike the other and create particles. Vendulka Humlová reports new ALICE Collaboration measurements of one such process in this 2025 arXiv paper. The team studied incoherent production of J/psi mesons, bound states of a charm quark and an antiquark, in lead-lead collisions, a channel sensitive to how gluons fluctuate inside nuclei.

The collisions ran at a nucleon-nucleon energy of 5.02 TeV, and the analysis sorts events by photon-nucleus energy and by momentum transfer, which reflects the size scale being probed. At small momentum transfer, the production rate rises as the photon energy grows. At larger momentum transfer, that growth is suppressed compared with the trend at low transfer. The authors note that this is the first study of incoherent photoproduction at the LHC mapped against both variables together.
arxiv-2510-11220:
Rayleigh-Bénard convection, fluid heated from below and cooled from above, is a classic test case for turbulence simulation. Shijie Qin, Kun Xu, and Shijun Liao simulate its two-dimensional form in this 2025 arXiv fluid dynamics paper. They solve the Navier-Stokes equations by direct numerical simulation in double precision, varying only the time-step size used by the solver.

They find two kinds of final flow, one vortical and one zonal, with completely different statistics. As the time-step shrinks to very small values, the two flow types alternate frequently, suggesting each type's time-steps are densely distributed. Because time-step size is tied to numerical noise, the result means stochastic numerical noise hugely influences the final flow and its statistics. That clashes with the Navier-Stokes model's own assumption that small disturbances are negligible, a logic paradox the authors say needs more investigation.
arxiv-2510-11420:
Programs for quantum computers mix quantum operations with ordinary classical logic, including decisions made mid-computation from fresh measurements, and compilers need a representation that captures both. Mark Koch and a large team introduce HUGR in this 2025 arXiv quantum computing paper. HUGR, the Hierarchical Unified Graph Representation, is an intermediate representation designed for mixed quantum-classical programs and the tooling that compiles them.

The design stresses expressivity and extensibility, aiming to cover near-term and future quantum devices and new programming abstractions as they appear. Its graph structure is machine-friendly and supports pattern-matching compilation techniques, while an MLIR-inspired design lets tools reason at several levels of abstraction and lower smoothly between them. Safety is built in through strict static typing and linear quantum types, so compilation tools can be built quickly without fear of breaking programs. A full specification and a reference implementation are open-source.
arxiv-2510-11520:
Outdoor navigation remains risky for people who are blind or have low vision, and AI assistants trained on ordinary image datasets rarely learn the hazards and landmarks that matter to them. Kedi Ying and co-authors build a dataset aimed at that gap in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Their mmWalk dataset is simulated and combines multi-view sensing with accessibility-oriented features for safe outdoor walking.

The dataset holds 120 manually controlled walking trajectories in scenarios, with 62,000 synchronized frames and over 559,000 panoramic images across color, depth, and semantic channels, including corner cases and accessibility landmarks. A companion benchmark, mmWalkVQA, adds over 69,000 visual question-answer triplets in nine categories for safe walking assistance. State-of-the-art vision-language models, tested zero-shot and few-shot, struggled with its risk assessment and navigation tasks. A model fine-tuned on mmWalk, validated on real-world datasets, performed effectively, showing the dataset's value.
arxiv-2510-11620:
Long chains of thought make models smarter and more fragile: one bad planning step derails everything after it. Siheng Xiong, Ali Payani, and Faramarz Fekri dissect where the derailments start in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Analyzing raw traces, they trace most errors to planning steps, not the execution that follows.

Their framework, Multi-Path Plan Aggregation, interrupts single-pass reasoning at intervals to generate several candidate plans and aggregate them into a refined plan, via a lightweight LoRA module. For training, they introduce online Step-DPO, a process-level preference method using twisted sequential Monte Carlo to supply step-by-step supervision. Across math, science, and logic benchmarks, the method beat both a DeepSeek-R1 distillation baseline and outcome-reward reinforcement learning. It used only ten percent of the supervised data and five percent of the preference pairs.
arxiv-2510-11820:
Anna R. Barth and nine co-authors show how sound can steer the thickness of dense slurries. Many suspensions, mixes of particles in liquid, thicken suddenly when sheared, a headache for mixing and pumping. Gentle acoustic vibration can soften that thickening in real time. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives the first measured account of the effect, which smart-material designers need for full control.

The team probed suspensions under acoustic perturbation and folded the results into a universal scaling picture. In that picture, viscosity follows one master function that crosses between two critical points: frictionless jamming and frictional shear jamming. The sound's effect can be captured as an effective repulsion pushing particles apart. Its strength comes out roughly equal to the acoustic energy density in the liquid. With that rule, the framework predicts a suspension's viscosity under new sound settings without fresh measurements. The authors show such predictions directly.
arxiv-2510-11920:
Omkar Dhungel and seven co-authors show a gentle way to probe superconductors with diamond dust. Nitrogen-vacancy centers are atomic defects in diamond whose fluorescence reports the local magnetic field. Sprinkling nanodiamonds on a superconductor lets teams sense its magnetism by light, with no microwaves and almost no disturbance. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests the approach on thin films of YBCO, a famous high-temperature superconductor.

Working at very low fields, with wiggles of about one millitesla, the team watched the Meissner effect, the superconductor's expulsion of magnetic field, through cross-relaxation field sensing. From the glow's changes they extracted two key numbers: the transition temperature where superconductivity switches on, and the penetration field where magnetism first breaks in. The method tolerates rough surfaces, which many sensing techniques cannot. It suits studies of flux vortices in samples with complex shapes.
arxiv-2510-12020:
Ivan R. Vasquez and A. Oliveros stress-test a modified theory of gravity against the universe's whole biography. In f(Q) gravity, Einstein's theory is rebuilt around nonmetricity, the failure of rulers to keep length under transport. Their 2025 arXiv paper chooses an exponential form for the modification and studies it with dynamical systems methods, which reduce the cosmic equations to an autonomous flow with equilibrium points.

Because the exponential spawns transcendental equations, the critical points are located by careful approximation and then tested for stability in terms of the model parameters. The model passes the basic historical audition: it exhibits the three main domination epochs, radiation, matter, and dark energy. The authors then switch on a linear interaction between dark matter and dark energy. The coupling shifts the equilibrium structure and leaves a nontrivial mark on the late-time de Sitter attractor, the universe's final resting state.
arxiv-2510-12220:
Bai and co-authors introduce Hierarchical Koopman Diffusion, a framework for fast image generation with a readable process, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models produce high quality images but sample slowly because they denoise step by step. One step methods are fast yet hide the intermediate stages that make diffusion editable and controllable.

The method rests on Koopman operator theory, which lifts nonlinear dynamics into a space where they evolve linearly. In that lifted space the diffusion trajectory has a closed form solution, so sampling takes one step while intermediate states stay open to manual changes. A layered design splits the dynamics across spatial resolutions, with separate Koopman subspaces handling coarse and fine detail. Experiments show competitive one step generation quality. Studying the operators' spectra also gives a principled way to read and steer the generative process.
arxiv-2510-12620:
Mayer and a large team simulate the birth of a star with radiation and magnetic fields in a moving mesh code, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. In the run, a jet launches itself. They implemented radiative transfer with flux limited diffusion in the AREPO code. Splitting the radiation terms into explicit and implicit parts keeps the timestep practical. The scheme passed standard tests for radiation diffusion, gas coupling, and radiative shocks, and works with local timestepping.

As a demonstration they collapse a one solar mass molecular cloud core down to the second Larson core, the embryonic star. A fast jet erupts self consistently from the second core, nested inside a slower magnetic outflow from the first core. Magnetic fields amplify enormously in the second core, which is ringed by a small disk. They present the run as proof their method handles the multiscale, high resolution physics of protostar formation.
arxiv-2510-13220:
He and colleagues make AI agents improve themselves at test time in this 2025 arXiv paper. Agents typically cannot learn complex skills on the fly, behaving like clever but clueless interns in new environments. To measure that gap, the authors introduce a benchmark where an agent plays the same text adventure game across consecutive episodes. The agent must improve between attempts. In this setup, reflection, memory, and reinforcement learning baselines all struggle.

Their framework, EvoTest, evolves the entire agentic system after every episode without any fine-tuning or gradients. An actor agent plays, while an evolver agent studies the episode transcript and rewrites the configuration. It revises the prompt, logs effective state-action choices into memory, tunes hyperparameters, and learns tool-use routines. EvoTest consistently raised performance, beating reflection and memory baselines and even online fine-tuning methods, and it was the only approach to win any of the games outright.
arxiv-2510-13920:
Ye Yuan, Mohammad Amin Shabani, and Siqi Liu tackle query-focused table summarization, where a system must describe spreadsheet-like data in plain sentences that answer a user question. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that older table-to-text models need costly retraining, while prompting large language models with whole tables wastes tokens and exposes private data.

They propose FACTS, an agentic workflow that builds reusable templates offline, before any question arrives. Each template pairs an executable SQL query, which pulls the needed numbers, with a text template that turns results into a summary. Because templates serve many tables with the same layout, summarization stays fast, and only table schemas go to the language model, protecting the data itself. On standard benchmarks, FACTS consistently beat the baseline methods tested.
arxiv-2510-14020:
Rohan Shenoy offers an elementary proof of the discrete renewal theorem, a classic result about processes that restart after random waiting times, in this 2025 arXiv note. Renewal processes model anything from machine repairs to arrivals separated by gaps, and the theorem describes the long-run rate at which events occur when the gaps between them are bounded.

Shenoy deliberately avoids the standard heavy machinery: no Markov chain theory, no complex analysis, and no generating functions, only elementary real analysis. He introduces the one-dimensional discrete renewal process through a board game example, making the setup concrete before proving the theorem in the common special case where interevent times are bounded. The note also supplies background and history on the Erdős-Feller-Pollard theorem, the celebrated earlier result in the same line. Readers see where the discrete renewal theorem sits in the development of probability theory.
arxiv-2510-14220:
Dibert and a large collaboration describe how they calibrated the SPT-SLIM mapping instrument against the sky during its first deployment on the South Pole Telescope, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Before its measurements of faint spectral lines can be trusted, the detectors' responsivity, how strongly they answer to sky brightness, must be pinned down under observing conditions.

During two weeks of on-sky operation in the 2024-2025 austral summer, the team measured detector response as the telescope changed elevation, which changes the atmospheric load. They combined those data with atmospheric opacity readings from a site radiometer, simulated South Pole atmospheric spectra, and laboratory-measured detector responses. From these they modeled each detector's responsivity to sky loading. They used the model to calibrate observations of the Moon and cross-checked the result against the Moon's brightness temperature as it varies with phase, validating the calibration chain end to end.
arxiv-2510-14520:
Tenyo Takahashi settles an open problem in modal logic by showing that a property of logics can be decided algorithmically, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modal logics extend logic with operators for necessity and possibility, and most questions about them, beyond consistency and exceptions, are undecidable: no algorithm can answer them in general.

The property at stake is being a union-splitting in the lattice of all normal modal logics, a notion about how a logic sits among its extensions. Takahashi provides a semantic characterization of union-splittings in terms of finite modal algebras. This converts an infinitary question into a finite check and thereby proves decidability. It answers a problem posed in 2007. Clarifying the connection further, the paper shows that in this lattice, having a decidable axiomatization problem and being a decidable formula are themselves decidable properties. This resolves another long-standing question from 1997 for this setting.
arxiv-2510-14720:
Moretti, Loreau, and Benzaquen model, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the global race between rising food demand and the forests and soils that farming consumes. A larger, wealthier population wants more food, especially meat. Meeting that demand expands and intensifies agriculture, which drives deforestation and degrades ecosystems. The damage then feeds back on yields, raising future land needs.

Their spatially explicit model links demand paths to crop and livestock production and land conversion, and it reproduces the joint trends seen since 1960. Comparing scenarios yields three lessons. Supply-side fixes alone, such as organic conversion or lower livestock density, often backfire: they trigger compensatory land expansion that erases the ecological gains. Demand-side change, especially eating less meat, relieves both expansion and intensification pressure consistently. Only substantial demand cuts, around forty percent of the projected excess by 2100, increased forest area and reduced degradation at the same time.
arxiv-2510-15320:
Yunlu Wang, Yunlong Xiao, Pengcheng Hong, and Ronggang Ping set up a future test of fundamental symmetries in the decays of a charmed baryon. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies parity and charge-parity symmetries, whose breaking helps explain why the universe holds more matter than antimatter. The focus is the three-body decay of the Xi_c baryon into a Xi baryon plus two pions.

Working with the helicity formalism, which tracks particle spins through the decay, the team derives the complete angular distribution formula for the decay and its secondary steps. They fold in the effects of polarized electron and positron beams, since the planned Super Tau-Charm Facility would collide such beams. The paper then evaluates how sensitively the asymmetry decay parameters could be measured under different data volumes and beam polarization choices. The authors present the results as a theoretical framework to guide that future experiment's symmetry program.
arxiv-2510-15620:
On-device assistants rank texts with cross-encoders, but scoring every candidate fully is slow and memory-hungry. Jiahao Zhou and colleagues from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Huawei address this in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their insight is that only relative order matters for top-K selection, not exact scores for each candidate. Rankings also settle early, in middle layers, which opens the door to pruning candidates sooner. Their system Grating prunes clusters of candidates progressively while bounding memory through sliding windows.

On rerankers up to eight billion parameters, Grating cuts latency by up to eighty-nine percent. Peak memory falls by up to ninety-five percent in microbenchmarks, with no precision loss. Three real on-device applications show smaller but still clear gains.
arxiv-2510-15720:
Reinforcement learning agents can act unsafely while learning, which blocks real-world deployment. Edwin Hamel-De le Court, Gaspard Ohlmann, and Francesco Belardinelli propose a safety method in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their algorithm, ProSh, adds a risk budget to the state of a cost-constrained learning problem. A learned cost critic estimates danger, and a shield filters the agent's action distribution. The shield keeps every sampled action safe in expectation, without needing a model of the environment.

The authors prove an upper bound on expected cost that holds throughout training. The bound depends only on the backup critic's accuracy. Under mild assumptions, experiments confirm safety even during the training phase itself.
arxiv-2511-00220:
Pouya Ghari, Simone Sciabola, and Ye Wang address a common flaw in tuning large pre-trained models: one reward score rarely captures all that matters. A text model may need to be clear, safe, and on topic at once. A drug model faces a similar mix of goals. Tuning on one score alone can distort the rest.

Their method cycles through several rewards in turn, fine-tuning the model on each one in repeated rounds. The approach extends leading reinforcement learning methods, and the team backs it with theory. Tests on text, biological sequences, and small molecules beat strong baselines, which suggests the cycling helps balance competing goals.
arxiv-2511-00320:
M G Masteghin and six co-authors map the full damage left by focused ion beams, fine tools used to cut and build at the nanoscale. Most checks measure only the beam's bright core, where most ions land. The faint tail matters for precise jobs like placing impurities in a chip, yet it is usually missed. The team uses an advanced electron microscopy method that records diffraction at every scan point.

By comparing patterns from known exposures with spots dosed by a gallium beam, they detect damage at extremely low levels. A noise-based score proved more sensitive and robust than standard dark-field imaging. The fuller profile helps users judge beam performance beyond simple sharpness and tailor settings for delicate work.
arxiv-2511-00520:
Hòa Bùi and Alberto De Marchi speed up cutting plane methods, a classic way to solve nonlinear discrete optimization without relaxing whole-number decisions into fractions. The methods are powerful in theory but erratic in practice. Recent work showed that building cuts at projections of infeasible points onto the feasible set helps greatly, and the authors ask whether cuts at feasible points near the optimum help even more.

Their hybrid pairs the global guarantees of cutting planes with the local search of projected gradient methods, which scout promising regions and supply tighter cuts. The focus is binary problems with convex, differentiable goals, where projections reduce to mixed-integer linear programs. Experiments across solver setups confirm better solutions found faster. The framework extends naturally to wider discrete domains.
arxiv-2511-00620:
Autumn Toney-Wails and Ryan Wails test whether a language model's confidence means what probability says it should. Certainty is often read from token logits, with probabilities and entropy standing in for trust. In gambling-like scenarios with known odds, though, a well-behaved model's token probabilities should track the theoretical distribution of outcomes, a stricter demand than mere accuracy.

The authors probe GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-Chat with ten probability prompts, such as rolling a six-sided die, with and without fairness cues. Both models answered every scenario validly and perfectly. Yet their token-level probabilities and entropy values consistently diverged from the theoretical distributions. Certainty signals, the study warns, should not be confused with calibrated probability in high-stakes decision support.
arxiv-2511-01020:
Ana Bokulic and Filip Pozar construct the first noncommutative corrections to a broad class of theories where electromagnetism is nonlinear. Noncommutative geometry deforms spacetime so that positions fail to commute, and the deformation here is applied through a Drinfeld twist, with the effects passed into the matter sector by the Seiberg-Witten map.

Two sources of nonlinearity now interact: the one already present in nonlinear electrodynamics, and the one from the noncommutative deformation. Starting from a static, symmetric dyonic black hole with spherical shape, carrying both electric and magnetic charge, they solve the equations of motion order by order in the deformation parameter. Corrections to the metric and the gauge potential are then computed for several leading nonlinear theories.
arxiv-2511-01120: Carla Mariana da Silva Pinheiro studies multiplicative statistics in a unitary random matrix ensemble whose probability measure carries a deformation controlled by a parameter. Earlier work on such deformations handled a bounded or decaying parameter. This paper extends the results to a growing parameter, kept under a controlled rate. It derives the asymptotic expansion of the statistics. It also shows that the underlying statistics relate to the study of the lower tail of the KPZ equation, a central model of random growth.
arxiv-2511-01220:
David Sommers and colleagues introduce SQDMetal, an open source workflow to model the electromagnetic behavior of superconducting quantum circuits. Such tools matter greatly when designing quantum devices, but the standard tools are mostly commercial, and open parallel alternatives have been scarce.

SQDMetal is a Python interface that links Qiskit Metal for design, Gmsh for meshing, Palace for large parallel runs, and ParaView to view the results. Mesh studies show strong agreement with two leading paid packages on eigenmode and capacitance numbers. Models of resonators and transmon qubits match experiments well. Extras include getting Hamiltonians by the energy participation ratio method, kinetic inductance effects, and full 3D device geometry.
arxiv-2511-01420:
Christoph Lenzen tackles gradient clock synchronization, the problem of keeping neighboring clocks in a large network close to each other even when no two clocks in the network agree exactly. Earlier theory gave tight bounds, but those bounds rest on pessimistic assumptions: worst-case measurement errors guaranteed for the whole life of the system, and oscillators always drifting at their worst rate.

Lenzen builds a gentler model that asks only that measurement and frequency errors stay stable over short periods. In that model he re-analyzes existing methods and beats the established lower bound on local skew, sometimes dramatically. He also shows how to keep the schemes self-stabilizing and how to extend them to synchronization against an external time reference.
arxiv-2511-01720:
Mahammad Nuriyev built a team of artificial specialists to animate non-player characters in interactive worlds. A game character must chat naturally, stay in persona, and also act on the world through tools, three jobs that strain a single model. His system splits them among three experts, all adapted from the Qwen3 language model with low-rank adapters.

One expert handles tool calling, a second interprets tool responses, and a third carries on direct dialogue, with a commonsense, persona-grounded setup deciding which speaks. The system ran fast with modest resource use on L40S graphics cards, comfortably meeting efficiency requirements. Entered in the Commonsense Persona-Grounded Dialogue Challenge 2025, the multi-expert entry ranked second overall, and the code is publicly available.
arxiv-2511-02520:
Nikita Evseev, a mathematician in analysis, repairs a gap between two notions of a derivative for maps into abstract spaces. A Lipschitz map from a Euclidean domain into a metric space is known to be metrically differentiable almost everywhere: zoom in far enough and its stretching looks like a simple scaling pattern. When the target is a Banach space with a separable predual, that pattern has a linear version, the weak-star differential. For a general metric or Banach target, such a linear derivative may fail to exist.

Evseev introduces weak weak-star derivatives, a relaxed concept designed to exist in the general case. Within that framework the metric differential again has a linear representation, and its size can be computed as the norm of an associated linear operator. The construction restores, for rough target spaces, the bridge between the geometric and the linear pictures of differentiation.
arxiv-2511-02620:
Roy Rinberg, Adam Karvonen, Alexander Hoover, Daniel Reuter, and Keri Warr defend the crown jewels of AI companies, the model weights, against theft through the front door. Whoever runs an inference server could smuggle the weights out hidden inside ordinary-looking model responses, a steganographic exfiltration that normal monitoring would miss. The authors formalise the threat as a security game and build a verification framework that provably limits how much information such a channel can carry.

Verification means characterising every legitimate source of randomness in model inference, so anything unexplained becomes suspicious; two practical estimators measure those sources. Tested on open models from three to thirty billion parameters, the detector squeezed the exfiltratable information below 0.5 percent of responses at a false-positive rate under 0.01 percent on the largest model, slowing an attacker more than two-hundredfold. Protection, the authors conclude, need not cost providers much.
arxiv-2511-02720:
Explaining why a vision network labels a photo is hard for non-experts. Vojtech Kur and five colleagues built LLEXICORP, a 2025 pipeline that explains convolutional networks in plain words. It builds on concept relevance propagation, a method that traces a prediction back to channels in the top layers and finds images that excite each channel most.

Older workflows made experts name those concepts and write the explanations by hand. LLEXICORP instead hands the task to a multimodal language model, with prompts that keep naming and explaining apart for faithfulness. The text can be pitched low for experts or high for lay readers. Tests on ImageNet photos with a VGG16 model suggest the pairing can open up network decisions to far more people.
arxiv-2511-02920:
James Owen and Douglas Lin propose a new way to form the broad-line region around an active galactic nucleus, the fast-moving gas that gives these objects their wide spectral lines. High above the accretion disc, the air cools enough for dust to condense. Their 2025 paper models the disc's vertical structure with that condensation and the central glare included.

The dusty upper air grows tall and is held up by radiation pressure. It is also unstable: denser gas raises the dust survival temperature, makes more dust, traps more light, and gets pushed harder. Simulations show fountains of dusty gas launched upward, stripped of dust by the central light, then falling back. The churning clumps move at over a thousand kilometers per second, matching broad-line speeds.
arxiv-2511-03520:
Yannik P Wotte and colleagues build MORLie, a framework that shrinks large physical simulations by respecting their Lie group geometry. Many systems live on curved manifolds where rotations and motions act naturally, yet classic reduction flattens that structure into linear subspaces. MORLie instead approximates the full system with a smaller system that still lives on a Lie group.

Unlike older group methods, the framework handles dynamics that lack symmetry, a common practical case. Non-intrusive variants learn the small model from data alone. A key bound shows the method can beat the classic width limit that caps all linear approaches. Tests include a deforming body tracked through noisy point clouds.
arxiv-2511-03620:
Philipp Hager, Onno Zoeter, and Maarten de Rijke release CLAX, a library that rebuilds classic click models with modern gradient training. Click models explain why users tap some search results and skip others, and the classic versions stay readable but train with an older expectation method. Neural versions train fast yet lose that readability.

CLAX swaps the old optimizer for direct gradient steps inside the JAX framework, keeping the classic structure intact. Any part, from embeddings to custom modules, can plug into the model for end-to-end training. Runs on a billion-scale search log from Baidu show the speed on offer. Search teams gain models that both explain clicks and train like modern neural nets.
arxiv-2511-04120:
Xinyuan Li is the lead author among seven authors on RIDE, a framework that rewrites mathematics problems into harder, still well-posed versions to test real reasoning in language models. High scores can reflect leaked training data or shallow pattern matching, while crude rule-based perturbations often create broken questions and no clear difficulty scale.

Item Response Theory supplies the difficulty measure. Responses from thirty-five models acting as students train a difficulty ranker, whose signal then guides a rewriting model through reinforcement learning. Applied to competition benchmarks, rewritten problems cut performance across twenty-six models by about twenty-two percent on average. The drop exposes limited robustness behind headline mathematics scores.
arxiv-2511-04320:
Kuankuan Sima, Longbin Tang, Zhenyu Yang, Haozhe Ma, and Lin Zhao present MacroNav, a learning framework for robots navigating unknown environments under partial views. Good navigation needs detail, connectivity, and global structure at once, and capturing all three cheaply enough for real-time decisions has resisted earlier approaches.

A lightweight context encoder, trained with multi-task self-supervised learning, produces navigation-centred spatial representations at several scales. A reinforcement learning policy joins those representations to graph-based reasoning for action choice. Experiments showed robust environmental understanding, and real-world deployments beat leading navigation methods on success rate and path-weighted success while using less compute, according to the reported results.
arxiv-2511-04520:
Nabyl Quignon and three colleagues propose THEval, a framework for judging talking head videos. Generated faces now look close to real, but scoring tools lag behind. Current checks cover broad quality and lip sync, plus slow user studies.

THEval uses eight metrics across quality, naturalness, and synchronization. Fine-grained measures track the head, mouth, and eyebrows, along with overall face quality. The authors favor metrics that run fast and agree with human preferences. A shared yardstick like this helps builders compare talking head systems honestly as the outputs grow harder to judge by eye.
arxiv-2511-05220:
Jinghui Pi and co-authors study how quantum particles fade in dissipative systems whose spectrum has an imaginary gap that closes. Such systems sit in non-Hermitian physics, where point-gap topology, tracked by winding numbers, can reshape real-time behavior.

Using a saddle-point method, they find that in the trivial case, gap-closing points can also be saddle points. The local response then falls as a single power law, set by the saddle's order. In the non-trivial case, the pattern splits in a distinct way. Their scaling laws give a clean read on long-time decay.
arxiv-2511-05320:
Klára Bendová and co-authors test how to pull court-established facts out of criminal court opinions in Europe. Standard crime data hold little about the act itself, while verdict texts hold rich accounts of what a court found proven.

The team works on public Slovak decisions and tries two routes: pattern matching with regular expressions, and large language models. A simple pattern method sets the baseline. Their study gauges how well each route finds the fact passages, a step toward data sets that can support crime research and fair policy checks at scale.
arxiv-2511-05720:
Kawshik Kumar Paul and Sawmik Kumar Paul describe a Jenkins pipeline that keeps the controller light by pushing heavy builds to a remote Docker host. In standard setups the controller runs the builds itself, which drains its resources and hurts reliability. Jenkins is the widely used automation server at the center of their design.

Here Jenkins runs in a container with persistent storage and sticks to orchestration and reporting. Secure connections hand build and packaging work to remote nodes. The system adds time-stamped backups, sealed artifact packaging, and automatic notices. In their evaluation, builds moved faster, the controller used less CPU and memory, and artifacts arrived sooner. They pitch the setup to small and mid-sized DevOps teams.
arxiv-2511-05820:
Zishuo Xu, Dezhong Yao, and Yao Wan recommend web APIs for software mashups, and explain each pick. Developers combine public APIs to build apps fast, but the choice set is huge. Older recommenders return a fixed number of results and give no reasons, which limits trust and fit.

Their framework, WAR-R1, builds on a lightweight language model. It emits a set of APIs plus a plain-language justification for each. Special start and stop tokens let the model decide how many APIs a mashup needs. Training mixes supervised fine-tuning on an annotated corpus with reinforcement learning that rewards accuracy and reasoning quality together. On a standard data set it beat prior methods on accuracy while giving grounded explanations.
arxiv-2511-05920:
Chirag Seth, Mehrdad Pirnia, and James Bookbinder model how to ship fresh produce while it is still fresh. Fruits and vegetables spoil fast, supplies swing, and quality rules are strict, so their supply chains are hard to run. Sensors from the Internet of Things now report conditions along the way, which the team puts to work.

Their adaptive model accounts for delays, travel time, and temperature drift that eats into shelf life. It reacts to temperature feedback to correct course during transit. Compared with robust, distributionally robust, and stochastic optimization models, the adaptive version extended shelf life by more than eighteen percent in experiments. The authors argue freshness, often ignored in logistics planning, can be planned for directly.
arxiv-2511-06220:
Mohammad Farhad, Sabbir Rahman, and Shuvalaxmi Dass hunt for flaws that survive software patches. A patch can leave latent weaknesses behind when a fix is incomplete or an issue was overlooked, and those leftovers may later become zero-day exploits. Their system, HYDRA, predicts which patched functions still carry hidden risk.
