The larger hope is that the discrete variant can grow into the multi-dimensional form needed for further progress — replacing a powerful but heavy tool with one built from counting and symmetry.
arxiv-2512-05420:
Wusheng Wang and Masahito Hayashi redesign quantum message authentication so the verifier, not the signer, starts the process. Many quantum signature schemes are signer-initiated: signing material must be spread in advance, even if nobody ever verifies anything. In systems where checks are sporadic — spread-out services, audit trails — that advance cost is waste. Their verifier-initiated scheme has the verifier request proof only when needed; the signer responds once, and checking then proceeds without further interaction.

The security rests on quantum zero-knowledge techniques, so checking a signature reveals nothing about the signer's secret beyond its validity. The authors give a general principle turning suitable quantum proof protocols into such signatures, plus a concrete building on elementary qubit hardware. The result is information-theoretic protection against forgery and privacy against curious verifiers, with no reliance on hardness assumptions.
arxiv-2512-05520:
Jonas Bresch, Oleh Melnyk, Martin Schoen, and Gabriele Steidl maximize the generalized Rayleigh quotient without ever multiplying by a matrix's adjoint. The Rayleigh quotient is a central object in numerical linear algebra — its extremes are eigenvalues, and its generalization drives everything from vibration analysis to data science. Standard algorithms lean on adjoint products, which makes them fragile when the available adjoint is only approximate, a common mismatch in practice.

The authors' algorithm is stochastic, zeroth-order, and Riemannian: it climbs the quotient's landscape using only function values, respecting the geometry of the constraint set. They prove the iterates converge to the set of global maximizers with probability one, with the gradient's norm vanishing at a sublinear rate. Numerical experiments show excellent performance against leading algorithms. For applications where adjoints are unavailable or untrustworthy, the method removes a hidden single point of failure.
arxiv-2512-05720:
Dominic Bair, Sagnik Jana, and Yulan Qing ask what happens to a graph's geometry when its edges get random lengths. The setup is first-passage percolation: each edge of an infinite graph receives a random length, drawn independently from one distribution. Many graphs have non-positive curvature, a property that keeps their geometry tame and tree-like in the large.

The team proves this tameness almost never survives the random stretching. Both Gromov hyperbolicity and the coarse CAT(0) property are almost surely lost. Even a special well behaved route, a Morse geodesic ray, loses its Morse character after percolation. The one thing that does hold is that the random map is radial, a technical property about how rays from a fixed point behave. The results show how fragile negative curvature is: chance alone bends a tame space out of shape.
arxiv-2512-06120:
Sarah Millholland and Joshua Winn survey what the James Webb Space Telescope can reveal about exoplanets beyond their atmospheres: their dynamics, the physics of how they spin, bulge, and interact. Nearly six thousand exoplanets are known, yet for most we hold only an orbit, a radius, and a mass. Webb's light gathering power and precision open subtler measurements. A planet raised into an egg by its star's tides tells of its interior and orbital history. Rotational flattening betrays a planet's spin period.

Rings could appear as extended shadows in transit. Moons, entirely undetected so far, might announce themselves through timing and transit shapes. The paper lays out the expected signatures, phenomenon by phenomenon. The field's questions are shifting. The dynamics era will watch planets move and flex.
arxiv-2512-06520:
Zihan Pengmei, Spencer Guo, Chatipat Lorpaiboon, and Aaron Dinner make graph neural networks practical for huge molecular simulations. A simulation of a protein tangled with nucleic acid can hold thousands of building blocks, and reading its motion by hand picked features is slow and brittle. Graph networks learn the features by passing messages between nearby atoms, but on big systems they eat memory and crawl.

The team's fix gathers local detail into summaries as the network goes, shrinking the graph while keeping atomic detail where it counts. That cuts memory and run time sharply. Systems with thousands of residues can now be analyzed on a single graphics card within minutes. On smaller systems with enough data for fair checks, the method also read the dynamics better and made its reasoning easier to follow. The work opens routine learning based study of the large complexes that fill real cells.
arxiv-2512-06820:
Antonin Novak, Andrzej Gnatowski, and Premysl Sucha tackle a scheduling problem inside hospital laboratories, where blood and other samples arrive all day with mixed urgency. Before testing, samples are spun in a centrifuge in batches, so staff must decide when to start a load. Spin too early and urgent samples wait for the next round; spin too late and the ones already loaded sit idle. Travel times from ward to lab add further uncertainty.

The team builds several control rules, pairing a stochastic planning model with a detailed simulation of lab events. Tested on real data from a university hospital, using knowledge of likely travel times cut the typical wait for life-critical samples by about five minutes. The gain nearly matched what a perfect-foresight method could achieve, a striking result for emergency care. Routine samples, by contrast, saw no real change.
arxiv-2512-06920:
Alexandr Plashchinsky proposes a cheap way to steer small language models with reinforcement learning, without hiring human raters or training a separate judge model. Standard practice rewards exact right answers, or scores from people, both of which are sparse or costly. His framework instead compares meanings. A larger parent model writes a reference answer, and the smaller child model earns reward for replies whose internal meaning-vector sits close to the parent's.

Tested across five language tasks, the method steadied the popular PPO training method. Rewards rose more smoothly than with a simple right-or-wrong signal. Because the signal is dense, every answer earns a graded score rather than a bare pass or fail. Plashchinsky pitches the approach as a practical path for aligning smaller models under the guidance of bigger ones, where budgets rule out the heavier machinery of preference-based training.
arxiv-2512-07020:
Jessica N López-Sánchez, Erick Munive-Villa, and Tanja Rindler-Daller simulate dark matter halos made of an ultra-light scalar field whose particles interact with each other. In this picture each halo holds a dense, steady core, a soliton, wrapped in a lighter envelope. The authors merge multiple solitons in three-dimensional simulations and watch the combined halos settle, testing both repulsive and attractive versions of the self-interaction across a wide range of strengths.

Repulsion puffs cores up: they grow more massive and spread wider, with thinner centers than in the non-interacting case. Attraction does the reverse, packing centers tighter until, past a critical mass, collapse threatens. Known formulas for core size still hold with interactions switched on, and the team extends the core-to-halo mass relation beyond the standard fuzzy dark matter setting.
arxiv-2512-07120:
Julian Allagan and co-authors count special colorings of a family of graphs called 2-trees, turning the counts into structural fingerprints. The coloring rule is strict: every triangle must use exactly two colors, never one and never three. The constraint echoes distributed systems, where components should avoid both total concentration and total isolation. Unlike the classic chromatic polynomial, which gives every 2-tree of a given size the same fingerprint, these counts actually distinguish structures.

For theta graphs the counts turn out to be Stirling numbers of the second kind, with a separate closed form for two colors. For fan graphs the two-color count is a Fibonacci number, and higher counts follow an explicit sum built from precomputed terms and Stirling numbers. Both families can be computed quickly.
arxiv-2512-07220:
Yu-Hsueh Chen and Tarun Grover test whether a classic model of spreading activity fits a new information-based way of carving nature into phases. The new proposal groups states that can be reached from each other by short evolution without correlations stretching too far, a property called local reversibility, measured by a Markov length. Their test case is the Domany-Kinzel model, a lattice where sites switch on and off, with an active phase and an absorbing dead phase divided by a directed percolation transition.

Tensor network simulations support local reversibility inside the active phase. Approaching the transition, the Markov length grows without bound, unlike equilibrium transitions where it vanishes outright. The shared information between distant regions scales exactly as directed percolation predicts.
arxiv-2512-07420:
Md Raqibul Islam and eight co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on particle physics computing. Colliders spray out narrow bursts of particles called jets, and sorting jets by type guides the analysis. Deep learning sorts them well, but its reasons are often hard to read.

Their network, called KIGNet, builds four graph views of each jet. Each view weights particle links by a physical trait, such as angle, momentum share, or mass. Three views rest on the Lund jet plane, a map grounded in quantum chromodynamics. A mapping tool then shows which traits drive each sorting choice. Angle and relative momentum carry most of the weight, matching known physics of radiation in jets. Tests on simulated data and on real CMS collision data beat earlier methods. The network also forms cleaner inner groupings on the real data.
arxiv-2512-07620:
Natasha Latouf, Chris Stark, Avi Mandell, and Vincent Kofman wrote this 2025 astronomy paper. It asks how future telescopes can spot water on an Earth-like planet around another star. Their tool is the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, which will study reflected starlight.

Water leaves a broad dip in a planet's reflected light at a known wavelength. The team tests whether coarse photometry, rather than full spectroscopy, can catch that dip. They vary the exposure time, the sharpness of the light split, and the number of sample points. Placement of the points matters as much as their count. At least three well-placed points are needed for a strong detection. How much water the planet holds shifts the observing time required. Detector noise turns out to drive the final choice between methods. When noise is high, photometry yields more planets; when noise is low, spectroscopy wins.
arxiv-2512-07720:
Fan Yang and eleven co-authors wrote this 2025 computer graphics paper on digital avatars. Building a lifelike upper-body avatar from a single photo is still hard. Reconstruction models are fast and stable, but their textures blur and motion stiffens.

Video generation models take the opposite trade in this field. They synthesize realistic, lively results, yet bodies warp and identities drift. The authors combine the strengths of both camps in one framework. A three-dimensional reconstruction model supplies firm structure and appearance priors. Those priors guide a real-time autoregressive video diffusion model. The video model then renders crisp detail and fluid motion on top. Texture blur and stiffness fall away under that guidance. Structural errors common in pure video generation are also prevented. Tests show fewer artifacts and clear gains in visual quality. The method targets live uses such as gaming and virtual reality.
arxiv-2512-08020:
Daniel W Cranston, a graph theorist, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025 about a long standing open problem in graph theory. Albertson conjectured that any graph with a given chromatic number must have a crossing number at least as large as that of the complete graph on the same number of colors. Earlier work had settled the claim only for small values.

Cranston verifies the conjecture for chromatic numbers up to twenty four. He also sharply restricts what a counterexample could look like for the next two values. Beyond that, he rules out broad ranges for the size of a smallest counterexample at each value. For very large chromatic numbers, the excluded range widens further. The paper moves the boundary of the problem and narrows the search for anyone hoping to finish it or break it.
arxiv-2512-08220:
Leandro M Chinellato, Oleg A Starykh, and Cristian D Batista, condensed matter physicists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about chiral solitons in quantum spin chains. Solitons are localized twists that travel through a chain, and the quantum versions are hard to treat because interactions are strong. Their work builds a direct lattice way to quantize these objects.

The framework extends a famous duality between the sine Gordon and Thirring field theories down to the lattice itself. By building the soliton operators explicitly, the authors show how their odd dynamics appear in the excitation spectrum and correlation functions. One sharp result: the main tunneling amplitude flips sign depending on whether the spin is integer or half odd integer. They also identify marks of these excitations in the dynamical spin structure factor, which neutron scattering measures, opening a path to testing deep field theory ideas in real materials.
arxiv-2512-08320:
Qingyuan Hu, Christopher M Poskitt, Jun Sun, and Yuqi Chen, computer security researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is defending cyber physical systems, the software that runs power plants, factories, and other vital infrastructure. Detectors are usually trained once on expert made or fuzzed attack data, which can leave them blind to subtler, unseen attacks.

Their framework, Evo Defender, turns training into a contest. A smart attacker uses guided fuzzing to invent diverse new attack strategies, while the defender learns incrementally from each round and adapts. The team implemented the system on two realistic testbeds, a chemical process model and a robotic arm workstation, injecting hundreds of attack scenarios. On unseen attacks, Evo Defender beat leading baselines while using training data more efficiently. The authors argue that a defender which keeps challenging itself ends up faster and tougher than one trained once and frozen.
arxiv-2512-08420:
Zeno van den Heuvel, Benoit Tabone, Ewine F van Dishoeck, and colleagues posted a data paper on arXiv in December 2025. They compute how often collisions with hydrogen molecules excite or calm the hydroxyl molecule OH in warm gas. OH is a cornerstone of interstellar chemistry, yet the collision data behind its infrared lines were incomplete at high temperature.

Their new rates extend to higher rotational levels and temperatures well above earlier sets. They come from quantum scattering calculations for both forms of hydrogen, matched against a trusted 2017 study where they overlap. One pattern stands out: collisions with the simpler hydrogen form excite OH less, because it lacks a quadrupole moment, though the gap shrinks as gas heats up. The rates follow scaling rules for extrapolation. A first test shows collisions rule low OH populations around newborn stars, even against chemical pumping. The full set is public in the LAMDA database.
arxiv-2512-08620:
Nathan Morris works in complex geometry, on flat vector bundles over curves and the loci where special Hodge structures appear. He asks how large those loci can be inside a moduli space that tracks both curves and bundles. The size is measured by codimension, and it is tied to rank and level.

Morris proves that when rank and level are small compared with the genus, the codimension must be positive. The proof extends a known rank bound by Landesman and Litt and applies it to the isomonodromy foliation on the moduli space. A side result bounds the rank of the monodromy group Lie algebra for a flat bundle moved to a nearby curve. Together, the results limit where these special loci can sit.
arxiv-2512-08720:
Shah Faisal gives a lower bound for how well oval solids in higher dimensions can be placed inside symplectic space, stated through a capacity of those solids.

The proof studies a class tied to a region near a chosen torus in that space. It uses a string based count of descendants of the torus, due to Tonkonog, to obtain the bound. The result links the size of a placed solid to a quantity that is defined purely from the solid itself. That link gives a clean test for when a placement must fail, since the bound can be checked from the solid alone, with no need to build the placement first.
arxiv-2512-08920:
Jessica Yin and coauthors introduce OSMO, an open source tactile glove for human to robot skill transfer. Video demonstrations by humans provide abundant training data for robot policies. Video alone, however, cannot capture the rich contact signals that matter for manipulation tasks.

The glove carries a set of tactile sensors with three axes, spread across the fingertips and palm. It works with leading hand tracking methods, so data can be collected. By fitting the same glove to both the human teacher and the robot, the design shrinks the visual and tactile gap between them. Continuous shear and normal force feedback transfer directly, with no need for image editing or inferred forces. A robot policy trained only on human glove demonstrations performs a hard wiping task that needs steady contact pressure. Its success rate clearly beats vision only baselines, mainly by removing contact related failures. Hardware and firmware are released.
arxiv-2512-09020:
W B Hoogendam and a large team present two months of spectrophotometric observations of the interstellar comet designated 3I ATLAS, the third known interstellar object. Such objects are building blocks ejected from other solar systems, so they offer rare access to the makeup of distant young systems. Observations use an integral field spectrograph on the University of Hawaii telescope.

Their data include the earliest blue sensitive spectrum of the comet, taken about half a day after the discovery announcement. Later spectra confirm cometary activity, including emission from nickel and a carbon nitrogen molecule. Spectral slopes vary with wavelength across the approach toward the Sun. Synthetic photometry shows mostly stable color evolution over the period, with measured colors in several band pairs reported in detail. The team notes that continued observations after closest approach to the Sun will give further insight into what may be an extreme composition for this visitor.
arxiv-2512-09120:
Piotr Gruza, Leszek Aleksander Kołodziejczyk, and Mateusz Łełyk work in mathematical logic, on the strength of fragments of Peano Arithmetic, the standard axiom system for whole-number arithmetic. Earlier work had sorted theories by properties called tightness, neatness, and solidity, which describe how tightly a theory pins down its own meaning. A known result showed that full Peano Arithmetic and some other strong systems are solid.

An open question asked whether a weaker theory sitting strictly inside Peano Arithmetic could still be solid. The authors answer yes for arithmetic. At every level they construct solid theories, and also tight but not neat ones, between a standard fragment and the full system, and their solid examples cannot even interpret the full system. They also give simple solid subtheories of set theory and of second-order arithmetic, plus examples that separate the related properties from each other.
arxiv-2512-09220:
Małgorzata Curyło leads a large radio astronomy team working to sharpen pulsar timing, the precise tracking of pulses from spinning neutron stars. Timing millisecond pulsars supports tests of fundamental physics, studies of neutron star interiors, and searches for very slow gravitational waves. Better timing depends on better templates for the average pulse shape.

The team builds those templates from polarization, using all four measures of the radio waves' polarization state and tracking how the pulse shape changes with frequency. They apply the method to millisecond pulsars timed by the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array in Australia. Timing errors shrank by up to roughly a fifth to a third. The paper also presents the first detailed polarization measurements of these pulsars across both pulse phase and frequency from the Parkes telescope's wideband receiver, and releases the data, plots, and code.
arxiv-2512-09320:
Jinyoung Kim leads a team engineering magnetism in ultrathin films of strontium ruthenate, a quantum material known as SrRuO3. In very thin form, the material sits at a crossover between non-magnetic and ferromagnetic states, because its low-dimensional states pile up electronic density at certain energies. Near such a boundary, small nudges can switch magnetic behavior.

The authors tune the film by adding electrons, moving its Fermi level across the high-density point. Using photoemission measurements that resolve both spin and angle, plus transport tests and theory, they directly picture the spin-split band structure. They show how that structure drives the film's magnetic and electrical properties. The findings show magnetism can be designed by controlling the density of states at a phase crossover. The authors offer that route for building tunable quantum materials on purpose, rather than by accident.
arxiv-2512-09420:
Jørgen Vold Rennemo revisits a lemma in algebraic geometry due to Okounkov, giving it a full proof. The setting is a scheme, a geometric space, equipped with a torus action, a symmetry by multiplications. The lemma concerns generating functions built from Euler characteristics of sheaves, a standard tool for tracking data over a space.

Start with a factorisable sequence of torus-equivariant coherent sheaves living on the symmetric powers of the space, the spaces of unordered collections of points. Okounkov's lemma says the generating function of their Euler characteristics equals the plethystic exponential of a simpler generating function built from sheaves on the original space. Such identities turn hard counts over many points into compact formulas. Rennemo's paper supplies the full argument for a result that other work relies on, clarifying a useful piece of machinery in this part of K-theory.
arxiv-2512-09520:
Fabrizio Pavan and colleagues study how light confined in optical cavities can change the topological behavior of a chain of sites. The chain is the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a test bed for topological physics. Tracking topological phase transitions driven by an environment is a challenge. A tool, mean chiral displacement, can read out the invariant from one particle's motion.

The authors follow one particle's out-of-equilibrium dynamics, coupled to cavity modes through hopping terms between cells. When the cavity frequency exceeds the hopping strengths, the coupling makes the mean chiral displacement jump abruptly, even at short times. It leaves a signature in the chance the particle survives at the edge where it started. At frequencies near the hopping, topological order competes with dissipation and the displacement varies smoothly, carrying information about the driven, lossy topology. The work shows single-particle dynamics can witness environment-induced topological change.
arxiv-2512-09620:
Fabrizio Canfora and colleagues compute non-perturbative corrections to the Casimir energy for a scalar field confined between two parallel plates. The Casimir effect, an attraction from the quantum vacuum, is calculated for simple linear boundary conditions. Here the plates carry non-linear boundary conditions, either Dirichlet-like or Neumann-like, governed by a coupling constant, mimicking features of a non-Abelian gauge theory with surfaces embedded in the bulk.

The authors report the first evidence for a boundary mass generated non-perturbatively, scaling with the inverse square of the coupling, and compute the correction it induces in the standard Casimir energy. Their method builds the boundary conditions into the action through corrections to the boundary fields, rather than imposing them afterward. The result shows how strong boundary effects can reshape a textbook quantum effect in ways ordinary perturbation theory cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-10120:
Maris Basha, Anja Zai, Sabine Stoll, and Richard Hahnloser introduce VocSim, a benchmark that asks what audio embeddings actually know. General purpose sound representations should place different recordings of the same event near each other, whether the event is speech, an animal call, or a door slam, with no task specific training. VocSim tests that intrinsic geometry directly: frozen embeddings, no parameters updated, no labels used beyond a label free correction for anisotropy. The benchmark gathers a large collection of single source clips from nineteen corpora, spanning human speech, animal vocalizations, and environmental sounds, deliberately excluding mixtures.

A simple pipeline built on frozen speech model features ranks strongly and stably across domains. Weakness appears where it matters: on blind tests with low resource languages, local retrieval collapses toward chance, exposing a cross lingual generalization gap in speech representations.
arxiv-2512-10620:
Andrea Braides, Andrea Pinamonti, and Margherita Solci study fractional Sobolev spaces on thin films, slabs whose thickness shrinks toward zero. These spaces measure functions that are rough in a fractional sense, and the regime here is the delicate one of low integrability, where the fractional order sits below one half. The question is what the spaces become as the film flattens.

The authors prove the thin-film spaces converge to a fractional space on the flat base alone. But with the order raised by one half, a gain that reflects the collapsing direction. The statement is made precise through a dimension-reduction notion of convergence, under which suitably scaled Gagliardo seminorms form equicoercive functionals. Limit results are also proved as the fractional order approaches its two endpoints, completing a picture that earlier versions of the work had left open.
arxiv-2512-10720:
Lingjing Kong and co-authors give generative models a causal skeleton key. Image and text generators are powerful black boxes, and popular interpretation tools such as sparse autoencoders, while empirically striking, come with no guarantee that the features they find are the true ones. The authors aim to put interpretation and control on proved foundations instead of plausible stories.

Their lever is causal minimality, the preference for the simplest causal explanation. They build a theory of hierarchical selection models, where high-level concepts arise from constrained compositions of lower-level variables. And derive conditions under which learned representations must match the true hidden variables, component by component. Applied to leading text-to-image diffusion models, the constrained method extracts the models' own hierarchical concept graphs, revealing how their knowledge is organised. Those grounded concepts then work as levers for fine-grained steering of the output.
arxiv-2512-11120:
Michele Silverstein and fellow authors report the first radio spotting of an ultracool dwarf at a frequency of three hundred forty megahertz. Ultracool dwarfs are tiny, cool stars whose magnetic action produces flares and aurora like radio emission. That frequency band is sensitive to material at distances from the star that other bands miss, and passing eruptions may also be detectable there.

The observations came from VLITE, an instrument that rides along on the Very Large Array radio telescope. Its target was EI Cancri, a nearby pair of magnetically active dwarfs with an unusually slow candidate spin period. Detecting the system at this frequency opens a largely unexplored window on ultracool dwarf behaviour. The authors present the spotting as a first step toward understanding how these small stars emit across the radio spectrum.
arxiv-2512-11220:
Fucai Li, Jinkai Ni, Ling-Yun Shou, and Dehua Wang prove global results for a system coupling a flowing fluid with a cloud of particles. The model pairs the Navier Stokes equations for a viscous, density varying incompressible fluid with a kinetic equation for particles dragged by a nonlinear friction force. Such mixtures appear in sprays, sediments, and industrial flows.

The hard part is the long time limit as viscosity vanishes, where the fluid should approach the inviscid Euler equations while friction still drains energy. The authors first prove that small disturbances of equilibrium stay controlled forever, with uniform estimates and sharp rates of settling. They then build global solutions of the inviscid system as the vanishing viscosity limit and prove strong convergence over all time, with a rate that differs sharply from the pure fluid case. New techniques developed here may serve other two phase problems.
arxiv-2512-11320:
Rajrupa Banerjee and colleagues express the quantum entanglement inside oscillating neutrinos purely in terms of quantities experiments can measure. Neutrinos switch among three flavours as they travel, and that flavour system can be viewed as a three part quantum state. Whether its entanglement is genuinely three way or merely pairwise matters for a quantum information reading of flavour change.

The authors show one standard three party measure vanishes identically, meaning the state belongs to the W class of entangled states. Other measures, including partial tangle and concurrence fill, capture the total sharing beyond pairs and can be written through observed appearance and disappearance probabilities. Simulations for the planned DUNE experiment show these measures vary with energy in distinctive patterns. Near maximal mixing, entanglement concentrates between the muon and tau flavours, offering experiments a new quantum lens on flavour evolution.
arxiv-2512-11520:
S. A. Khrapak and A. G. Khrapak connect two ways of understanding how much heat a dense liquid can store. One approach, a scaling law, predicts how the excess heat capacity of simple liquids falls with temperature as a power law. Another, the two phase model, pictures a liquid as a mixture of gas like and solid like behaviour, with a rigidity parameter measuring the balance between them.

The authors show the scaling law is not an independent coincidence. It emerges naturally inside the two phase model, because the rigidity parameter itself is scale invariant. When a quantity does not change under rescaling, power law behaviour follows. The short paper ties a phenomenological recipe used for real liquids, including those in planetary interiors and industrial settings, to a physical picture of liquid structure.
arxiv-2512-11620:
Kanisorn Sangchai and co-authors show how to build robot brains from ready made AI parts. A Large Action Model joins seeing, reasoning, and acting in one loop. Training such a model from scratch is huge, and the results can be hard to check or explain.

Their design wraps neural parts in logic based checks. The robot turns its plans into PDDL code, a strict planning language that a person can review before action. That human in the loop step cuts made up or unsafe actions. Tests on a multi sense robot show the parts work well together. The lesson is that smart robot action can come from careful assembly, not just giant training runs.
arxiv-2512-11820:
Darren J Edwards presents a long manuscript claiming a proof that P differs from NP, the most famous open problem in computing. The claim rests on a new frame called the N-Frame model and a rank measure named SPDP rank. A compiler turns fast programs into tidy polynomial forms with low contextual entanglement width.

From there, rank bounds for fast programs are set against a lower bound for hard counting problems, yielding a clash if P equaled NP. Extra parts claim the argument dodges the known relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization barriers. The author is frank that community checking and machine verification remain future work. Readers should treat the separation as a claimed architecture, not a settled result.
arxiv-2512-11920:
Dong Liu and Yanxuan Yu present CXL-SpecKV, a memory system that eases the biggest cost in serving large language models. During text generation, key value caches swell and eat GPU memory, capping batch size and throughput. Their design moves those caches off the GPU entirely.

It links remote FPGA memory over Compute Express Link, a fast interconnect. A speculative prefetcher guesses which cache entries come next and loads them early. An FPGA engine compresses and decompresses cache data, cutting bandwidth needs up to four fold. On top models the system reached 3.2 times the throughput of GPU only setups and cut memory cost 2.8 fold, with no accuracy loss. Code is open source.
arxiv-2512-12520:
Abby Liu and twelve co-authors probe surface conduction in topological insulator films in a 2025 paper. These materials conduct on their surface while the bulk stays quiet, and tuning the mix of bismuth and antimony in (Bi1-xSbx)2Te3 moves the key Dirac point to cut bulk flow. Magnetic transport tests showed electron dominated conduction, with signs tied to topological surface states.

The team asks whether twin boundaries, internal seams about 100 nm apart, add extra conducting paths. Theory found a raised density of states at 60 degree twin boundaries, with 2D carrier density over 3 times 10 to the 13 per square centimeter. Boundary conductivity was bounded at 7.3 times 10 to the minus 4 siemens, with mobility up to 142.
arxiv-2512-12620:
Aheli Poddar, Saptarshi Sahoo, and Sujata Ghosh study syllogistic reasoning in large language models in a 2025 paper. Syllogisms are classic logic arguments, like all A are B, and all B are C, so all A are C. The team tests 14 large language models on both symbolic inference and natural language forms of such arguments.

Some models reached perfect symbolic scores, the authors report. That raises a question: are these models becoming formal reasoning machines, rather than mirroring the nuances of human reasoning? Syllogistic skill was not a uniform emergent property across models. The paper maps where models stand and where this research direction is heading, with code released in public.
arxiv-2512-12820:
Sourav Nayak, Dhriti Sundar Patra, and Vladimir Rovenski study a class of shapes in geometry called weak nearly C-manifolds. These shapes come from recent work that loosened the rules for older structures known as metric f-manifolds. Such structures link geometry, foliations, and some ideas in physics.

The authors find conditions under which one of these manifolds splits, at least locally, into a product of simpler parts. They also give a full description of the case in lower dimensions. Their theorems yield new results for the older, stricter class of manifolds as well. The work sharpens the basic theory of these spaces.
arxiv-2512-12920:
Alexey Cruz-Garcia and co-authors look for hyperuniform patterns, arrangements that are more evenly spread than random ones yet not on a strict grid. Such patterns can give materials useful traits, and making them with tens of thousands of parts is a prized goal.

The team shows that a pattern of this kind can grow from the vortex structure in a superconductor. They used pristine samples of a copper oxide compound, cooled in a magnetic field. Images over very large fields of view showed the vortex pattern spanning tens of thousands of components. The finding offers a template route toward large hyperuniform devices.
arxiv-2512-13320:
Shivam Parashar and co-authors report particle energization inside interacting solar storm clouds during the strong May 2024 event. Data came from the ASPEX instrument on India's Aditya-L1 spacecraft, parked between Earth and the Sun. Two analyzers viewing in perpendicular planes gave a new kind of vantage point.

They describe a special region where a shock, driven by one coronal mass ejection, plowed into a preceding one. The downstream zone lasted over 13 hours and acted as a site where protons and alpha particles gained energy. A second ASPEX sensor confirmed the energized particles. The view is the first of its kind from the L1 point.
arxiv-2512-13420:
Andrea Santoro, Marco Nurisso, and Giovanni Petri shift brain signal analysis from nodes to edges. Standard graph methods study signals sitting on brain regions, the nodes. Co-fluctuation between regions, carried on the edges, can hold dynamics that node signals miss entirely.

Using the one-dimensional Hodge Laplacian, they process edge signals from 100 unrelated Human Connectome Project subjects. Structural connectivity is recast in a form that supports this edge view. Edge based decoding of task states beat conventional node based methods in both static and dynamic settings. The findings suggest edge-focused methods reveal parts of brain functional organization that older pipelines overlook.
arxiv-2512-13520:
Abhishek Ghadai and Sayantan Majumdar report a memory effect in collagen networks that stiffen under strain. Collagen is a key part of the tissue that holds mammal cells in place. Materials pushed far from balance can store traces of past strain in their structure, and the authors test that idea in lab-made collagen gels.

Using shear tests and live imaging, they find a non-steady stress drop that recalls the Kovacs effect. It appears only when the gel is in its stiff, nonlinear range, and over a wider strain range than in other soft solids. The response also tracks with negative normal stress and local strain fields.
arxiv-2512-13620:
Olga Aryasova, Ilya Pavlyukevich, and Andrey Pilipenko prove limit theorems for stochastic equations with sticky interfaces. Their diffusions move through many semipermeable hyperplanes. Local time builds up at each interface, and a random time change can make an interface sticky once enough local time collects.

They show that as the gaps between interfaces shrink to zero, the local-time terms merge into a single homogenized drift term. When interfaces are sticky, the limit diffusion also slows, so its diffusion coefficient drops in effect. The results give a form of stochastic homogenization for media layered with sticky, semipermeable barriers. The paper runs 28 pages and sets the theorem in a general multivariate frame.
arxiv-2512-13820:
Kyrill Michaelsen and Felix Tellander classify when one-loop Feynman integrals have a special algebra property. They study generalized hypergeometric systems, in the sense of Gel'fand, Kapranov, and Zelevinsky, tied to one-loop integrals. The key question is when the rank of the system does not depend on space-time size or propagator powers.

That question equals asking when a linked affine semigroup ring is Cohen-Macaulay. For massive one-loop integrals, they prove conditions that are both needed and enough, extending past normality results. For Feynman integrals, the property is fully set by an integer linear program built from the Newton polytope of the integrand. They also give a picture-based account of its solutions and a condition that is enough on its own for general one-loop integrals.
arxiv-2512-13920:
Haoyuan Cai, Sulaiman A. Alghunaim, and Ali H. Sayed develop DAMA, a unified framework for decentralized nonconvex minimax optimization. Minimax problems pit two objectives against each other and arise across machine learning. Doing them over decentralized multi-agent networks adds communication and bias problems.

DAMA blends online and offline stochastic minimax algorithms with several decentralized learning strategies. Its unified learning strategy subsumes bias-correction methods such as gradient tracking and adds variants with tighter network-dependent bounds. A probabilistic gradient estimator called GRACE unifies momentum and variance-reduction methods for accelerated gradients. A unified analysis gives a general performance bound with state-of-the-art sample complexity. This first part covers algorithm development and main results, with theory and experiments in Part II.
arxiv-2512-14420:
Nakamasa Inoue and six co-authors address a weak spot in image captioning research: automatic scores for captions become unreliable when images come from new domains. Their method, DISCODE, scores captions with a large vision-language model but adjusts the scoring at test time, with no extra training of the model itself.

An adaptive loss, guided by a bell-shaped prior distribution, steadies the scores, and the authors solve it with a formula rather than slow search. They also built MCEval, a benchmark spanning six domains, to test scoring methods fairly. DISCODE topped MCEval and four older benchmarks as a reference-free metric.
arxiv-2512-14720:
Agents powered by large language models are moving onto social media, where they read posts, watch media, and act among human users. Yet no comprehensive evaluation existed of how well these agents comprehend media content, understand user behavior, and make intricate decisions.

SoMe is presented as a realistic benchmark to close that gap for social media agents. A shared, realistic testbed matters because agent behavior online affects real communities, not just lab scores. The benchmark gives researchers and platforms a way to compare agents honestly before wider release, and to see where their social understanding still falls short.
arxiv-2512-15120:
Yuqing Xie and five coauthors automate one of reinforcement learning's most fiddly crafts: writing the reward function. In tasks with several goals at once, a good reward must blend many human designed heuristics, and hand tuning that blend is slow. Their framework, MORSE, learns the blend by itself.

MORSE sets up a two level optimization. The inner loop trains a robot policy to maximize the current shaped reward. The outer loop adjusts the reward itself to improve true task performance. To keep the search from settling too early, it injects noise guided by task results and by the prediction error of a fixed random network. In MuJoCo and Isaac Sim robot tasks, MORSE balanced competing objectives well. Its performance matched policies trained with manually tuned rewards, across a range of robotic jobs.
arxiv-2512-15320:
Nazerke T. Tleukhanova and a coauthor extend classic inequalities about Fourier series into a broader family of function spaces. Bochkarev's inequalities, of Hardy-Littlewood type, link the integral behavior of a function to how summable its Fourier coefficients are. The classical results describe trigonometric series in Lorentz spaces with second index above 2.

The new work moves to anisotropic grand Lorentz spaces, where the measure of a function can differ by direction and includes a grand, limiting flavor. Using extrapolation of linear operators, the authors derive Bochkarev type inequalities for these spaces and for arbitrary orthonormal systems, not just trigonometric ones. They also study the summability of Fourier coefficients for functions in the new spaces. The results generalize a classical chapter of harmonic analysis to a much wider setting.
arxiv-2512-15420:
Yeonwoo Cha and co authors present FlowBind in a 2025 paper on models that can turn any mix of inputs into any output type. Earlier flow based systems needed large paired data sets, heavy computing, and complex staged training. FlowBind aims to keep the quality while cutting those costs.

The method learns one shared latent space for all modes, with invertible flows linking each mode to that space. At use time the flows act as encoders and decoders for direct translation. Tests on text, image, and audio match prior quality while using up to six times fewer parameters and training ten times faster.
arxiv-2512-15920:
Deaglan Bartlett and co authors introduce a special issue on symbolic regression in physics in a 2025 article. It searches data for compact math formulas, offering readable relations rather than black box fits. A Royal Society discussion meeting in April 2025 gathered the field's current work.

The opening piece reviews the basics of the method and contrasts it with standard fitting. Use cases span machine led equation finding, modeling of emergent effects, and compact stand ins for costly model runs. Method topics include search space design, operator choice, keeping formulas simple, and feature choice. Open problems include scaling up, noise, and overfitting, while symmetry and limiting rules mark hopeful paths.
arxiv-2512-16020:
David Simonne and six co-authors report surface chemistry results in a paper released on arXiv in 2025. Platinum catalysts help make nitric acid and clean up pollution through ammonia oxidation, a reaction where ammonia reacts with oxygen on a platinum surface. Whether thin oxide layers form on the platinum during the reaction has long been debated.

Using X-ray methods that watch the surface while the reaction runs, the team studied the flat platinum face called Pt(111). They found that stable oxides do not form under working conditions. Short-lived oxide-like layers appear in oxygen-rich gas above light-off temperature, then vanish once ammonia arrives. The reaction instead follows a Langmuir-Hinshelwood path, where adsorbed ammonia fragments and oxygen compete to set whether nitric oxide or nitrogen gas comes out.
arxiv-2512-16220:
Alexis Hibbler, Kevin J McGown, and Enrique Trevino count special polynomials in research shared on arXiv in 2025. A number field is called norm-Euclidean when a division-with-remainder trick works in it, which makes its arithmetic tidy. Heilbronn gave a test that can prove a field fails to have that property when a prime ramifies completely.

The authors ask how often that test applies to fields built from Eisenstein polynomials, a family tied to the prime p. For odd degree at least 3 and prime at least 5, they prove a lower bound on the share of such polynomials where the test succeeds. As p grows, that share tends toward all of them. A corollary says a positive proportion of Eisenstein polynomials of any degree at least 2 generate fields that are not norm-Euclidean.
arxiv-2512-16520:
Felix Kloiber-Tollinger and Lukas M Sieberer build theory for watched quantum systems in a paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025. Measurement-induced phase transitions, where monitoring changes a system's entanglement pattern, were mostly studied for perfect detectors. Real experiments lose information, and many systems evolve through quantum jumps with non-Hermitian operators.

Their replica Keldysh field theory handles general quantum-jump processes for bosons and fermions alike. Perfect monitoring gives pure-state trajectories, sloppy monitoring gives mixed-state dynamics, and ordinary Lindblad evolution appears as a limiting case. Applied to imbalanced fermion counting with some jumps missed, the theory predicts area-law entanglement for any nonzero jump rate under perfect counting. With inefficient detection, subsystem entropy switches to volume-law scaling beyond a finite correlation length. Simulations back the analysis.
arxiv-2512-16620:
Kanwal Aftab, Graham Adams, and Mark Scanlon turn wall sockets into forensic clues in a 2025 paper posted to arXiv, aimed at a 2026 digital forensics venue. Locating where an indoor photo or video was taken could aid investigations of trafficking and exploitation, but rooms look alike worldwide and GPS fails indoors. Plug sockets, though, are standardized by country and region.

Their three-stage pipeline first detects sockets with a YOLOv11 model, reaching a mean average precision of 0.843. A classifier then sorts sockets into 12 types at 0.912 accuracy, and a final step maps types to countries at 0.96 accuracy when confident. Two purpose-built data sets, thousands of annotated images, support training. Tests on crowd-sourced hotel photos from the TraffickCam subset showed the approach working under poor light and amateur angles. Code, models, and data are open-sourced.
arxiv-2512-17020:
Saurya Das, Mitja Fridman, and Sourav Sur propose a fresh kind of equivalence principle violation. In their version, an object inertial and gravitational masses differ not by makeup, but by distance. The distance is measured from a gravitating body. Standard thinking ties any such gap to inner makeup and interactions.

The authors show the gap can instead be a function of separation alone. They sketch lab and observational ways to test the idea. A covariant frame for the same effect is laid out side by side. The claim can thus be judged in full relativistic terms. If borne out, the effect would add a distance dial to tests of a bedrock rule of gravity.
arxiv-2512-17120:
Kingsley Yeon and Mihai Anitescu speed up low-rank plus diagonal decomposition, a model for large covariance matrices that joins global shared factors with local fixes. Such matrices drive covariance estimation, factor analysis, and kernel learning at scale.

Their alternating algorithm fits the low-rank part, then the diagonal part, and provably cuts error while beating gradient descent and costing less than majorization methods. A randomized variant pairs Nystrom sketching for the low-rank part with stochastic diagonal estimates. It reaches machine precision with far fewer matrix-vector products than the ambient dimension, backed by error bounds. On S and P 500 return covariances it beat pure low-rank fits by a wide margin.
arxiv-2512-17220:
Yuqing Li and seven co-authors borrow an idea from psychology to help language models handle very long texts. People keep a global picture of what they read, called a mindscape, and use it to place each new detail. Standard retrieval systems lack that picture, so they lose track of evidence spread across a long document.

Their system, MiA-RAG, first builds a mindscape by summarizing the text level by level. Both the search step and the writing step then lean on that global view. Search queries get richer wording, and answers are formed inside one coherent frame. Across long-text and two-language test sets, MiA-RAG beat the standard systems it was compared with.
arxiv-2512-17320:
Lu Wei, Yuta Nakashima, and Noa Garcia built EMMA, a tougher exam for tools that claim to erase a concept from an image generator. Erasure is meant to strip out things like a celebrity's face or a living artist's style without retraining the whole model. Past exams used few concepts and plain, direct prompts, which made weak tools look strong.

EMMA grades five erasure methods over 13 measures in five domains, from objects to copyrighted styles. It probes sneaky prompts that hint at the banned concept, lookalike concepts that should survive, and bias by gender and ethnicity. Every method stumbled on hinted prompts and on lookalikes. Some even made bias worse than the original model, a warning for anyone shipping erasure as a safety fix.
arxiv-2512-17420:
Yasufumi Araki and Jun'ichi Ieda work out the theory of an odd electrical effect at the seam between two magnetic materials. An alternating current in a heavy metal stirs the magnetism of a neighbor layer through the spin Hall effect. That stirring feeds back as reactance, a lag between voltage and current, as if a tiny coil hid in the seam.

At low frequencies, below the neighbor's natural ringing point, the feedback acts just like an inductor. Better still, its sign flips depending on how spin crosses the seam, through a damping-like push or a field-like push. Watching that sign gives engineers a clean electrical probe of an interface they cannot see, useful for sorting spintronic materials.
arxiv-2512-17520:
Peter Lundqvist and coauthors report new low frequency radio views of three famous supernovae, the exploded stars SN 1979C, SN 1986J, and SN 2006X. The images come from LOFAR, a European radio telescope array, through its Two-metre Sky Survey and its international stations. Their 2025 paper reads these faint signals for clues about each blast and its surroundings.

SN 2006X itself stayed invisible, and the silence caps the density of gas around it at about 10 hydrogen atoms per cubic centimeter under their model. SN 1979C still glowed at 4.6 mJy almost 40 years after exploding, with a fading pattern pointing to a star of about 13 solar masses. SN 1986J gave a first sharp LOFAR image at 6.77 mJy, showing how radio telescopes can track supernova leftovers for decades.
arxiv-2512-17720:
Joanna Sliwa and three co-authors stop a fine-tuned model from forgetting its schooling. LoRA, the popular cheap way to specialize a big model, adds small trainable patches instead of retraining everything. The catch is catastrophic forgetting: the model masters its new math task and quietly loses older knowledge it was never asked to rehearse.

Their fix, LaLoRA, first maps which of the patch's settings the model holds with confidence, using a Laplace approximation of the loss landscape. Updates then steer away from bending those confident settings, while free directions stay open for the new skill. The guard applies only to the small patch, so costs stay low. On a Llama model tuned for math, the learning-forgetting balance improved, with one dial controlling the trade.
arxiv-2512-17920:
Rahul Baxi asks why chatbots follow orders worse when prompts are squeezed shorter. Past tests mixed two kinds of failure: breaking a stated rule and getting facts wrong. His Compression-Decay test scores those two apart, across five squeeze levels, for nine leading models and eight ideas.

Rule breaking formed a U shape in almost every run, worst at middle length, not at the shortest length. Rule scores and fact scores barely moved together, and rule effects were 2.9 times larger. A further test pinned much of the blame on helpfulness training: muting it raised rule compliance by 598 percent on average. The fix, he argues, starts with training habits, not prompt length.
arxiv-2512-18020:
Brahim Mahmoudi and four coauthors name a new kind of software flaw: LLM code smells. As chatbots get wired into apps, sloppy wiring can quietly drag down quality. No formal list of such flaws existed for the code that calls a language model.

The team defines five recurring bad habits in that calling code, drawn from past studies. They extend an existing checker to spot the five, then scan 200 open source systems that use language models. The flaws showed up in 60.50 percent of the systems, and the checker flagged them with 86.06 percent precision. A shared list gives developers a way to clean up AI wiring early.
arxiv-2512-18220:
Handhika Satrio Ramadhan, M Naufal Athaullah, and Ilham Prasetyo revisit cosmic strings in a Dirac-Born-Infeld theory, a model where fields have a built in speed cap. An older study said such strings can never reach the neat BPS state, where forces cancel and binding energy drops to zero. The verdict hinged on one fixed shape for the field's energy hill.

Letting the hill shape be chosen to fit, the team finds BPS states do exist. The demand for them picks out one hill, shaped like a sine wave's kin, and yields exact first order equations for the string. The strings hit the energy bound dead on, and they melt back into the classic string as the cap fades.
arxiv-2512-18320:
Sun-Hyun Youn rebuilds the tennis serve from physics alone, with no motion capture fitting. Most serve studies film pros and learners or let AI sift the footage, which shows what top players do but not why the body must move that way. Youn models the upper body as 12 linked segments and demands each serve type meet the air flow facts of a real ball flight.

Solving backward for the joint paths, then forward for the forces, gives a surprise. Flat, slice, and kick serves look near alike on film, yet their inner force patterns differ sharply. The wrist, which barely seems to move, must fire strong, fast changing twists to fight gravity and the swing's coupling.
arxiv-2512-18920:
Oliver Huang and five co-authors argue that data analysis tools should start with the story, not the chart. Analysts naturally build narratives as they explore, asking questions, plotting, and revising what the data mean. Most software treats that narrative as an afterthought, severing the link between evidence and the evolving reading. Their framework, Narrative Scaffolding, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and presented at IUI 2026, makes narrative the primary interface.

Their system takes narrative-first input, generates views aligned with the analyst's stated intent, and supports reflection through insight provenance and inquiry tracking. In a within-subject study of twenty users, scaffolding produced broader exploration, deeper reflection, and narratives that held up better. Six chart literacy experts confirmed the outputs matched intent and encouraged careful exploration. Sensemaking, the work suggests, improves when the story stays visible.
arxiv-2512-19320:
Yayuan Li, Jian Zhang, Jintao Guo, and Zihan Cheng fix a blind spot in model merging, the craft of fusing specialist models into one. Merging usually aligns feature directions and calls the job done. Features, though, also carry magnitude, and common merge steps quietly distort it, dragging performance down.

Their plug-in framework, MAGIC, recalibrates magnitudes layer by layer in both feature and weight space. Three variants cover different needs, and no real retraining is required. By restoring the scale that fusion perturbs, the merged model keeps more of each specialist's behavior. The work argues magnitude deserves the same care that direction has long received.
arxiv-2512-20020:
Yuecheng Cai and Jasmin Jelovica give ship designers a shortcut from whole-hull behavior to the stress inside a single panel. Their hybrid framework pairs a coarse homogenized model of the hull girder, built as an equivalent single layer, with a graph neural network for local detail. The coarse model efficiently predicts global displacements, and boundary degrees of freedom along stiffened panels are extracted from it.

A mapping and reconstruction procedure converts those global quantities into detailed boundary kinematics, which feed a heterogeneous graph transformer together with panel geometry and loading. Trained on high-fidelity three-dimensional finite element panels, the network predicts stress and displacement fields for any panel. Three box-beam validations show global error governed by the coarse model while local accuracy stays high, a combination suited to design optimization loops.
arxiv-2512-20120:
Mohammad Helal Uddin, Liam Seymour, and Sabur Baidya prune vision transformers with a calculus-aware scalpel. Transformers pay quadratic attention costs and carry much redundant work. That blocks deployment where latency is tight. Past pruning treats tokens or heads apart. It leans on heuristics or first-order signals. HEART-ViT gauges second-order, curvature-weighted sensitivity for both at once. It uses fast Hessian-vector products to do so.

Pruning calls are made per input, under set loss budgets. Token and head cuts are unified in one frame. A structural lesson emerged. Token cuts give most of the savings, while head cuts polish what is left. On ImageNet tests, the method cut compute by near half and latency by over a third. Accuracy matched or beat the base models after fine-tuning. Gains held on edge hardware too.
arxiv-2512-20520:
Chehak Malhotra and co-authors benchmark language models at a task hospitals actually need: predicting shock in intensive care patients. Early warning of shock enables interventions that save lives. The team pits large models, including the clinically trained GatorTron, against smaller biomedical encoders and classic embeddings.

Clinical notes from over seventeen thousand ICU stays in MIMIC-III were filtered by stay length and shock index, leaving a small, imbalanced cohort. Fine-tuning with focal and cross-entropy losses addressed the imbalance. GatorTron-Base earned the best weighted recall, yet overall the large models merely matched the small ones. The authors conclude that language models are not inherently better at forecasting clinical events, and future training should target clinical trajectories.
arxiv-2512-20720:
Shibam Das, Debanjan Karan, Babli Khatun, and Nilay Kundu derive new rules for cosmological correlators, the statistics that describe the infant universe. Such correlators live on de Sitter spacetime, the setting of cosmic inflation. The team ask what basic principles, unitarity and analyticity, force these quantities to look like.

Their cutting rule expresses the jump in a correlator as products of simpler jumps from one internal line being cut. Extra auxiliary pieces, built from real and imaginary parts of wave-function coefficients, appear for the first time. Checks in several models agree with standard methods. The framework also stretches to loop corrections and derivative interactions, widening its use.
arxiv-2512-20920:
Ningyuan Liu, Jing Yang, Kaitong Cai, and Keze Wang attack the memory wall that blocks full fine-tuning of mixture-of-experts language models. Updating every parameter requires caching the intermediate activations of each layer for the backward pass, and for large models that cache dwarfs the hardware most teams own. Existing frameworks spread memory across many graphics processors or offload it, trading hardware and speed for feasibility.

Their framework, RevFFN, redesigns the transformer blocks to be reversible, so each layer's inputs are rebuilt from its outputs during backpropagation instead of stored. The expressive design of the expert architecture stays intact while peak memory drops sharply. Full-parameter fine-tuning of these models becomes practical on a single consumer-grade or server-grade graphics processor.
arxiv-2512-21620:
Sumit Roy builds a model of undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, an aggressive soft-tissue cancer, and of its treatment. The model is a system of nonlinear differential equations. It combines Gompertz-type tumor growth, necrotic loss tied to the tumor surface, surgery with residual disease left behind, recovery, immune interaction, and radiation scheduling.

Roy analyzes the model's behavior and proves several results. The growth equation has a threshold below which the tumor cannot survive and may disappear. After surgery, an early inflammatory stage is followed by proliferative recovery. For the tumor-immune part he identifies equilibrium states and local stability conditions. The radiation scheduling problem is posed as optimal control, and its best strategy turns out to be of bang-bang type, meaning treatment is either fully on or fully off. A theme is that relapse depends on residual disease, recovery dynamics, and timing, not growth alone.
arxiv-2512-21720:
Shizhe He, Christopher Ré, Dan Biderman, and their co-authors analyze the design of agentic language model systems through information theory. Products like deep research assistants and coding agents share a hidden pattern: a smaller compressor model distills raw context into compact text, and a larger predictor model reasons over the digest. Designers currently choose these components by expensive trial and error.

Treating the compressor as a noisy channel, the authors estimate the mutual information between context and compression. That single number, computed without reference to any task, strongly predicts downstream performance. Across five datasets and three model families, bigger compressors were more accurate and more efficient, packing more information per token. One mid-size compressor conveyed over five times the information per token of its smaller sibling. Scaling the compressor beat scaling the predictor: put a capable compressor on the device, paired with a smaller cloud model.
arxiv-2512-22020:
Neutrino mass matrices with two texture zeros make testable predictions, and modular symmetry can generate them. Bhabana Kumar, Debajyoti Dutta, and Mrinal Kumar Das realize seven different two-zero textures inside a left-right symmetric model. Matter multiplets are singlets of the modular A4 group, with weights chosen to produce each pattern.

For every texture they compute the Majorana mass for neutrinoless double beta decay and branching ratios for lepton-flavor-violating processes. The textures are then confronted with DUNE and T2HK, sharpened by JUNO and reactor measurements of the solar and reactor mixing angles. Under inverted ordering, two textures collapse to tiny islands near CP-conserving points, a highly predictive outcome.
arxiv-2512-22420:
Rui Li and five co-authors present Nightjar, a serving system that turns speculative decoding on and off as conditions demand. Speculative decoding speeds language model replies by drafting tokens cheaply and verifying them in parallel. That helps under light load but backfires when servers are compute-bound, and keeping the draft model resident eats memory needed for larger batches.

Nightjar first tunes the speculative length to the current batch size. A multi-armed bandit planner then decides when speculation stops paying, and disables it proactively. During disabled phases, the draft model moves to the CPU only when graphics memory is under pressure, freeing cache space for bigger batches. Tests showed up to about fifteen percent higher throughput and twenty percent lower latency than standard speculative decoding.
arxiv-2512-22720:
Murtaza Nikzad and Kerem Atas explain how RSA encryption, the workhorse of secure communication, collapses when its prime numbers are chosen badly. Two attack vectors anchor the paper. Fermat's factorization method cracks keys whose two primes sit too close together. The greatest common divisor attack exploits different keys that accidentally share one prime factor. Anyone can then compute that factor from the public moduli.

The analysis leans on landmark measurement studies: one famous scan found over sixty-four thousand vulnerable TLS hosts sharing factors, and a 2023 study tracked Fermat factorization in deployed systems. Weak random number generation in embedded devices emerges as the main culprit. The authors close with mitigations, proper entropy collection and prime validation checks, arguing these old failures remain prevalent in real implementations.
arxiv-2512-23420:
Antika Yadav and Prasad Vilas Chanekar study control co-design for systems governed by parabolic partial differential equations, where the design and the controller must be chosen together rather than in sequence. Co-design matters because a plant optimized without its controller, or a controller tuned to a fixed plant, can both leave performance on the table. For heat-like PDE dynamics, though, the joint synthesis problem is infinite-dimensional and hard to attack.

The authors set up the co-design problem for this class, then derive an approximate version whose constraints are matrix-algebraic, a problem that numerical methods can grip. They solve the approximation with a gradient-based method and prove the solution also stabilizes the original PDE system, so the simplification does not sacrifice the safety property. Examples justify the approach. The paper offers a tractable route into co-design for distributed thermal and diffusion processes.
arxiv-2512-23620:
Monica Guica reviews two subjects that turn out to be deeply linked: the Kerr/CFT correspondence, a proposed small-scale description of rotating black holes. The second subject is solvable deformations of two-dimensional quantum field theories, T-bar-T and J-bar-T. The counting of black hole states can be tied to very special deformations of two-dimensional conformal field theories. The exactly solvable deformations return the favor with insight into black hole interiors. The review runs to nearly two hundred pages.

The Kerr/CFT chapters stress hard conceptual problems, especially recent evidence that the classical geometry of extremal black holes is unreliable. The deformation chapters are self-contained and field-theoretic, covering the finite-size spectrum, thermodynamics, scattering, and holographic dictionaries. A highlight is the extended symmetry structure of the deformed theories, which matches the asymptotic symmetries of the dual spacetimes exactly.
arxiv-2512-23720:
Matt Bowring, Ben Anderson, and Ben Tiffany built a circuit board that computes with coupled oscillators. Their electronic Ising machine attacks hard graph problems, the NP-hard kind, by annealing. A network of nonlinear electronic oscillators evolves until its phase pattern settles into a stable configuration, and that pattern encodes the answer.

The paper reviews the theory behind this energy-minimization style of computing, then presents the custom printed circuit board design in detail, with simulations and experimental results from the hardware. The board is meant to be low-power and high-speed compared with running the same search on a conventional processor. The authors close by flagging open research directions for this emerging family of computing architectures, which tries to let physics itself do the optimization.
arxiv-2512-24320:
Adam Boocher, Noah Huang, and Harrison Wolf attack two old conjectures in algebra. The conjectures give lower bounds for the Betti numbers of graded modules. Those numbers encode the shape of a module's resolution. The authors recast the bounds as arithmetic. The new home is the Boij-Söderberg cone.

Inside that cone, a counterexample would leave a numeric trace. It would match an explicit Diophantine obstruction from a pure resolution. Number theory sorts those obstructions fully in codimension three. Delicate links emerge between Betti tables and classic Diophantine equations. New cases fall in codimensions five and six. Those concern Gorenstein algebras. There, studying the variety cut out by the equations settles the conjecture.
arxiv-2512-24420:
Brandon Robinson builds a prized symmetry into neural network field theories. Such theories usually describe free-like fields. In two dimensions they lack a local stress tensor. That gap blocks Virasoro symmetry, the algebra at the heart of conformal field theory. Robinson's Log-Kernel design removes the block. A special prior on the spectrum enforces local conformal symmetry.

The Virasoro algebra then emerges from the statistics of the network ensemble. The derivation is done on paper, not just in simulation. Numerics check the construction. The measured central charge lands close to the predicted value of one. Vertex operator dimensions match as well. Finite width adds weak interactions that shrink as the network grows. Fermions and boundary conditions extend the frame. The super-Virasoro algebra appears there, with matching correlators.
arxiv-2512-24720:
Li and Orlov connect products of random Hermitian matrices to Hurwitz numbers, which count branched coverings of the Riemann sphere. The matrix product generalizes the familiar one-matrix model of random matrix theory. The coverings counted have free ramification over zero and infinity and a special brickwork pattern elsewhere, built from swaps with no fixed points.

Products of normal random matrices receive parallel treatment. Readers in mathematical physics get a bridge between random matrices and enumerative geometry. Such links let results from one field compute quantities in the other, and they clarify how multi-matrix models encode covering data.
arxiv-2512-24820:
Torjus Steffensen, Vegar Stubberud, Emilie Hennisen, and colleagues report a circuit-free way to monitor arterial pulse through the skin using nanophotonics. A soft silicone film carries a strain-sensitive nanophotonic surface on one face and a bio-inspired adhesive structure on the other. Pulse-driven strain shifts diffracted colors, which an unmodified smartphone camera can read.

No laser, spectrometer, or electronics at the sensing site are needed, unlike earlier mechano-optical devices. Measured optical response matches color-mixing models. Health sensing readers get a passive patch concept for cardiovascular monitoring. Large-area nanoimprinting makes the dual-function film, pointing toward cheap, simple wearables.
arxiv-2601-06620:
Gui-Qiang Chen and two co-authors prove a big result on flows with a vacuum edge in 2026. The flow laws are those for a thick fluid that can be squeezed. Their case has round symmetry and starts from large, rough data.

How such flows act over all time with vacuum is key to thick flows. A true vacuum edge moves and speeds up in a set way at its rim. It shows up in the flow of thin sheets of water, they note. Large-data cases in more than one dim had stayed open till now. Two blocks made them hard: a flaw at the core point and wear at the edge. Their proof deals with both blocks for the round case. It is a mark in the study of flows that meet empty space.
arxiv-2601-07520:
Mara Pompili and Daniel Smertnig study when certain algebras have unique factorization, using a computational approach. Their 2026 preprint covers locally acyclic cluster algebras and their class groups. Class groups measure how far a ring is from having unique factorization. To make progress, the authors introduce a new class of rings called finite Laurent intersection rings.

These new rings include several known families. Among them are locally acyclic cluster algebras, full-rank upper cluster algebras, and some generalized upper cluster algebras. Laurent phenomenon algebras also fit inside the class. A single framework lets results proved once apply across all these settings. The paper should interest algebraists who study cluster algebras and factorization theory together.
arxiv-2601-07720:
Peihang Wu extends bundles over the boundary forms of Shimura varieties, in a 2026 preprint on pure math. Shimura varieties are shapes in geometry at the heart of modern number theory. Their integral canonical models extend them over bases from number theory. Toroidal forms add boundary layers so the spaces become complete. Wu builds canonical extensions of principal bundles over these forms.

The bundles involved carry level structure fixed at a prime p, of hyperspecial type. Automorphic vector bundles, which code automorphic forms in geometric terms, also get extensions. Such extensions let scholars study how the bundles decay at the boundary. That matters for the arithmetic of Shimura varieties and their cohomology. The paper serves those who work on arithmetic geometry. It supplies foundational constructions that later work on these spaces will use. The work is base work: dry on its face, yet much later work will stand on it.
arxiv-2601-07820:
Manar Ali and colleagues test whether language models ask for clarification when they should. In human conversation, both sides work to maintain shared understanding. A listener who is unsure can request clarification. The authors ask whether models can play that listener role. Their 2026 preprint uses reference games, tasks where a description must pick out a target. Uncertainty in such games is natural and measurable.

The testbed links model uncertainty to clarification requests. A well-aligned model should ask more when its uncertainty is high. Asking too little risks confident errors; asking too much burdens the user. Reference games give clean scores for that balance. The paper speaks to scholars in dialogue systems and human-computer interaction. It treats clarification as a skill to measure, not a nuisance.
arxiv-2601-08020:
Layton A. Hall and Samuel Alperin revisit self-imaging, the periodic reappearance of a wave's pattern as it travels. Self-imaging is a hallmark of paraxial, quadratic-wave evolution. Across two centuries of realizations, uniform recurrence planes along the axis were considered fundamental. The pattern was assumed to repeat at evenly spaced planes. Their 2026 preprint introduces canonical clocks and hidden geometric freedom in this setting.

Challenging the uniformity assumption opens new designs for optical systems. If recurrence planes can be placed with more freedom, imaging devices gain flexibility. Canonical clocks give a principled way to describe the timing of recurrences. The work blends optics history with modern geometry. The paper serves scholars in wave optics and mathematical physics. It shows a textbook phenomenon still has structure left to find.
arxiv-2601-08620:
Antonio Loison and a large team wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a test for search-aided AI writing. The test is called ViDoRe V3. The systems in view are Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines, or RAG. A RAG system finds source texts first, then writes a reply based on them. Real work puts hard demands on such a system. It has to take in visual parts like tables, charts, and images.

It must join facts from more than one source. It must ground each claim in a source a reader can check. Past tests miss much of that strain. They tend to use text alone, or a single source. They can grade the search step and the writing step apart from each other. ViDoRe V3 grades the full pipeline in hard, real-world cases. Teams that build search tools for firms gain a tougher test of what they ship.
arxiv-2601-08920:
Md. Jahidul Islam builds a tool to merge health scans of more than one type into one clear view. One scan may show bones well. The next may show soft tissue well. A merged view can guide a doctor more than each scan on its own. Past merge tools trade off: they keep broad match high, but lose fine local form.

His tool is called W-DUALMINE. It uses two expert paths, one for each type of scan fact. Each path is weighed by how much trust its input earns. The merge also keeps the link stats of the source scans safe. A reader in health scans gets a merge plan that aims for both broad truth and fine form.
arxiv-2601-09020:
Larissa Inacio and four co-authors study a faint pull between things in salt water, and what it means in a cell. The pull is the Casimir effect, a force from wave noise in the gap. Salt was thought to screen it fast. The team shows a shared part of the pull that salt does not screen. It reaches far past what past work thought.

That far reach holds at the spans found in a cell, such as gaps near actin strands. It may shift how strands pull and push in the cell frame. A reader in bio physics gets a force they may have set to zero too soon. In salt water, faint wave pulls can act at cell scale.
arxiv-2601-09120:
Chen-Wei Liang and three co-authors build a chain to draft patent claims in more than one land's form. A claim is the part of a patent that sets what it guards. Draft tools fail on three points. They bend poor to new lands. They miss how a claim ties to past art. And their grade of a draft can not be trusted.

Their chain has three stages. Stage one weighs how the new claim ties to past art. Stage two drafts in the form of the target land. Stage three grades the draft by one shared scale. A reader in law tech gets a chain built for cross land work, with grades a team can check.
arxiv-2601-09320:
William Dorrell and Peter Latham ask how the wiring of brain like nets sets what they can learn. Such nets show in more than one brain zone, and in the smell path of bugs and the sense path of a fish. In all, a thin input fans out to a vast mid layer. A last layer then reads the fanned code to sort inputs.
