eliot-ara-vos-prec-1920:
Ara Vos Prec, published in London in 1920, gathers the poems Eliot wrote in the lean years before The Waste Land. The title, from Dante, means 'Now I pray you', and the book holds some of his sharpest short work.

Alongside French poems, it includes 'Sweeney Erect', 'A Cooking Egg', and 'Whispers of Immortality'. Sweeney, the coarse modern brute, stalks through several pieces, set against Donne, Webster, and the ghosts of a finer past. The verse is bitter, funny, and tightly made. Readers can watch Eliot's voice harden here into the one that would soon shake poetry.
eliot-poems-1920:
T. S. Eliot published Poems in 1920, gathering the short works that had first made his name in London and America. He was then working at a bank and editing a literary journal. The slim volume is the complete set of his early poems in book form.

The poems are cool, witty portraits of modern city people. Prufrock worries through a drawing-room evening, and Portrait of a Lady watches another social visit go thin and sad. Short satires mock hollow manners with clipped, musical lines. Readers in 1920 met a new kind of poetry here: ironic, learned, and quietly bleak about modern life.
eliot-sacred-wood-1920:
T. S. Eliot gathered his early criticism in this 1920 volume, and it changed how English poetry was read. These essays, written while he worked at a bank and taught evening classes, argue for a new standard of taste.

The famous piece, 'Tradition and the Individual Talent', claims a poet must absorb the whole past of literature and then surrender the self to it. 'Hamlet and His Problems' introduces the objective correlative, his test for whether a work's feelings are truly earned. Other essays rank poets and clear ground for modern verse. Few slim books of criticism have carried this much force.
europmc-pmc10817020:
Zhang and Dhalla review how swelling signals drive heart and vessel disease in this 2024 paper. Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of illness and death around the world. Certain cytokines, which are small proteins that carry signals between cells, stir up swelling, called inflammation. Three of the most studied are interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor, and the interleukin-1 family.

The review traces how these signals interact with cell stress and calcium handling inside heart cells. It covers their roles in blocked arteries, blood clots, heart attacks, and heart failure. It also covers rhythm problems such as atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven heartbeat. Proof from lab and clinic work shows these signals matter, the authors say. Whether they can serve as warning markers or drug targets is still unclear, so they call for more research.
europmc-pmc11126520:
GBD 2021 Causes of Death Collaborators break down 288 causes of death worldwide from 1990 to 2021 in this 2024 study. Regular, detailed reporting on why people die is fundamental for public health choices. Such counts also show how each cause lifts or drags life expectancy. They matter most after large death spikes such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

The analysis drew on 56,604 data sources in total. They included death registration, verbal autopsy, surveys, and cancer registries, the team reports. Verbal autopsy means interviewing families about a death's symptoms. Most cause-specific death rates were fitted with an ensemble model that blends several models. Counts cover 204 countries and 811 subnational locations by age and sex. Years of life lost were estimated for each cause. The authors say the comparisons reveal each cause's true weight.
europmc-pmc1308820:
Abernethy and co-authors validated a revised performance scale for palliative care in 2005. The Karnofsky scale is the standard for patient function. A community-focused variant suited palliative settings better. Their Australia-modified version blends both scales for any care setting.

All three scales were scored for 306 trial patients in South Australia. Ratings totaled 1,600 timepoints across settings. The median score was 60 on all three scales. The new scale agreed with the original in 87 percent of ratings. Most disagreements sat within one level on the 11-level scale. Kappa values backed the strong agreement between scales.
europmc-pmc1326220:
Fournier and co-authors compared genomes of a drug-resistant hospital bacterium in 2006. A. baumannii was drug-sensitive in the 1970s. It is now a major hospital infection threat worldwide. Two strains were sequenced: an epidemic resistant strain and a susceptible one.

The resistant strain genome measured about 3.9 million base pairs. It held an 86,000-base resistance island, the largest then known. Forty-five resistance genes clustered inside that island. The susceptible strain, linked to body lice, lacked the island. Fournier shows resistance arrived as one large acquired block. The work used full genome reads of both strains.
europmc-pmc1351920:
Hotez and co-authors argued for joining tropical disease control to big disease programs in 2006. Global funds had surged for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria. Together those three cause 5.6 million deaths yearly. They also drain 166 million disability-adjusted life years per year.

Neglected tropical diseases overlap the same poor populations. Three billion people live on under two dollars a day. The authors propose a rapid-impact package delivered alongside big-three programs. Shared delivery could cut costs and widen reach. Hotez argues success against the big three may require fighting neglected diseases too.
europmc-pmc1440920:
Some RNAs do work in the cell rather than code for proteins. Pedersen and co-authors swept the human genome for such folded RNAs in 2006. They compared our DNA with that of seven other species, from chimp to puffer fish. Their method scores shapes that stay alike across species, a sign the shape does a job.

The sweep found about 48,000 candidate structures. It caught many known working RNAs, plus 169 fresh candidates for microRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune genes. Some hits may guide chemical edits to RNA or help insert a rare building block. Pedersen warns some hits are false, but the list gives labs clear leads to test.
europmc-pmc1464820:
A gene tree and a species tree can tell different stories. Degnan and Rosenberg explored that clash in 2006. As species split, gene copies sort by chance, so a gene's history may not match the species path. They used a chance-based model of that sorting.

Their proof holds for any species tree with five or more species. For some branch lengths, the most likely gene tree differs from the species tree itself. Degnan warns that picking the most common gene tree can thus give a wrong answer with growing data. The pair close with ways to dodge this trap in genome studies.
europmc-pmc1538620:
Claudins seal the gaps between cells, and their levels shift in cancer. Hewitt, Agarwal, and Morin surveyed the whole family in 2006. They tracked all 21 human claudin genes across 266 normal and cancer tissues, using a large public database plus lab tests.

Most claudin genes spoke more softly in cancer. Three, CLDN3, CLDN4, and CLDN7, spoke louder in many cancers, including pancreas, bladder, ovary, and colon. CLDN5 ran high in blood vessel lining, a possible target for drugs that starve tumors. Hewitt flags CLDN18 as a candidate marker for stomach cancer. The survey covered the whole claudin family, in healthy tissue and in cancers.
europmc-pmc1550420:
Tiny gene tuners called microRNAs go awry in colon cancer. Bandrés and co-authors measured 156 of them in 2006, comparing tumors with nearby healthy tissue. Only a few microRNAs had known jobs, yet changed levels had been tied to cancer growth.

Thirteen microRNAs differed clearly between tumor and healthy tissue. The strongest shifts hit miR-31, miR-96, miR-133b, miR-135b, miR-145, and miR-183. Levels of miR-31 also tracked the tumor's stage. Bandrés suggests the microRNA pattern could help predict how colon tumors behave and how patients fare.  Such profiles may also help separate tumor subtypes that behave in unlike ways.
europmc-pmc1637120:
Grouping proteins into working modules from interaction webs is a crowded craft. Brohée and van Helden benchmarked four clustering algorithms in 2006. Interaction data carry false links and missing links, so tools must be robust.

They built a test web from 220 known yeast complexes, then made 41 warped versions by adding or cutting links. Four methods, MCL, RNSC, SPC, and MCODE, were run at varied settings. The team measured how sensitive each was to its parameters and to noise. Brohée gives users a grounded guide for picking settings instead of trusting defaults.
europmc-pmc1851020:
Turner, Mamo and Karlsson reviewed in 2007 how heat-loving microbes and their enzymes could power biorefineries. A biorefinery turns plant biomass into chemicals and fuels using microbes and enzymes. Hot processes mix better, dissolve feedstocks faster, and resist contamination, but most enzymes fail when heated.

Thermophiles are microbes that thrive at high temperatures, and their enzymes keep working where normal ones unfold. The review covers their use in converting carbohydrate feedstocks, with worked cases for lignocellulose, the woody part of plants, and starch. It also assesses tricks that make enzymes more heat-stable, either by changing the protein or its conditions. A final thread covers genetic vectors, the carrier DNA used to install enzyme genes in heat-loving host microbes for production.
europmc-pmc1895920:
Hagmann, Thiran and co-authors mapped in 2007 the structural wiring of whole living human brains with diffusion MRI. This scan type follows water along white matter bundles, letting researchers trace the cables between brain regions without surgery. A full connection map is a long-standing goal in neuroscience.

Their method builds large, individual connection datasets for a whole brain, usable in living or dead, human or animal subjects. For two human volunteers, the resulting networks followed an exponential pattern in how many connections each node holds. A few nodes carry many links, but the numbers fall off smoothly rather than in a long tail. Globally, both brains showed small-world organization, with short paths between any two regions. The pipeline turns one scan session into a complete network dataset per person.
europmc-pmc1978520:
Körding and co-authors asked in 2007 how the brain decides whether two senses report the same event. Seeing a movement and hearing a sound nearby may share one cause. Or they may be separate. The team built an ideal-observer model, a maths model of the best possible judge. It infers whether cues share a source and where that source lies.

Human subjects did two tasks locating sounds and sights together. The model closely predicted their non-linear way of combining cues. People integrated cues when they were close, and split them when far apart. The results show people infer causal structure during basic perception. This happens constantly and without conscious effort, not only in high-level thinking.
europmc-pmc2124920: A medical paper with a bulkhead suture of the intestine. The intestinal seam. This article preserves that surgery. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
europmc-pmc2125120: A medical paper with studies upon experimental pneumonia in rabbits, studies in immunity. The rabbit pneumonia's defense. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131120: A medical paper on the effect of antiserum against the soluble toxic substance of Bacillus coli. The E. coli antiserum. This article preserves that immunology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140420: Stomachs need acid to digest protein, and this paper measured exactly how hydrogen ion concentration governs the process. The researchers tested digestion across pH levels. The acidic breakdown, quantified. The article preserves that biochemistry research.
europmc-pmc2140720: Glowing bacteria shine brighter or dimmer with the heat, and this second study tracked temperature's effect on their light. The researchers warmed and cooled the cultures. The luminous intensity, charted. The article preserves that bacteriology research.
europmc-pmc2140820: A biology paper on the metabolism of tumors in the body. The cancers' fuel. This article preserves that oncology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2323620:
Husain and Nachev reviewed the parietal cortex in 2007, a brain region at the top and back of the head. Standard theory split brain processing into two streams, one for space and action and one for objects. Damage to the right lower parietal lobe often causes spatial neglect, where patients ignore one side of space.

The authors argued that this simple split does not fit the lower parietal lobe. They summed up brain scans and lesion studies showing plainly non-spatial jobs for this region. Those jobs include holding attention over time and spotting key events in a stream of events. Upper parietal zones do handle space and guide action. Lower zones, they concluded, do something that fits neither classic stream.
europmc-pmc2394820:
Terwilliger and colleagues described an automated structure-building wizard in 2008. In X-ray crystallography, scientists build an atomic model into an electron-density map, a cloud showing where atoms sit. They then refine the model, use it to sharpen the map, and rebuild, cycling many times.

The PHENIX AutoBuild wizard runs that whole cycle on its own. It belongs to the PHENIX software project for crystallography. The wizard works from starting phase information obtained by any of the standard routes: comparing similar crystals, using heavy-atom signals, or molecular replacement with a known structure. The authors noted that rival automated tools still struggled at low resolution and at finishing partial models. AutoBuild was built as a second-generation answer to those gaps, aiming at complete, accurate models with little manual work.
europmc-pmc2467420:
Kramer and colleagues, writing for the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance Board of Trustees Task Force on Standardized Protocols, set standard scanning protocols for heart MRI in 2008. Cardiac magnetic resonance can measure heart size, blood flow, and scar tissue, but each centre scanned differently, making results hard to compare.

The document lays out shared modules: safety and stress-test equipment, left and right heart function, contrast dye dosing, and first-pass perfusion, which tracks dye through heart muscle. It then gives disease-specific protocols. For blocked-artery disease these cover fresh heart attacks, long-standing damage and viability checks, and two drug stress methods. Further sections cover vessel imaging of the limbs and chest, abnormal coronary arteries, and lung vein checks. Valve disease, heart muscle diseases, congenital defects, and heart masses each get their own protocol.
europmc-pmc2467520:
Hooft, Straver, and Spek presented a statistical method for pinning down a molecule's absolute structure in 2008. Crystallographers can often solve a molecule's shape but not its handedness: which mirror-image form it takes. Handedness matters because the two forms of a drug can act very differently in the body.

Their approach uses Bijvoet differences, tiny intensity gaps between paired X-ray reflections that carry the handedness signal. Rather than forcing a yes-or-no call, they apply Bayesian statistics in a maximum-likelihood framework. That yields a probability for each possible structure, including the standard Flack parameter used to report the answer. The method was aimed at biologically active molecules, where weak signals are common. A probability statement, they argued, is more honest than the sharp verdicts older methods gave on thin evidence.
europmc-pmc2518220:
Curia, Longo, Biagini, Jones, and Avoli reviewed in 2008 the pilocarpine model, a standard animal model of temporal lobe epilepsy. In this model, injecting rodents with the drug pilocarpine triggers a long seizure episode. A quiet latent period follows. Finally, spontaneous recurring seizures begin. That sequence mirrors the human disease, which often follows an early injury and involves scarring in the hippocampus, a brain area central to memory.

The authors compared methods across many laboratories, since results shift with rodent species, strain, sex, age, dose, and drug combinations. They weighed death rates, timing of the first spontaneous seizures, neuron damage, and how brain networks rewired under each protocol. They conclude the model stays valuable for studying how epilepsy develops, especially if standardised to cut deaths and reduce variation.
europmc-pmc2527820:
Beckermann and colleagues asked in 2008 whether stem cells from bone marrow help pancreatic tumours grow their blood supply. These mesenchymal stem cells travel through the blood and settle in wounds and tumours, but why tumours attract them was unclear. The team tracked the cells in dishes and in mice carrying human pancreatic tumours.

The stem cells moved toward growth signals the tumours release, including PDGF and VEGF, and blocking drugs could stop that migration. Within hours they entered tumour-like spheres grown in the laboratory. Labelled cells injected into mice gathered in the tumours and interacted with vessel walls. Crucially, the cells released VEGF themselves, and tumours given them grew denser blood vessel networks. Silencing VEGF in the stem cells removed that boost.
europmc-pmc2535620:
Kan and colleagues studied daily deaths in Shanghai from 2001 to 2004 to see who is most harmed by dirty air. Four pollutants were tracked: fine particles, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone. The team asked whether season, sex, age, and schooling changed how strongly pollution tracked with mortality across the city's four years of daily records.

All four pollutants were linked to deaths from all causes and from heart and lung disease. A standard rise in particle levels, for example, came with a 0.25 percent increase in daily mortality, and the other gases showed larger effects. Pollution bit harder in the cool season than the warm one. Women, older people, and residents with little schooling proved more vulnerable than others facing the same air.
europmc-pmc2565420:
Groenewegen reviewed the basal ganglia and motor control in this 2003 paper. The basal ganglia are a set of deep brain structures, including the striatum, pallidum, substantia nigra, and subthalamic nucleus. They connect with the cortex and thalamus in a series of parallel loops that stay largely separate from one another.

Those loops serve not only movement but also thinking and emotion. Groenewegen argues a main job of the basal ganglia is learning and selecting the most fitting motor or behavioural programme for the moment. Their internal wiring suits such selection in children and adults alike. He also weighs whether childhood clumsiness partly reflects basal ganglia dysfunction, comparing their role with the cerebellum's in developing motor control.
europmc-pmc2575520:
Covington, Maloof, Straume, Kay, and Harmer combined several genome-wide data sets in 2008 to measure how much of a plant's genome its body clock controls. Earlier microarray studies of the model plant Arabidopsis disagreed wildly, putting clock control at anywhere from 5 to 15 percent of genes. The team reanalysed the experiments with standardised methods to find the true scale.

Combining data sets proved far more powerful than any single run. The unified analysis found 3,975 clock-regulated genes, and between 31 and 41 percent of all expressed genes showed circadian, roughly daily, rhythms in abundance. Clock-regulated genes clustered in hormone and stress-response pathways, suggesting the clock steers how plants answer nearly every hormone and stress. The authors also identified DNA elements in gene promoters that set the time of day each gene peaks.
europmc-pmc2630720:
van de Sande-Bruinsma and colleagues confronted antibiotic use with resistance across Europe in 2008. They reported for the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System Group and the European Surveillance of Antimicrobial Consumption Project Group. Drug effectiveness is a shared resource being eroded by overuse, and new antibiotics were drying up. The study merged the continent's two big tracking databases. One covers drug use, the other drug resistance.

They compared outpatient drug use, adjusted for population size, against resistance trends. The check covered three drug-and-germ pairs in 21 countries over 2000 to 2005. The routine tracking data did show a link. Higher national use went with higher national resistance. The authors present the joint analysis as support for steps that cut drug use at national level. They caution that country-level data cannot untangle how prescribing and resistance truly connect.
europmc-pmc2631520:
Ma and Huang proposed a statistical method in 2009 for picking reliable cancer genes by pooling several microarray studies at once. Single studies measure thousands of genes in few patients, so the marker genes they select are unstable. Pooling raises power, but studies differ in design and gene counts dwarf sample sizes. Their method, called Meta Threshold Gradient Descent Regularization, was built for exactly this setting.

The method lets each experiment keep its own settings while selecting one shared set of cancer-associated genes across all of them. It also accounts for genes acting jointly rather than one at a time. In simulations and in real pancreatic and liver cancer data sets, it outperformed existing approaches at recovering dependable markers. The authors offer it as an effective route to robust gene selection.
europmc-pmc2638020:
Barr and co-authors mapped the shapes of a large family of human proteins in work published in 2009. The proteins, called tyrosine phosphatases, remove chemical tags from other proteins and so help control cell signals. Faults in them are tied to many diseases, which makes them targets for new drugs.

The team solved the three-dimensional shapes of 22 family members and compared them with shapes known before. The basic fold was shared, yet the surfaces differed a great deal from one protein to the next. Many carried an extra pocket beside the main working site, a spot that could help drugs pick one member only. Tests of working speed also varied widely. Three members, named PTPD1, PTPD2, and HDPTP, proved unable to do the chemistry at all.
europmc-pmc2656620:
Brisse and colleagues sorted in 2009 the family lines of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a germ that lives harmlessly in many people yet causes hospital infections of urine, lungs, and blood. Some rare lines cause distinct diseases, such as a liver abscess illness spreading in Asia. Knowing which lines are dangerous could sharpen control.

The team typed 235 samples from patients and the environment, checking their genes, capsule coats, and power to sicken mice. Clear clones emerged, each tied to its own source and behavior. Two clones wearing the K1 coat linked to liver abscess and lung infection. Two nose and throat diseases each matched a single narrow clone, so those named subspecies count as clones too. One K2 clone was fiercely virulent in mice, the other not. Coat genes, it turned out, can jump between lines, blurring the coat as a danger sign.
europmc-pmc2667420:
Guh and colleagues pooled 89 studies in 2009 to measure how often overweight and obese people go on to develop other diseases. Extra weight was known to raise many risks, but firm numbers for each illness were scattered. The team searched two large databases for solid forward-looking studies and merged their results.

Eighteen linked illnesses met their standards. Overweight raised the odds of type II diabetes, most cancers, heart and vessel disease, asthma, gallbladder disease, joint wear, and chronic back pain. The strongest single link was diabetes in women, at nearly four times the risk of normal-weight women. Obesity raised the same risks further in nearly every case. Two cancers, of the food pipe and prostate, showed no clear link. The numbers give doctors and planners a shared scale for the harm done by extra weight.
europmc-pmc2771920:
Brennan and co-authors showed in 2009 that glioblastomas, the most common malignant brain tumors, fall into subclasses defined by which signaling pathways are active. Tumors grouped under one name differ widely, and sorting them by switched-on pathways could guide targeted drugs. They ran targeted protein analysis on twenty-seven surgical glioma samples, then checked the patterns against genome and expression data from two hundred forty-three tumors in The Cancer Genome Atlas.

Three subclasses emerged in roughly equal shares. One ran on EGFR signaling, with receptor amplification and mutation plus strong Notch activity. A second was driven by PDGF signaling, mostly through excess ligand. The third had lost NF1, a brake on the RAS pathway, and showed lower overall MAPK and PI3K activity. Each class matched a known gene-expression subclass, tying protein signals to signature gene changes.
europmc-pmc2791220:
Fellay and a large team, including the NIAID Center for HIV/AIDS Vaccine Immunology (CHAVI), scanned the genomes of two thousand five hundred fifty-four people with HIV-1 in 2009. They sought common DNA variants that help some people keep the virus at low levels without treatment.

The scan strongly confirmed three links found in an earlier, smaller study, and all sat in one genome region tied to immune defense. Added effects from both common and rare variants appeared in that same region, plus a cluster for virus entry receptors on chromosome three. No variant outside those areas held up, which narrowed where control of HIV-1 seems to be written in DNA.
europmc-pmc2799520:
Chen and a large team tested in 2010 whether one short DNA stretch, called ITS2, could serve as a standard barcode for naming medicinal plants. A barcode here means a short gene region whose spelling differs enough to tell species apart. The group compared seven candidate regions across medicinal species.

ITS2 copied most reliably, showed a clear gap between variation within and between species, and beat the other candidates. Tested on more than six thousand six hundred samples from four thousand eight hundred species, it named the right species in more than nine of ten cases. The team proposes ITS2 as a standard barcode for medicinal plants and a wider plant naming tool.
europmc-pmc2832020:
Khanna and colleagues found in 2010 why diabetic wounds stay inflamed instead of healing: their cleanup cells fail at eating the dead. Wound macrophages must clear away apoptotic cells, meaning cells that died on schedule, before inflammation can end. The team took macrophages from wounds of diabetic mice and tested that eating job, called efferocytosis.

Diabetic wound macrophages cleared dead cells poorly, leaving a heavy burden of them in the tissue. The same burden appeared in wound tissue from diabetic patients. Forcing extra dead cells into wounds stoked inflammatory signals and muted calming ones. When cleanup worked, macrophages switched into an anti-inflammatory mode, tying the eating job directly to healing.
europmc-pmc2841820:
Livshits and colleagues followed middle-aged British women in the Chingford Study for fifteen years to test whether blood markers of inflammation predict knee osteoarthritis seen on X-rays. Osteoarthritis, the wearing breakdown of joints, lacks any accepted early warning marker. Nearly a thousand women gave X-rays and blood at set visits across the study.

The share with clear knee damage rose from about fifteen percent to nearly half over the period. Women who developed it ran higher body weight and higher levels of two inflammation markers, CRP and IL-6. Higher IL-6 at year five independently forecast damage at year ten, alongside age and starting weight. Women in the top IL-6 quarter faced nearly triple the odds of the bottom quarter.
europmc-pmc2856220:
Hedström, Svensson, Bergström, and Michno charted every fracture treated in children and teenagers around Umeå, Sweden, in 2010, using a hospital injury database running since 1993. Over ten thousand fracture events appeared in the records through 2007. The team mapped which bones broke, how the injuries happened, and how patterns shifted with age, sex, and calendar year.

Falling caused most fractures, and the far end of the forearm was the commonest break. Rates peaked at eleven to twelve years in girls and thirteen to fourteen in boys, with boys breaking bones half again as often as girls. Fracture incidence rose about thirteen percent over the decade to 2007, which the authors partly blame on changing activity patterns in children.
europmc-pmc2877420:
Limmathurotsakul and colleagues tracked in 2010 a rising tide of melioidosis, a severe soil-borne infection, in northeast Thailand. The culprit is Burkholderia pseudomallei, a bacterium living in soil and water that enters through skin cuts. They counted every culture-confirmed case admitted to the region's main hospital across a decade.

More than twenty-two hundred cases gave an average rate near thirteen per hundred thousand people a year. The rate climbed steadily, from about eight to over twenty-one per hundred thousand across the study years. Men, people over forty-five, and people with diabetes, known or hidden, faced the highest risk. Deaths ran above forty percent, making melioidosis the region's third deadliest infection after HIV and tuberculosis by 2006.
europmc-pmc2901520:
Egecioglu and co-authors showed in 2010 that the hunger hormone ghrelin also drives craving for tasty food through the brain's reward hub. They targeted the ventral tegmental area, a midbrain node that feeds dopamine to reward circuits. Mice missing the ghrelin receptor and rats given a receptor blocker both ate less of a rewarding food when offered a free choice against plain chow.

Rewarding food normally triggers a dopamine surge in the accumbens, a reward center, and that surge vanished in receptor-free mice. Injecting ghrelin straight into the hub boosted one-hour intake of rewarding food but not of chow. Blocking the receptor also killed the learned place preference for the tasty food. Hunger chemistry thus sets how much pleasure food is worth pursuing.
europmc-pmc2912920:
Arain, Campbell, Cooper, and Lancaster asked in 2010 what a pilot or feasibility study actually is, after finding the terms used loosely across medicine. A 2004 review had urged that such small preliminary studies stick to description and sample size planning rather than testing treatments. The team re-screened seven major journals for 2007 and 2008 and also surveyed trial registries, funders, and editors.

Fifty-four pilot or feasibility papers turned up, about half of them pilot trials of interventions. Practice had barely budged: many still ran hypothesis tests their small samples cannot support. Worse, registries, grant bodies, and journals each defined the terms differently, and some had no policy at all. The authors press for shared definitions so pilots do the sizing and feasibility work they exist for.
europmc-pmc2919420:
David and colleagues, working in Cynthia Kenyon's laboratory, reported in 2010 that ordinary proteins clump with age in the worm C. elegans, not just the disease proteins famous for aggregating. Sticky clumps define Alzheimer's and similar illnesses, yet whether normal aging itself is clumping-prone was unknown. Using systematic proteomics, the team separated the insoluble fraction of young and old worms and named its contents.

Several hundred normal proteins became insoluble and aggregation-prone as the worms aged. The set was not random debris: it was rich in proteins that influence how other proteins fold and clump. In tests, these age-clumped proteins nudged disease-linked proteins toward aggregation and worsened their toxicity. Aging itself tilts the whole protein pool toward clumping, which may explain why age is the master risk factor for aggregation diseases.
europmc-pmc2919520:
Cornuet, Ravigné, and Estoup upgraded in 2010 DIYABC, software that infers population history from genetic data using approximate Bayesian computation. The approach simulates millions of datasets under competing histories, like splits and admixtures between populations, and keeps the histories whose simulations resemble the real data. Version 1.0 widens what the software can digest and, crucially, lets users check whether a chosen model actually fits.

It now accepts DNA sequence data alongside microsatellites and handles five locus types, including sex-linked and mitochondrial markers with balanced or skewed sex ratios. Simulated tests showed mixing data types can sharpen scenario choice and parameter estimates. The new model-checking step, long neglected in this field, flags histories that merely win a contest without truly explaining the data.
europmc-pmc2949620:
Drummond and Suchard introduced a Bayesian method for dating family trees when evolution speeds up and slows down across branches, in a 2010 article. Strict clock models assume one steady rate, an idea real lineages often break.

Their approach lays many local clocks over different parts of a tree and averages over the possible placements using computer sampling, while estimating the tree itself at the same time. That setup lets users test the single-rate idea directly against a huge range of alternatives. Worked examples cover mammal, primate, and influenza histories, with new ways to display the resulting rate patterns.
europmc-pmc2954820:
Huang, Lee, Marcotte, and Hurles mapped genes where losing one copy matters, a state called haploinsufficiency, in a 2010 genome study. One working copy is not always enough, and such genes cause many dominant diseases.

They contrasted several hundred known sensitive genes with over a thousand genes repeatedly damaged in healthy people, so judged tolerant. Sensitive genes tended to be longer, more conserved, busier in early development, and more connected in gene networks. A model built on those traits scored all genes, and high scorers indeed clustered among dominant disease genes and mouse lines with faults from a single lost copy.
europmc-pmc3009720:
Globisch and co-authors measured a sixth DNA base, hydroxymethylcytosine, across mouse tissues in a 2010 study. They also hunted for further bases. Such bases would prove an active removal pathway for methylation marks. The new base forms from the classic methyl mark, and its job was unknown.

Using an ultra-sensitive isotope method, they found the base in every tissue and cell type, richest in brain nerve cells. The expected follow-on bases of a stepwise removal chain were essentially absent, arguing against that demethylation route. The base looks more like a stable feature of nerve cells than a passing step.
europmc-pmc3117820:
Ralf Hass and colleagues compared human repair cells drawn from adult and newborn tissues in a 2011 mini-review in Cell Communication and Signaling. These versatile cells, found near blood vessels in most tissues, can renew themselves, turn into several cell types, and calm immune responses. Sources range from bone marrow and fat to placenta and cord tissue.

The review contrasts the sources on growth speed, surface markers, and range of cell types they can form. Neighbouring cells, low oxygen, and small regulatory RNAs all shift how each population behaves, so cells from different tissues are not interchangeable. For doctors hoping to use them in healing, the paper maps which source suits which job and what still needs testing.
europmc-pmc3139420:
Craig Johnson and colleagues found a hidden protein in a pig virus in a 2011 paper in the Journal of General Virology. The virus causes the most costly swine disease worldwide, harming breeding and breathing, yet its protein set was thought complete. Suspecting a missed reading frame, the team purified virus particles and searched them for unknown pieces.

Ali Zomorrodi and Costas Maranas introduced OptCom, a framework for modeling the metabolism of microbial communities, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. Microbes rarely live alone, yet what each member contributes to a community's chemistry, and who trades what with whom, remains poorly understood despite abundant sequencing data. Existing models typically optimized a single goal, which misrepresents real communities.

It handles any mix of cooperative and competitive interactions and any number of species. Ian Holmes, Keith Harris, and Christopher Quince introduced Dirichlet multinomial mixtures, a statistical model for microbial community data, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Metagenomic surveys produce tables counting how often each organism appears in each sample, tables that are sparse and uneven in size. Older clustering methods ignored those quirks, so the authors built a generative model that respects them.

Each community is described by a probability profile over taxa, drawn from one of a few mixture components; the components act as community types, sometimes called enterotypes. Annette Michalski and colleagues introduced the Q Exactive, a benchtop mass spectrometer for proteomics, in this 2011 paper in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics. Protein analysis by mass spectrometry demands speed, sensitivity, and resolution at once. The new instrument couples a quadrupole mass filter, which selects ions almost instantly, to an Orbitrap analyzer, which weighs them with high precision, a pairing not reported before.

Abrantes, van der Loo, Le Pendu, and Esteves reviewed a fast killing rabbit disease and the virus behind it, in a 2012 article. The virus first appeared in China in 1984 and swept the world, killing adult European rabbits within two to three days of infection. Australia and New Zealand even released it on purpose to control pest rabbits.

Infected rabbits die mainly of acute liver destruction, with bleeding in lungs, heart, and kidneys from runaway clotting. All deadly strains form a single type, though two subtypes circulate, and harmless relatives may have come first. No other species is known to die of it. Control in rabbit farms rests on vaccination and strict hygiene, which are hard to apply to wild rabbits. The review gathers what is known about the virus's spread, evolution, and possible future use as a medical tool.

Lawrence and colleagues ran tests to see whether living with other species changes how a population adapts to a new setting. Most lab studies of adaptation use one species alone, yet in the wild organisms always adapt in company. The team therefore grew bacterial communities side by side with matching single-species cultures and watched how each changed.

Species changing together did not follow the path they took alone. Community members shifted toward split, complementary use of resources, carving up the setting rather than all chasing the same solution. Those shifts also changed how the whole system worked. The results say adaptation in nature cannot always be foretold from single-species tests.

fitzgerald-flappers-and-philosophers-192:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published Flappers and Philosophers in 1920, riding the instant success of his first novel. The eight stories had mostly run in The Saturday Evening Post, which paid him handsomely. Together they form the flapper canon in its first collected form.

Bernice Bobs Her Hair turns a dull cousin's visit into a small war of popularity, ending with scissors. The Offshore Pirate sails a rich girl into a staged romance that turns real. Other tales cover icy debutantes, headstrong boys, and young people testing every rule their parents kept. Fitzgerald's dialogue sparkles, but regret already shadows the fun. The book defined the Jazz Age heroine for America.
fitzgerald-this-side-of-paradise-1920:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published This Side of Paradise in 1920, when he was twenty-three and fresh out of the army. The novel grew from his Princeton years and his courtship of Zelda Sayre. It sold out its first printing in days and made him the spokesman of his generation.

Amory Blaine, handsome and self-absorbed, drifts through prep school, Princeton, and the war, falling in and out of love and ambition. The book mixes prose, verse, and play script with youthful confidence. Amory ends poorer, sadder, and beginning to understand himself. Fitzgerald named a generation's restlessness here and invented the Jazz Age novel in the process.
frus-1861-d120:
Charles Faulkner, the outgoing American minister to France, wrote to Secretary of State Jeremiah Black on 19 March 1861. The letter is document 120 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Faulkner wrote in the last days of the Buchanan order in Paris. Within weeks Seward would replace Black, and Dayton would replace Faulkner. The letter marks the old guard handing over the most delicate post in Europe as the Union split. Faulkner's Virginia roots made his loyalty a point of talk in that tense spring. Loyalty in that spring was a coin whose worth each man's acts would fix.
frus-1861-d20:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford on 26 March 1861. Sanford was the new American minister to Belgium, based in Brussels. The letter is document 20 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford was an eager, well connected envoy who made Brussels a listening post for the Union. Seward's March letter belongs to the first set of orders sent to Lincoln's new men abroad. It set the terms on which Sanford would watch Europe for the Union cause. Sanford later raised funds and arms for the Union on his own bold account.
frus-1861-d220:
Guidance for Mr. Marsh left Washington on 20 September 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 220 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d120:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 August 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 120 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d20:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 17 February 1862, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 20 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d220:
William Stuart answered on 25 June 1862 with a letter to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 220 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting head of the British legation during Lord Lyons's absence.

A stand-in envoy walks a fine line, firm for his government yet careful not to commit it too far. Stuart's letters show that care in formal, measured prose. His reply came as the Seven Days battles opened outside Richmond. News that soon reached Washington and sharpened every question between the two governments that summer. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d320:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 28 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 320 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote on the first day of the second Bull Run battle, in a Paris still working from July's picture of the war. His report adds the French court's reading at the very moment the facts were changing across the ocean. Papers like this one, filed late in the volume, reward readers who follow dates rather than document order. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d420:
From the American legation in Madrid, Horace J. Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 May 1862. The dispatch is Document 420 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Late May brought word of Union advances in Virginia and the West, and Perry's job was to make that news count in Spain. Spanish officials also had to weigh France's deepening grip on Mexico, next door to their own stake in the Americas. Reports of this kind gave the State Department its picture of Madrid's mood. They are worth reading as the ground-level half of a conversation whose other half is Seward's string of instructions.
frus-1862-d520:
Two days after Antietam, on 19 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 520 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record.

Seward wrote before the battle's full result was known in Washington, let alone its meaning abroad. His orders in that week kept to first principles: the Union would win, foreign interference was unwelcome, and neutral duties must be honored. Pike at The Hague would soon have better news to use, including Lincoln's emancipation order of 22 September. The dispatch catches the correspondence mid-turn, as the autumn's new facts began their slow journey into every legation's instructions.
frus-1862-d620:
Jacob S. Haldeman, the American minister at Stockholm, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 December 1861. It is Document 620 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Swedish file.

Haldeman served the joint kingdom of Sweden and Norway, a poor, seafaring north whose people were then emigrating to America in growing numbers. His December report reached Washington in the Trent winter, when every court's attitude was being tallied. Sweden's sympathy for the Union was genuine and its weight small, a combination that made for pleasant, undemanding correspondence. The letter begins the volume's Scandinavian file, the far edge of the Department's European map.
frus-1862-d720:
On 6 November 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Friedrich Hassaurek, the American minister in Ecuador. The letter is document 720 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last paper in this part of the volume. It answers Hassaurek's dispatch of early October.

Seward's reply closed the Ecuador file for the year in the printed record. His outward letters set the brief for each post; for a far Pacific legation, they also carried the news of home that an envoy needed. This one shows the full span of the State Department's reach in 1862. It ran from the courts of Europe to a lone post high in the Andes.
frus-1863p1-d120:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 16 March 1863 to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 120 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of the day took the next head of the brief in line. Seward's points for London were the war's points in Europe: fair dealing, the blockade's rights, and the warships in British yards. This letter holds its slice of that work. In the row of four it is a mid-piece, and its worth is in the row as much as in itself.
frus-1863p1-d20:
On 25 December 1862, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London. A Christmas Day dispatch is a fair sign of how full the legation's plate was. The letter is document 20 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams closed the year with reports on the ground he had held: Britain had not backed the South, and its government trod with care. His letters also tracked the press and the public mood, which Seward weighed with the cabinet's acts. This dispatch ends the 1862 run of the London file in the volume, a quiet cap to a year of strain.
frus-1863p1-d220:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 22 June 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 220 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d320:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 12 November 1862. The note is document 320 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The questions reaching the British legation were the war's daily friction: stopped ships, seized cargoes, arrested men, and the rights of a neutral flag. Stuart's letters deal with that traffic. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d420:
Washington's business with Britain on 23 March 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 420 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Notes on this route often dealt with single ships, single cargoes, or single men. Small cases mattered, because each one tested what neutrality would allow. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d520:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State sent an official note to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 20 May 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d620:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State sent an official note to William Stuart, the British chargé d'affaires in Washington on 16 September 1863. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d120: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on November 12, 1943, and a second Stalin letter of the same date follows it in the volume. This one is Document 120 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two letters in a day from Moscow, as the president sailed, suggests urgent or divided business, though the record names no topic for either. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d20: T. V. Soong, China's Minister of Foreign Affairs, wrote to Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, on June 21, 1943. The message is Document 20 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hopkins was Roosevelt's closest aide, and foreign envoys often worked through him. The catalog's title carries no date; its older note supplies June 21. No topic is recorded, so the note's errand must be read in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d220:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt cabled Washington from Ankara on 14 November 1943, in telegram 1871, sent an hour after his previous report that day. It carries one hopeful signal from the Soviet ambassador in Ankara, Sergey Vinogradov, about Turkey's fears of Russia.

Vinogradov had told Foreign Minister Numan that if Turkey's worry was only about excessive Soviet demands in the Balkans, and not a general mistrust, a fair settlement should be easy to find. Numan answered that if Ankara could be sure Russia held no ambitions in the Balkans, the two countries could resume the cordial, close friendship they had shared for many years. The cable was repeated to Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d320:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 408/1 at Cairo on 26 November 1943, answering the American proposal for a supreme commander over all operations against Germany. After careful study, they state at once that on military grounds they profoundly disagree.

Total war, they argue, is not a military affair alone. Nearly every big problem carries political, economic, and domestic weight. The commander would have to consult both governments on almost everything. He would become an extra link deciding only minor matters. The Foch parallel from the last war fails, since Foch never held so many fronts. They also attack the clause letting the Combined Chiefs reverse his orders, warning of troops marching on orders later countermanded in confusion.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d420:
John Jernegan, third secretary of the American embassy in Iran, wrote to Major John Henry at Tehran on 3 December 1943. Henry was General Hurley's aide. The letter sets down the main facts behind the Declaration on Iran, signed two days before, as far as Jernegan's knowledge ran. It is the fullest inside account of how that document came to be.

Prime Minister Soheily asked Eden and Dreyfus on 29 November for a joint statement covering Iran's help in the war, the treaty pledges of independence, and her economic needs. Hurley won British agreement, and Dreyfus supplied the draft, shortened from Jernegan's own. The Soviets hung back until Roosevelt made a strong personal request of Stalin on 1 December and Stalin consented. That night the draft was accepted with small changes, signed at the final session's end, and shown to Foreign Minister Saed, who initialed a copy and agreed to hold its release.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d520:
President Roosevelt wrote to Brendan Bracken, Britain's Minister of Information, on December 18, 1943. Bracken was one of Churchill's closest friends and ran Britain's wartime information and propaganda effort. The letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A letter from an American president to a British cabinet minister outside the usual chain shows the personal web that bound the two governments. Bracken stood near the center of Churchill's circle, and Roosevelt knew the value of that friendship. For readers, the message is a reminder that the alliance was held together by personal ties as well as by treaties, staffs, and formal notes.
frus-1944-quebec-d120:
In telegram 780, sent the same evening as his personal appeal, Churchill forwarded Roosevelt the text of a War Cabinet message to Moscow. The British government had cabled the Soviet leadership about Warsaw on September 4, 1944. Churchill wanted the president to see exactly what London had said before the Quebec Conference.

The message told Moscow that British public opinion was deeply moved by Warsaw's suffering. It said people could not understand why no material help had reached the Poles, or why Soviet-held airfields were closed to American aircraft. If the Poles were overwhelmed within days, the shock would be incalculable. The refusal, London said, clashed with the spirit of Allied cooperation.
frus-1944-quebec-d20:
President Roosevelt replied to Prime Minister Churchill on August 8, 1944. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, among the letters preparing the September conference.

Roosevelt answered from a Washington intoxicated by victory in France yet facing hard choices: how fast to press Germany, how to treat liberated France, and how to supply the final campaigns. His August letters to Churchill mixed command decisions with the politics of the alliance. For readers, this reply shows the President setting the terms on which the two leaders would meet at Quebec a month later.
frus-1944-quebec-d220:
Roosevelt's memorandum of September 20, 1944, is only a few lines long. Its substance is the map attached to it, reproduced in the volume. On that map the president drew lines and notations in red, blue, and green pencil, sketching his own idea for dividing Germany after the peace.

The editors call it, in Roosevelt's words, a very rough suggestion made by him, among others, for a subdivision of Germany. The map is probably the one he was working on with three colored pencils when Morgenthau called at noon on September 15. It shows the zones question being settled not only in conference papers but in the president's own hand.
frus-1945-50-intel-d120:
The National Intelligence Authority wrote to Attorney General Clark on 8 August 1946. The board addressed the cabinet officer who oversaw the FBI, in the middle of the Latin American dispute. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A letter from the whole authority carried the combined weight of State, War, and Navy. Sent to Clark, it told the Justice Department where the board stood on the division of foreign intelligence work. Readers have reached the ruling stage of the summer's fight. The papers that follow, Hoover's protests and Leahy 's direction, show the ruling being received. Few episodes in the volume display the 1946 system working as designed so completely.
frus-1945-50-intel-d20:
Secretary of War Robert Patterson and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal wrote jointly to Secretary of State Byrnes on 29 September 1945. Two cabinet officers signing one letter is itself a signal. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The military departments wrote together because the OSS order had pushed them into a shared corner. The War Department held the spy units, the Navy its own services. Both faced a State Department newly armed with analysts. A joint letter shows the two services settling their differences to face the civilians as one. Readers see coalition building at cabinet level, the necessary first step before the long negotiation over a central intelligence system could begin.
frus-1945-50-intel-d220:
A memorandum from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) reached the National Intelligence Authority on 11 September 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 220 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d320:
On 17 July 1947 the 14th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 320 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. For a reader now, the draw is the nearness: this is the meeting as its own staff chose to keep it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d420:
On 2 May 1950, W. Park Armstrong wrote again to Under Secretary of State James Webb. The memo is document 420 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By the spring of 1950 the shape of American intelligence was still open to change. The State Department's share of that work depended on aides like Armstrong making their case in writing. His May memo is one more round in a long contest over who would speak for the facts abroad. Weeks later the Korean War began, and debates like this one turned at once into wartime tasks.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d120:
President Roosevelt pushed back on the Germany planners in this private memorandum of 29 September 1944. Writing to the Secretary of State, he questions the rush to settle the treatment of German industry. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

No good purpose, he says, would be served by sounding out British and Russian views just now. The European Advisory Commission, in such a case, sits on a tertiary level, not even a secondary one. The real nub is keeping Britain out of complete bankruptcy when the war ends. He also attacks a leak: somebody has told the press that Germany is to be made wholly agricultural, and, he insists, no one wants that.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d20: Churchill replied to Roosevelt on 16 November 1944, two days after the president's last letter. Document 20 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta preserves his side of the exchange, as published by the Office of the Historian. The November letters show both men turning from campaign season toward the practical questions of where and when the Big Three would meet.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d220:
Ten billion dollars, not six: the Treasury raised Moscow's bid in this memorandum to the President of 10 January 1945. “A $10 Billion Reconstruction Credit for the U. S. S. R.” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It argues that Russia can pay, chiefly in goods America lacks.

The credit would buy reconstruction goods in the United States, at two percent interest over thirty-five years. Repayment would come mainly in strategic raw materials that are short at home. Russia's means are set out in three parts. She can sell those scarce materials. She can earn dollars through tourist trade, exports, and a favorable balance with the world. And she holds a gold stock put at two billion dollars, with yearly output in the hundreds of millions.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d320:
President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill joined the Combined Chiefs of Staff at Malta on February 2, 1945, to review an interim report. Roosevelt praised how much the military talks had achieved in so short a time. The leaders then went through the report paragraph by paragraph.

One clause on basic pledges drew debate. General Marshall warned about the British wording. It put supplies for freed areas on the same level as battle needs, beyond what was required to stop sickness and unrest. That shift, he argued, would change the claim those supplies had on scarce shipping and gear. The record catches a president and a prime minister doing staff work, line by line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d420:
Bohlen left only three words for one Yalta luncheon — no notes available — and this editorial note builds what it can around them. Times and guests come from the official trip log. Admiral Leahy's memoir supplies more: the talk centered on voting procedure in the assembly of the planned world body.

Churchill, Leahy writes, agreed orally to an arrangement at that lunch. The United States, Britain, and the Soviet republics would hold equal voting power in the assembly. A mark on Hiss's notes for the afternoon plenary confirms the subject was live that day. The note shows editors squeezing a key bargain out of a memoir's single paragraph.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d120:
Charles Bohlen confirmed Ambassador Harriman's place at Berlin in a telegram sent July 4, 1945, over Secretary Byrnes's signature. The message is document 120 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Harriman had twice asked whether the President and the Secretary wanted him at the meeting, and had heard nothing since Stettinius resigned.

Both the President and Byrnes desire him present, Bohlen writes, and he should bring Edward Page with him. Washington also thinks Harriman should reach Berlin a day or two early to look over housing and arrangements for the civilian staff. Official instructions will follow. The short cable ended the ambassador's anxious wait and put his knowledge of the Russians at Truman's service.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d20:
Truman opened the Hopkins mission in this top secret message to Stalin of May 19, 1945. He was sure Stalin shared his sense of the difficulty of dealing, by exchange of messages, with the complicated questions they faced. Pending a possible meeting, he was sending Harry Hopkins with Ambassador Harriman to Moscow. They would discuss these matters personally with Stalin.

Hopkins would return immediately to Washington to report to the President in person. They planned to arrive in Moscow about May 26. Truman asked whether that time suited Stalin. The message, sent by Navy channels, revived Roosevelt's most trusted channel for the hardest errand of the spring.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d220:
The British Chiefs of Staff laid out the daily rhythm for the staff talks in a memorandum dated July 15, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/9, is document 220 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It was drawn up at Babelsberg as the delegations gathered.

Following past practice, each side's chiefs would hold their own meetings in the morning. The Combined Chiefs of Staff would meet together at 2:30 in the afternoon. The attached program runs four days. First come the Japanese situation and Pacific operations. Then come British participation and command questions. Next come basic objectives and other nations' roles. Last come the directive to the Southeast Asia commander, Russian participation, and the planning date for the war's end. An editor's note lists the subjects the Soviet delegation asked to add when Truman met Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d320:
Finland is the subject of a short memorandum written at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945, by Thompson, a secretary at the London embassy, for Assistant Secretary Dunn. Stalin, it recalls, had told Churchill on June 14 that he saw no reason to delay restoring diplomatic relations with Finland. Finland, Stalin said, was meeting the armistice terms.

The memo argues that the United States stands in a stronger position than its allies. America had never been at war with Finland, though it broke off relations in June 1944. Thompson urged that Washington resume ties as soon as it could do so without badly offending the Russians, and use the conference to clear the way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d420:
President Truman's coal message to Churchill is transmitted in a Washington cable to Winant of June 24, 1945. The coal famine threatening Europe this coming winter, Truman writes, has impressed him with the urgency of the problem. He proposes directing the military authorities in Germany to exert every effort to raise German coal production.

All coal above minimum German needs, he urges, should go for export. Without immediate concentration on German coal, he warns, turmoil and unrest will strike the very areas of western Europe on which the continent's stability depends. Truman also proposes like pressure on France and Belgium to raise their own output, and a directive to his own commander.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d520:
Poland's claims and allied control collide in Dunn's memorandum to the Secretary, written at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945. At present, Dunn writes, Marshal Zhukov claims he has no control over the areas of eastern Germany which have been unilaterally placed under Polish administration. Those areas contain the mining resources of Upper Silesia and a large part of Germany's food surpluses.

Before any joint economic policy for Germany can be agreed, whether on reparations or on the Control Council's responsibilities, it is necessary to know what Germany those policies relate to. This government, Dunn states, approves in principle territorial adjustment for Poland's benefit, but opposes unilateral action in this as in other territorial settlements.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d620:
Edwin Pauley, the U.S. member of the Allied reparations body in Moscow, wired the Secretary of State on June 24, 1945. His top secret message is document 620 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It links East European farm and oil goods to the war against Japan.

Pauley says the U.S. has in effect waived reparations claims on Rumania and Hungary, save for harm to U.S. property. Yet U.S. occupation forces in Germany are fed and fueled from America. Rumania, Hungary, and Austria hold surplus oil and farm goods that could supply them instead. If the Soviets, who expect some of those goods as reparations, passed them on as reverse lend-lease, two gains would follow. The war on Japan would be helped, and the net sum drawn from Germany would rise.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1020:
Soviet delegates circulated this proposal on the Königsberg area at Potsdam on July 22, 1945. It records approval of a Soviet request on East Prussia's future. Pending final settlement at the peace settlement, part of Germany's Baltic coast would pass to the Soviet Union.

The new Soviet western border would run from a point on the western shore of Danzig Bay. From there it passes eastward, north of Braunsberg and Goldap. It ends where the borders of Lithuania, Poland, and former East Prussia meet. The line would give the Soviet Union the northern part of East Prussia, with the city of Königsberg.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1120:
The Soviet team tabled this formal proposal on 18 July 1945, the second day of the Potsdam Conference. Early papers staked out each side's opening demands. Only later did the real trading begin, once all three teams had shown their first hands.

Moscow came to Germany set on gaining ground after the Soviet Union's vast losses in the war. Its dead ran into the tens of millions, a fact its envoys raised often. A proposal from the opening round shows the Soviet bid in its first, fullest form. Later papers can then be measured against it to see what the bargaining wore away.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1220:
Hurley wrote to the Secretary of State on 29 July 1945. His dispatches from China came often that summer. Each carried the state of a country split between a Nationalist government and communist armies, with Japan's defeat near and civil war looming behind it.

The secretary read China news beside the German bargaining. The two files met in Soviet intentions, which touched both. This cable is one piece of that dual picture. It shows an envoy at a hard post keeping his chief informed in the summit's last days. The crisis he reported would outlast the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1320:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 20 July 1945. Formal papers were the currency of the summit: each one a claim in writing, offered for the other teams to take, amend, or refuse. This one came at the end of the first week.

By then the American stands on the chief questions were known, and drafting had turned to terms that might close. A proposal of this date belongs to that sharpening phase. It survives in the official record in the team's own words. Readers can weigh it against the final protocol to see what the week of trading did to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1420:
Herschel Johnson, the American minister in Sweden, wrote to the secretary of state on 6 July 1945. Johnson's post in Stockholm kept Washington in touch with a neutral capital close to the war's edge. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Neutral capitals were listening posts in 1945, full of envoys, rumors, and quiet feelers from all sides. A minister's letter from Stockholm in the week before Potsdam adds that northern view to the volume. Readers meet a lesser-known channel here: the reports that flowed in from the war's margins. It sometimes carried word of moves the main capitals had not yet seen. It widens the map before the summit papers begin.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-120:
John McCloy, the Assistant Secretary of War, wrote to Secretary of State James Byrnes on July 27, 1945. McCloy was one of the War Department's most trusted hands. He dealt with occupation problems and the hard seams between war and peace. His letter reached Byrnes at Potsdam in the conference's final week.

Letters between the War and State chiefs show the two machines meshing. Armies would have to run much of what diplomats agreed. McCloy wrote with that burden in view. Readers get a senior soldier-administrator's voice, direct and practical. The exchange stands in the second Potsdam volume, among the papers that shaped the closing days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-20:
An extract from Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes of July 19, 1945, covers what war facts to give the Russians. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The subject had split the U.S. and British chiefs in the papers printed in volume one.

General Hull told the chiefs that Britain wanted facts passed to Moscow on a combined basis. That, he said, had not been the Joint Chiefs' policy. Two intelligence reports on Japan were in hand, one combined and one purely American. Hull doubted the British would agree to hand over the combined report itself. He thought the U.S. chiefs would be willing to give Moscow the American report instead. General Marshall guessed at a British motive beneath the dispute. London, he thought, cared more about facts on special projects than about operational intelligence.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d720:
Document 720 is Hurley's letter to the Secretary of State dated August 1, 1945. The Potsdam Conference adopted its final protocol that day. Hurley wrote from China, where the war against Japan still ran. His letter joined the closing run of the second Potsdam volume's China papers.

Last-day timing gives the letter a hinge quality. It looks back at the conference and ahead to what followed. Readers see an ambassador positioning his mission for the peace. The document reminds us that Potsdam's choices landed worldwide. Embassies everywhere had to live with them, starting at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d820:
Melbourne reported from Rumania on July 26, 1945, in document 820. The acting representative in Bucharest wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His letters reach a near-daily rhythm in the volume's second week. This one joined the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

By late July, Melbourne's reports form a chronicle. Each adds a day's facts to a worsening file. Readers can watch a mission's position erode in real time. The document shows the worth of that persistence. Because he kept writing, the record of Rumania's turning is full. Silence would have served the other side.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d920:
Soviet delegates circulated this plan of reparations from Germany at the foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945. It sets a total sum of 20 billion dollars for consideration. About half would come from one-time removals of German national wealth within two years of the surrender. The rest would come as yearly deliveries in kind over ten years.

The plan prices the removals by industry, from war and chemical plants to foreign investments and shares. Yearly goods would include coal, sugar, chemicals, cattle, cement, and timber. Prices rest on 1938 levels, with set markups. The exchange rate is fixed at 3.5 marks to the dollar.
frus-1952-54v13p2-d820: A 1952-1954 FRUS editorial note from the Indochina volume's second part. Dien Bien Phu's shadow fell. This note provides that context. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
galsworthy-in-chancery-1920:
John Galsworthy continued his Forsyte family saga with In Chancery, published in 1920. The novel follows The Man of Property and the short piece Indian Summer of a Forsyte. Galsworthy tracked the rich, possessive Forsytes across decades of English change.

Soames Forsyte, divorced from Irene, wants an heir and pursues the young Annette Lamont. Irene, meanwhile, finds late love with Soames's cousin Jolyon, now head of the family's other branch. Old bitterness poisons every new happiness, and the war years hang over the younger generation. Galsworthy shows a proud family slowly learning that money cannot settle matters of the heart.
gao-gaoreports-b-295620: Spotless Janitorial Services mopped up a February 2005 protest at GAO, and the ruling is the call. The cleaners' grievance got scrubbed through the full review. The floors of justice were spotless. The ruling was squeaky clean. The review was thorough.
gao-gaoreports-b-298020: IPlus doubled its June 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer each, and the record stays clean.
gao-gaoreports-b-298720: Midland Supply doubled its November 2006 protest — two case numbers, one supply fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299720: Carson Helicopter Services fought a July 2007 award at GAO — two case numbers, one rotorcraft prize — and the combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the agency's pick; the call weighs each claim. Helicopter deals draw high-stakes protests; GAO's verdict lands the dispute.
gao-gaoreports-b-299820: PWC Logistics Services doubled its 2007 protest — two case numbers, one fight over a supply-chain deal — and GAO's combined ruling settles both.
