plos-pone-0341920:
Spotting strange traffic on a computer network early can stop attacks before damage spreads. Debiao Luo and co-authors combine several techniques into one detection system, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper on network safety.

Raw traffic is first broken into smoother waves to remove noise. A hybrid network then reads the signal two ways at once: attention heads catch far-apart links, while a memory network reads the sequence in both directions. A firefly-inspired search tunes the system's settings automatically. On standard test data the combined model beat earlier methods on both error rates and detection scores, with gains the authors checked statistically.
plos-pone-0343920:
Imane Bagheri, Atena Dadgari, and Naiire Salmani interviewed palliative care staff in 2026 about death doulas, non medical companions for dying people. Cancer patients at the end of life and their families often need more support than clinical teams can give.

Fourteen staff members described what must exist before the role can work: drivers pushing for it, proper recruiting and training, and basic structures to host it. Challenges included families not knowing the role and officials not recognising it formally. The study gives planners a grounded checklist for introducing doulas without confusion about who does what at the bedside.
plos-pone-0345620:
Juliana Amorim and colleagues hunt for new antibacterial compounds in nature's chemistry library, in this 2026 PLOS ONE computer study. Their target is an enzyme Staphylococcus aureus needs to make its golden pigment, which shields the bacterium from immune attack; blocking the enzyme should weaken the germ rather than kill it outright.

Starting from nearly three hundred thousand natural products, shape-based screening and then activity models narrowed the field to about two thousand strong candidates, with a few dozen predicted to bind extremely tightly. Five finalists held stable grips on the enzyme in molecular simulations. The list gives chemists concrete starting points for lab testing against a pathogen known for drug resistance.
plos-pone-0345720:
Md Yasin and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One paper on predicting two key measures of knitted cotton fabric before it is finished. Mills need to know a fabric's final width and its weight per square meter, yet both shift during production. The authors built a fuzzy logic model that takes stitch length, yarn fineness, and machine diameter as inputs.

The model was trained on more than thirty thousand real production records and then checked against fresh factory data. Its predictions landed very close to the actual width and weight values. Because the system rests on proven factory data rather than lab trials alone, the authors present it as a practical planning tool for textile mills that want fewer surprises in finished cloth.
plos-pone-0346820:
Mian Li and co-workers simulate, atom by atom, what happens when a common clay mineral soaks up water. The mineral, illite, is plentiful in oil shale, and its swelling can weaken rock. Their 2026 study runs computer models that vary heat, pressure, and water amount to watch the mineral's size, density, and stiffness change.

Water pushed the crystal to swell mostly along one direction. Pressure held the swelling back, while heat and more water sped it up. The mineral grew stiffer under pressure and softer as heat or water rose. Knowing these micro-level rules helps engineers judge rock stability for oil work and building projects where wet clay can cause trouble.
plos-pone-0347020:
Nasser A M Barakat and co-authors built a new electrode material in 2026 for turning urea in wastewater into energy. Urea is a common pollutant from farms and factories, and breaking it down with electricity can clean water while recovering power.

Thin carbon fibers were spun with nickel particles, plus phosphorus and nitrogen from a cheap starting chemical. Heat treatment tuned the nickel surface into a form ready for the reaction. In alkaline tests the best mix started working at low voltage and carried a strong current. Pairs of dirty water treatment and energy recovery make such catalysts worth developing further.
plos-pone-0348220:
Fanwei Meng and Bing Chen review infections picked up in hospital by children kept alive on heart-lung machines after heart surgery. The machines, known as ECMO, support children born with heart defects while they heal. Their 2026 study covers fifty-four children at one Chinese heart hospital over five years and compares those who caught infections with those who did not.

Fourteen children developed infections, mostly lung infections from tough Gram-negative bacteria. Having a breathing tube placed before surgery stood out as the one clear risk factor in the final analysis. Longer intensive care stays also appeared more often in the infected group. Death rates did not differ clearly. The results urge extra infection care around airway tubes in these fragile patients.
plos-pone-0348520:
Sangjin Lee, Sunggon Kim, and Yongseok Son build a faster defragmentation tool for flash-based solid-state drives. Even fast drives slow when heavy editing scatters a file's blocks across the chip, and the standard tool works through files one by one. Their 2026 system first collects file maps for everything, then runs many defragmenters in parallel, each owning one file and issuing requests without waiting.

On a common multi-core machine with a consumer drive, the tool finished cleanups up to nearly four times faster than the standard one. Throughput rose across workloads, and a program running alongside suffered less slowdown. Data centers juggling huge shared drives could tidy storage in shorter, less disruptive windows.
plos-pone-0348720:
Md Talha Jubaer and colleagues put a local scorecard for healthcare quality through tough math checks. The scorecard is used with left-out groups in Bangladesh. Their 2026 study drew on ratings from 311 local scoring groups. The groups spanned nine left-out communities. Each group rated fourteen items by consensus. The team tested the tool with classic stats and a modern item response model.

The scorecard held up. Ratings fell into three themes: access and fairness, how well offices respond, and mother and child health support. Together they explained over half the spread. The ratings also hung together well. One main thread backed a single overall score. Proof matters because scorecards steer real policy debates. Groups can now wield numbers shown to measure what they claim.
plos-pone-0348820:
Hung-Chun Huang and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE building a sideline triage score for lower-back, pelvis, and hip dysfunction in college athletes. These problems often precede back pain, but expert assessment is scarce, so teams need a field tool flagging who needs priority care and who can self-manage. Over eight hundred athletes from ten universities completed standardized history and functional testing, and experts judged each case as the reference.

Just over half needed priority assessment. The final score combined fourteen factors: a dozen raising concern, such as local pain, weakness, and higher body mass, and two safety-related findings that lowered it. The score separated the groups well, kept its accuracy under bootstrap re-checking, and calibrated nearly perfectly. A cutoff caught most priority cases while clearing most self-managers. The tool is presented as ready for prospective testing in team settings.
plos-pone-0348920:
Haruna Moshi and three colleagues examine why school-based deworming against schistosomiasis is delivered unevenly in Ghana, in this 2026 qualitative study. Preventive chemotherapy through schools is the main weapon against this parasitic disease, yet delivery in many districts falls short of World Health Organization targets and transmission persists. The researchers interviewed coordinators, head teachers, and school health teachers in two endemic districts of the Central Region.

Fidelity suffered where families feared the drugs or doubted the program, where supplies and money ran short, and where frontline teachers lacked training or incentives. It rose where awareness campaigns engaged the community, implementers felt motivated, and health and education sectors worked closely together. The authors conclude that faithful delivery is a system property, not a checklist, and must be built district by district.
plos-pone-0349020:
Javier Silva-Valencia and colleagues tracked lung exercise testing across Ontario over the years spanning the time before COVID-19 hit, the crisis itself, and the recovery since. These tests, such as the six-minute walk test, help doctors judge breathing problems and decide who needs long-term oxygen. The team used province-wide health records covering 2015 to 2023.

More than half a million tests were recorded, yet by late 2023 testing rates were still about a fifth below pre-pandemic levels. Recovery was uneven, lagging more for men and for some other groups. The shortfall matters because delayed testing can delay treatment decisions for people with chronic lung and heart disease.
plos-pone-0349120:
Maguy Saffouh El Hajj and colleagues reviewed why drug errors happen in local pharmacies, where most people collect their medicines. Hospital safety has drawn more study, yet busy counters carry real risk too. Thirteen studies, mostly from the United States and England, were woven together with a method that builds new themes from interview based research.

Five broad causes emerged from the weaving. Workload, staffing, and time pressure ran through many accounts, along with poor handoffs and weak safety habits. Checks confirmed fair trust in most themes. Local pharmacies need system fixes, like calmer workflow and better double checks, rather than blame aimed at single staff members working under strain.
plos-pone-0349220:
Nicholas Behn and colleagues gathered thirteen earlier studies to describe what life feels like when brain injury disrupts the thinking side of communication. After such injuries, people may struggle to follow conversation, find words, or read social cues, even when speech itself sounds fine. The review pools the voices of more than one hundred people with brain injury and sixty-six family members and friends.

Across the studies, eight themes emerged, starting with the plain fact that communicating is no longer easy. Participants described lost confidence, strained relationships, and services that overlook the problem. The authors argue that care should treat communication partners as part of the picture, since spouses, parents, and friends carry much of the daily repair work that keeps conversation going.
plos-pone-0349820:
Bandar Alghamdi and Sonia Rocha searched for low oxygen related genes that forecast lung adenocarcinoma outcomes in 2026. Tumors short of oxygen grow more aggressive and resist treatment, so their gene marks could guide care.

Comparing tumor and normal data, the team found hundreds of oxygen linked genes switched up or down. Up genes clustered in cancer and signalling pathways; down genes tied to immunity. Hub genes included known cancer players on both sides. Survival modelling then picked out genes whose levels track patient outcomes. Such marks may one day sort patients by risk and hint at drug targets in oxygen starved tumors.
plos-pone-0350020:
Charumita Vasudev and colleagues spoke at length with eighty six households in Uttar Pradesh and Goa, India, about food hardship during and after COVID. Field work ran from late 2022 into early 2023, with hundreds of interviews. Households mixed migrant and settled families, town and village homes, and varied caste and family types.

Everyday fixes came first: swapping foods, shrinking portions, and pooling what kin could share. Harder shocks forced harsher steps, like mothers eating last, selling goods, taking debt, pulling children from school, and delaying care. Settled village families leaned on kin and state food support. Migrants often lacked both, so place and movement shaped survival more than income loss alone.
plos-pone-0350120:
Mahunan Sossou and Dieu donné Gnonlonfoun reviewed intensive care records from Benin's national referral hospital for adults admitted with impaired consciousness. A dimmed or lost consciousness is common, dangerous, and little studied in low-resource intensive care. Records for four hundred sixteen patients admitted over two and a half years were used to estimate survival and find traits tied to death.

Two of every three patients died in the unit, half of the deaths within five days. Older age, deeper coma, low blood pressure, high temperature, and lacking oxygen therapy each raised the risk, while head injury cases fared comparatively better. The authors say simple admission readings can flag who needs attention first, and they make a plain case for reliable oxygen and basic monitoring before fancier equipment.
plos-pone-0350720:
Duc Quy Hoang and co-authors build a mammography reader that forces itself to look at suspicious spots, not just the whole breast image. AI readers can cheat by leaning on background patterns, which makes their answers hard to trust. Their hybrid system blends a compact local-detail network with a transformer that scans wider context, plus a branch that gathers evidence from the regions most likely to hold a lesion.

On a large public mammography collection, the full version topped strong rival systems on accuracy and balanced scores while using fewer resources. Its chosen regions often overlapped the lesions human experts had marked. Hoang and colleagues argue that showing its evidence makes the system easier for radiologists to check, a key step toward clinic use.
plos-pone-0350820:
Kanae Kondo and colleagues tracked cigarette sales and household tobacco spending in Japan across the COVID pandemic with national data stretching from 2014 onward. Sales series, spending surveys, and smoking rate data were modelled around the first emergency declaration and the later downgrade of COVID to a routine illness class.

Cigarette sales kept falling after the emergency, but more slowly than before. Price adjusted monthly tobacco spending jumped in the first emergency month, though later checks weakened that finding. Male smoking eased down year by year while female rates barely moved. Crises do not reliably cut smoking, the authors warn; stress and home time can blunt tobacco control.
plos-pone-0350920:
Farming shapes Vietnam's carbon footprint crop by crop, and An Thinh Nguyen and colleagues trained a neural network on three decades of data to weigh each land use. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered twenty-one farm product types from 1990 to 2019.

Most types moved with higher carbon dioxide emissions, including bananas, beans, cassava, coffee, and coconuts. Five moved the other way, among them rice, soybeans, and sesame. A four-layer network captured the links despite their tangled, non-linear shape. The authors say such product-level evidence helps policymakers target emission cuts where they count, instead of taxing all agriculture alike.
plos-pone-0351120:
Yao Zhao and Haoyu Zhou followed college students' sleep across all four undergraduate years in this 2026 study. Most earlier work measured sleep at single moments. These authors instead treated each student's nightly pattern as a smooth curve that changes over time. They used records from the NetHealth Project at an American university.

Wearable trackers produced more than sixty thousand daily sleep records for seventy-six students. Sleep grew longer across the four years, with clear seasonal swings tied to the academic calendar. Better grades and longer sleep went together throughout college. Each step up in grade average came with roughly twenty-seven extra minutes of sleep. Social activity levels also lined up with distinct sleep patterns, which argues for treating student sleep as a moving process, not a fixed habit.
plos-pone-0351220:
Heghine Gevorgyan and three colleagues probe how gut bacteria manage acid stress. Their 2026 study works with Escherichia coli fermenting sugars at an acidic pH. A protein switch called FhlA turns on the formate hydrogen lyase complex. That machinery converts formate into hydrogen gas, consuming protons as it goes. The team compared normal bacteria with mutants lacking the switch. They tracked the cell's main energy turbine, proton flows, and membrane properties at two growth stages.

Mutants showed weakened turbine activity and slower proton flux. The two systems, acid disposal and energy generation, clearly lean on each other. Older cultures of both strains carried more protective membrane groups and leaked fewer protons. Membrane voltage in the mutants stayed stubbornly unchanged. Bacteria, the authors conclude, balance their proton budget by coordinating several systems at once. Understanding that bookkeeping helps anyone fermenting microbes industrially, or fighting them medically, at low pH.
plos-pone-0351320:
Machines that tumble samples slowly can fake weightlessness on Earth, helping biologists rehearse space experiments. Andrada Pica and colleagues measured how well one such random positioning machine actually performs, in this 2026 PLOS One study combining motion sensors, computer modeling, and living nerve cells.

Sensors rode the frames while the machine ran in three modes. Modeling showed average gravity fell to between a hundredth and a thousandth of Earth's, with sideways spin forces staying tiny. Nerve cells grown under each mode reacted to the treatment. The authors offer the numbers as a reference so other labs can judge whether the simulation suits their experiments.
plos-pone-0352020:
Noumou Keita and seven colleagues reconstruct COVID-19's path through Mali from the virus's own genome. Their 2026 study is the country's first comprehensive genomic account. Mali recorded over thirty-three thousand confirmed cases between 2020 and 2025. The team analysed five hundred forty-eight Malian viral sequences. A high-quality subset, combined with close global relatives, powered time-resolved family trees. West African data are scarce in global surveillance, which makes every reconstructed introduction valuable.

Five distinct epidemic waves emerged. Early lineages gave way, wave by wave, to the dominant variants of 2023. Introductions traced mainly to Europe and North America. After each arrival, local transmission sustained itself. Viruses also flowed back and forth with neighbouring African countries. Molecular clock analysis dated the movements. For Malian health authorities, the reconstruction shows their epidemic was repeatedly reseeded from abroad, then homegrown. Border awareness and local genomic capacity both follow from that picture.
plos-pone-0352120:
Haeun Hwang and colleagues tested whether a cancer drug, omipalisib, can help brain cells clear out the tangled tau protein behind a family of dementias. Tau tangles grow when the cell's recycling system, autophagy, falters. The drug blocks a growth switch called mTOR, which normally holds recycling back. The team tried it in human cells engineered to make a mutant tau and in mice bred to develop tau disease.

In the cells, the drug loosened the mTOR brake, raised recycling markers, and lowered both a recycling backlog protein and the harmful modified form of tau, without killing the cells. Mice received the drug for two months starting at six months of age. The work supports the idea that freeing the cell's cleanup crew can cut tau buildup, a strategy now open to further testing in animals.
plos-pone-0352320:
Ahmad Sarraj and colleagues ran a small trial on whether brain stimulation adds anything to an intensive rehab method for people with long-standing paraplegia from spinal cord injury. The base method pairs imagining movements with strong sensory stimulation of the legs. Fifty patients were split among usual care, the method alone, and the method plus mild electrical stimulation of the scalp, over ten days.

Patients on usual care gained nothing measurable. Both active groups improved substantially and by the same amount on touch and pinprick sensation. So the sensory recovery seems to come from the peripheral method itself, with no extra gain from the brain stimulation on those measures. For clinics, that simplifies the recipe: the cheaper, simpler half of the pairing appears to carry the sensory benefit.
plos-pone-0352420:
Sandani De Vass Gunawardane and seven colleagues investigate a herbal capsule called Vernolac in this 2026 study. The product blends five Sri Lankan medicinal plants, including black seed and Indian sarsaparilla. Each plant has shown anti-cancer activity on its own. The team asked how the mixture might act against cancer as a whole.

Computer databases yielded one hundred fifty-five drug-like compounds from the blend. Their predicted protein targets overlapped with cancer-related targets at one hundred thirty-seven points. Network analysis highlighted fourteen hub proteins, many central to cell growth and death. Chemical profiling of the extract confirmed a rich mix of active plant compounds. The work maps plausible routes for the formula's effects, while stressing that laboratory and clinical proof must follow.
plos-pone-0353020:
Yusuf Başkıran and three colleagues compare three ways of performing a hysterectomy and their after-effects, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from a Turkish hospital. Records covered four hundred and sixty-six women whose wombs were removed for non-cancer reasons between 2020 and 2023, by the open abdominal route, by keyhole surgery, or through the vagina. The team measured vaginal length and sexual function scores before and after surgery.

Vaginal length shrank most after keyhole surgery, yet women's sexual function scores ended up similar across all three routes. Their partners' scores dipped after surgery, a finding the authors flag as tentative. The practical reading: surgical route changes anatomy measurably without clearly changing women's early sexual wellbeing.
plos-pone-0353120:
Bilgilisoy Filiz and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 on gel injections for knee osteoarthritis. More than one hundred adults with moderate knee wear will receive either a high-dose gel injection or salt water, then swap after three months, with neither patients nor assessors knowing the order. Pain, function, strength, and quality of life will be tracked for a year.

The crossover design lets each patient serve as their own comparison. Three-month results will judge benefit, while the full year watches safety. Gel injections are widely sold but unevenly proven, so a blinded trial with a dummy injection offers unusually firm evidence for patients weighing cost against relief.
plos-pone-0353420:
Marcos De Andrés Montero and seven colleagues present a method for untangling mass graves where bones from many people lie mixed together, in this 2026 PLOS ONE archaeology paper. Reassembling individuals is the necessary first step before any identification, yet field guidance has been thin. Their approach records the exact position of every bone in mapping software and adds a new coding system that tracks how complete each skeleton is.

Applied to a crowded sixteenth-century burial in southwestern Hungary, the method substantially increased the number of fully reassembled skeletons and suggested matches for many loose elements. Working spatially first, they argue, makes later bone-sorting techniques far more effective — a step toward naming the dead.
plos-pone-0353520:
Anggeriyane and colleagues published a plan in 2026 for mapping what is known about emotional and behavioral troubles in preschool children. Young children who struggle to manage feelings and behavior can face lasting harm later in life. Yet past studies are scattered across fields and use very different ways to measure the same problems.

Under the plan, the team will search six large databases for studies from the year 2000 onward, with no limit on language. Two reviewers will screen and chart the studies on their own, then group the linked factors into body, mind, family, and wider life domains. Readers get a clear map of what has been studied and where the gaps still sit.
plos-pone-0354020:
Agazhe Aemro and five colleagues count how often women across nine sub-Saharan African countries have ever tested for HIV, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis of national health surveys. The sample covers nearly one hundred and sixty thousand women aged fifteen to forty-nine. The average woman had tested about two and a half times in her life, but the typical woman — the median — had never tested at all.

Testing rose with age, education, wealth, employment, and knowledge about HIV, and varied enormously by region, with southern Africa far ahead. Having more partners, perhaps through antenatal and clinic contact, sharply raised counts. Over half of women had never tested, a gap the authors say needs community-level, region-specific campaigns.
plos-pone-0354120:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 study, race six inflammation scores drawn from routine blood counts to see which best predicts peritonitis in people on peritoneal dialysis. This infection of the belly lining is the Achilles heel of home dialysis and can end the treatment. More than two thousand patients from ten centers were followed.

About seven in every hundred patients developed peritonitis during follow-up. Three scores, built from ratios and products of blood cell counts, each more than doubled the estimated risk when high, and each separated future cases from non-cases moderately well. The relationships were curved rather than straight, rising steeply past certain levels. No score dominated the others. The authors suggest these free scores, computed from blood tests patients already get, could flag who needs closer watching and earlier teaching on sterile technique.
plos-pone-0354520:
Janet Antwi led a team of seven authors on this 2026 pilot study of a produce prescription program at a historically Black university in the United States. Fifty-five students received nutrition classes and cooking demonstrations; half also got personalized bags of fresh produce every two weeks. Intake was tracked with screeners, day recalls, and food questionnaires.

The produce group showed favorable shifts in how often several fruits and vegetables were eaten, though most group-to-group differences missed statistical significance. Antwi reads the patterns as promising and calls for a larger, fully powered trial.
plos-pone-0354920:
Femke W Overbosch and colleagues staged two table-top drills of a bird flu outbreak sweeping out of the Netherlands. Experts in health, society, and money sat first in split teams, then mixed. Their 2026 study had about forty experts across the drills. The team studied the written advice each setup produced. It also spoke with the experts before the drills. The goal was hunting for blind spots in how governments get outbreak advice.

Split teams disagreed on urgency. They disagreed on how bad things could get, and fiercely on school closures. Mixed talks showed each field's blind spots and built shared grasp of the problem. They also exposed tangled gaps in the rule books and basic systems. The authors suggest merging the advice teams for real. Gluing split memos together at the top, they argue, is worse.
plos-pone-0355020:
Rachel D Gordon and colleagues interviewed eleven adults with sickle cell disease who hope to have biological children. They explored what the adults know about fertility. They also explored what help they have been offered. Their 2026 qualitative study covered participants aged eighteen to thirty-five at an American center. It used open interviews analyzed for themes. The backdrop is evidence that the disease and some treatments impair fertility.

Five themes surfaced. Doctors rarely raised family building. Women felt unprepared for what pregnancy with the disease involves. Partners seemed to share the planning burden unequally. Costs shut down serious consideration of assisted reproduction. Above all, participants asked for earlier, repeated conversations. The authors urge sickle cell care to treat reproduction as routine, not taboo.
plos-pone-0355520:
Correction notice. Xin Pang and co-authors correct two figures in their published study of immune suppressor cells in oral cancer progression. After publication, readers flagged panels that appeared to overlap across different cell lines and conditions. This 2026 notice replaces the faulty panels with originals from the reported experiments.

The authors state that all three starting-time panels in one figure were incorrect and supply a corrected figure with its underlying data files. One panel in a second figure was likewise incorrect and is replaced. A panel said to show one cell line had overlapped a panel from another article showing a different line. The notice documents each fix so the experimental record can be checked.
plos-pone-0355620:
Cui Lin and colleagues followed rectal cancer patients home to test whether caregiver skill predicts stoma complications. A new ostomy demands careful daily care, and the family caregiver usually provides it. Their 2026 prospective study rated caregiver skill at discharge against set standards, then checked patients one month later.

Just over a third of patients developed a complication within the month, most often skin irritation or leakage. The skill gradient was steep. About three quarters of patients with low-skill caregivers had complications, against about one fifth in the high-skill group. Lin and colleagues argue discharge training should be tested against a clear skill standard, not given as a leaflet and a hope.
plos-pone-0355720:
Zehra Narlı Özdemir and coauthors published a 2026 clinical study in PLOS ONE on fatigue in people with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. That is an ultra-rare blood disorder in which red cells are destroyed by the body's own complement system. Fatigue is the complaint patients say never resolves, even on the standard drug eculizumab. Clinicians at eighteen Turkish centers surveyed just over a hundred treated patients face to face with a standard questionnaire.

More than a third of patients scored in the severe fatigue range despite treatment. Those patients had lower hemoglobin at diagnosis and at survey time, and they had spent longer on extra medications. In adjusted analysis, being female, having other illnesses, longer extra-medication use, and lower starting hemoglobin each tracked with severe fatigue. The results suggest that controlling the blood disorder alone does not lift fatigue, and clinics should track and treat it as its own problem.
plos-pone-0356220:
Naveen Kumar B and Aslam Abdullah Mohammed built a classifier in 2026 that helps detect when a drilled borehole has wandered off course. Borehole deviation matters in oil, gas, and water drilling because a crooked hole can miss its target and raise costs. Their method reads conventional well log data, the standard measurements recorded in every drilled well, and looks for the signature that the rock formation's response leaves when deviation occurs.

Using data that drillers already collect means the tool can be applied without new instruments down the hole. Catching deviation early lets drilling teams correct course before a small drift becomes an expensive sidetrack. The study applies machine learning classification to a stubborn, practical problem in field geology.
plos-pone-0356620:
Huiling Chen and five colleagues mine twelve years of United States food recall records to find what makes a recall high-risk, in this 2026 study. Their source is the Food and Drug Administration's enforcement reports from 2012 to 2024, covering nearly twenty-seven thousand food recall events. They classified each recall's hazard, product, reach, and region, then modeled which features accompany the most serious category, Class I, meaning a real chance of serious harm.

Yearly counts swung widely without a steady trend. Two hazards dominated: microbial contamination and undeclared allergens. Bacterial contamination recalls were classified as high-risk at consistently high rates across food categories, while allergen recalls varied much more. Once hazard type was accounted for, region, product category, and distribution scope added little. The authors say the classification system is driven mainly by the hazard itself, as its rules intend.
plos-pone-0356720:
Birhane Alem Berihu and seven colleagues measured folate levels in pregnant women in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, reporting in 2026. The region records some of the world's highest rates of neural tube defects, birth defects of the brain and spine that folate prevents. Four hundred women in their first trimester at five public hospitals gave blood samples and answered questions about their diets.

The results were stark: nearly ninety-nine in every hundred women fell below the blood folate level recommended for preventing these defects. Four in five also ate too narrow a range of foods, yet even women with varied diets were almost all deficient. Older mothers fared slightly worse, while dietary variety helped only a little. The authors argue that advice and occasional supplements cannot fix a gap this wide, and they call for mandatory fortification of staple foods at national scale.
plos-pone-0356820:
Tanchun Wang and five colleagues ask whether fatty liver disease simply speeds up normal liver aging, using large public gene-activity datasets in this 2026 study. The disease, now called MASLD, is common and worsens with age, but its molecular path over a lifetime is poorly mapped. The team combined well over a thousand liver samples from healthy donors and patients across a wide age range.

Healthy and diseased livers shared surprisingly few age-related genes, and some genes even moved in opposite directions with age. In healthy livers, aging genes centered on the cell cycle. In diseased livers, the changes instead involved protein cleanup systems, stress responses, and a pathway tied to cell death, and many tracked with scarring severity. The authors conclude the disease follows its own aging route, not just a faster version of the normal one, which matters for age-aware treatment.
plos-pone-0356920:
Shiho Hansen, Snefrid Møllersen, Anna Rita Spein, and Anne Cecilie Jávo present a protocol, published in 2026. It covers a survey of every upper secondary student in Finnmark, Norway's far northern county. The topic is problematic internet use. The study is designed for a multiethnic region. It will compare Sámi Indigenous adolescents with their non-Sámi peers. These groups are rarely examined side by side on digital behavior.

A bilingual questionnaire, in Northern Sámi and Norwegian, will measure compulsive internet use. It will also cover family, peer, and school norms. Strength of ethnic identity and experiences of ethnic discrimination are included. The analysis plan tests whether norms and identity protect against unhealthy use, or feed it. No results exist yet. The finished study should guide culturally fitting prevention in Arctic schools.
plos-pone-0357020:
Jiyoung Emily Lee led a team of eight authors studying the tear film of the eye, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. A thin lipid layer floats on tears and keeps eyes moist; its thickness varies more than doctors once assumed. The team ran a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of that variability and its clinical meaning.

Lee's findings help eye doctors read this subtle marker of dry eye disease and tailor treatment to it. Dry eye is common, uncomfortable, and often treated by trial and error. A measurable trait like lipid thickness, properly understood, can sort patients by cause. The study's care in describing normal variability is what makes abnormal readings meaningful in the clinic.
plos-pone-0357920:
Yan Nee Gan and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on preparing a pharmacy-led HIV prevention service for Malaysia. The prevention pill PrEP works, yet only a few thousand Malaysians took the free government supply in 2024, against hundreds of thousands who could benefit. Private pharmacies could widen access. This study reports a one-day Kuala Lumpur consultation where twenty-eight stakeholders stress-tested the model before its pilot.

The group worked through the barriers their earlier research had surfaced. They drafted fixes: build awareness and demand, protect privacy and confidentiality, keep it affordable, and fold in HIV self-testing. They also proposed digital checklists, simpler lab requirements, and a practical workflow guide, plus serious training. Training needs ran from drug basics to eligibility judgments and referral drills. The refined model is presented as ready for pilot testing, with cross-sector cooperation as its glue.
plos-pone-0358120:
Khomsan Yooyen led a team of six authors studying anemia in diabetes patients in northeastern Thailand, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Anemia and type 2 diabetes often occur together, and the pairing raises risks for the heart, kidneys, and eyes. The team ran a cross-sectional study to measure how common anemia is in this group and what drives it.

Yooyen's findings tell local doctors whom to screen and which factors to watch. Anemia is easy to miss because its tiredness looks like diabetes itself. Routine screening of the highest-risk patients can catch it early and cheaply. The study's value is local precision: national averages would hide the pattern in this region's clinics.
plos-pone-0358720: Mohammadi and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on guayule, a desert shrub grown as a source of natural rubber. They treated the plants with salicylic acid, a hormone-like chemical, and tracked changes in growth form. They also tracked how active the key genes for rubber making became. The work bears on efforts to grow more rubber at home instead of relying on rubber trees abroad.
plos-pone-0359620: Onyango and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE policy study set in Kisumu, Kenya. They read COVID-19 rules through a lens that weighs overlapping traits like sex, income, and social role. The focus was women who sell food in open, informal markets. The study asks how pandemic rules landed on this group in daily life. Its lessons apply when governments write emergency rules that hit informal workers hardest.
pmc-11126520:
Members of the GBD 2021 Causes of Death group report on deaths from nearly three hundred causes worldwide. Their counts cover more than two hundred countries and territories, plus many smaller regions within them, from 1990 to 2021. Regular reporting on why people die guides public health choices.

Alongside cause-by-cause deaths, the team shows how changes in each cause raised or lowered life expectancy. That breakdown reveals which gains came from fewer heart deaths, fewer infections, or other shifts. Leaders can use it to see where progress is real and where it is stalling.
pmc-13194920:
Octavio Reyes-Matte is first author on a 2026 methods paper on measuring bacterial cell size precisely at scale. Bacteria vary hugely in size, and size can evolve quickly, yet comparative size studies are rare because manual measurement is slow and standard imaging segments cells poorly. The team built a pipeline named MEDUSSA.

Deep learning first sharpens fluorescent membrane images, then segments individual cells, corrects errors, and measures each one regardless of shape, chaining, or clustering. Applied to six strains of one bacterial species, the method found over twofold volume differences, driven mainly by cell width. A partly working gene variant explained one strain's narrowness. The toolkit opens comparative study of how bacterial size evolves.
pmc-13197020:
Sima Fansa and colleagues offer a 2026 case report on amyloidosis found through gut symptoms. Amyloidosis is a set of diseases where misfolded proteins build up in organs and harm them. Gut involvement is common but often missed, since symptoms vary a lot.

Their patient was a 68-year-old man with long-term gut complaints. Tests showed AL amyloidosis, a form tied to abnormal proteins from immune cells, along with a slow blood cancer called lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Care combined chemotherapy with support for his gut symptoms. The authors urge doctors to weigh amyloidosis when gut symptoms persist, above all in patients with related blood disorders.
pmc-13199420:
Porntita Sae-li and colleagues surveyed Thai medical students on antibiotic knowledge and self-treatment in a 2026 study. Misuse of antibiotics fuels drug resistance, a major global threat. Future doctors who self-medicate set a poor pattern, so the team measured what students know and do.

More than five hundred students at a public university answered an anonymous online survey. Most knew drug names and the need to finish a course. Fewer than half grasped resistance in gonorrhea or how resistance spreads between people and animals. Senior clinical students scored higher than juniors. Junior status tied to using antibiotics for wrong illnesses and stopping courses early. Teaching should be tailored by year, the authors say.
pmc-13237220:
Osman and colleagues map the rocks of an Egyptian desert range by joining satellite images, fieldwork, and lab study of rock slices. The Gabal El-Faraid group, in the south-eastern desert, holds ancient rocks and zones where minerals collect along cracks and faults. Finding those zones from the ground alone is slow in such rough country.

Their method blends several satellite data types to tell rock types apart automatically, then checks the map on foot and under the microscope. Matching remote patterns to real rocks sharpens the map and flags ground most worth prospecting. The approach could speed mineral exploration across similar desert ranges.
pmc-13241520:
Schebek and colleagues at Freie Universität Berlin redesigned Boltzmann generators so they can sample large materials, not just small molecules. These neural networks generate equilibrium structures in one shot, avoiding slow molecular dynamics. Earlier versions failed to scale beyond modest system sizes. The new design pairs augmented coupling flows with graph neural networks that read local atomic environments.

Training runs on energies, and the model transfers to systems far larger than its training cells. Tests covered Lennard-Jones crystals, water ice phases, and the silicon phase diagram. Simulation cells passed one thousand atoms while free energies stayed accurate. Sampling ran faster and used fewer resources than earlier designs.
pmc-13242120:
Azmy Basiouny and colleagues at Cairo University braced the perineum to unblock obstructed defecation in twenty-nine patients. All had pathological perineal descent after a year of failed conservative care. Transverse perineal support surgery aimed to restore the pelvic floor's anchor. Constipation scores, pressures, and descent were gauged before and after.

Constipation scores dropped by over five points at six months. Push force rose while descent shrank appreciably. No mesh erosion or chronic pain showed. Nine patients kept their symptoms; all carried rectal intussusception and were older. Careful selection, the authors stress, decides success.
pmc-13244520:
Wanting Jiang and colleagues wrapped a potent but poisonous natural compound in a two-key delivery particle aimed at liver cancer. Their study appeared in Drug Delivery in 2026. Cantharidin kills cancer cells yet damages kidneys and liver on its own. Their solid lipid nanoparticles carry two homing ligands. One targets liver cells; the other extends circulation time, concentrating the drug in tumors.

In liver cancer cells the particles entered best and killed at the lowest dose. Over two-fifths of cells were pushed into programmed death, with survival genes flipped down and death genes up. In tumor-bearing mice the particles shrank tumors by nearly three-fifths, beating both free cantharidin and the standard drug sorafenib, with every mouse alive at two weeks and blood tests clean. The authors present the design as proof that smart packaging can domesticate a dangerous natural drug.
pmc-13244820:
An editorial expression of concern published in the Journal of Inflammation in 2026 alerts readers to problems in a 2023 article on radiation-induced lung injury. The earlier paper, by Zhuo Chen and colleagues, studied how that injury develops. After publication, the publisher received concerns about Figure 7 of the article, and further checking found image editing, described as beautification, in Figure 5.

The journal's editor-in-chief states that the authors could supply some, but not all, of the original data requested for checking the work. Without the full data, the results cannot be validated or replicated as claimed. Readers are therefore urged to treat the article's content and conclusions with caution. Chen agreed with issuing the notice, while the remaining authors did not answer the publisher's correspondence. The document is a formal warning flag on the record, stopping short of retraction while the concerns stand unresolved.
pmc-13244920:
Pong-isawaranan and colleagues studied in 2026 which factors predict depression among Thai adolescents as the country moved from the COVID-19 pandemic to its endemic phase. Six hundred five high school students from two schools in central Thailand completed standard scales for depressive symptoms, felt stress, coping styles, and social support between late 2023 and early 2024. The team used layered regression to weigh each factor's added contribution.

About 28 percent of students showed depressive symptoms. Felt stress was by far the strongest predictor, accounting for over half the variation in symptom scores on its own. Avoiding problems rather than facing them added a smaller but real share. Facing problems directly and social support did not predict symptoms once stress and avoidance were in the model. The authors urge school nurses to screen for stress and teach adaptive coping, with families brought into the effort.
pmc-13245320:
Alaoui Mrani, Azzouni, and El Abiad tested three sulfonamide compounds as rust shields for steel, in this 2026 RSC Advances study. Mild steel corrodes fast in hydrochloric acid, used in industrial cleaning and pickling, so inhibitors that cling to the surface are valuable. The team paired quantum-chemical calculations and surface simulations with electrochemical measurements on steel in strong acid.

All three compounds inhibited corrosion strongly at low concentration, with the best two blocking around ninety-five percent of attack. Electrical tests showed they slowed both halves of the corrosion reaction, and adsorption measurements indicated the molecules form a spontaneous protective film mixing physical and chemical bonding. The protection held up reasonably as temperature rose. Surface imaging confirmed the film, supporting sulfonamides as candidates for acid corrosion control.
pmc-13246820:
de Andrade, Novoa, and Pisa mapped the paperwork rules for telemedicine worldwide in this 2026 scoping review in Neurological Sciences. Video visits grew explosively, but what doctors must document, how consent is recorded, and how long records are kept vary by jurisdiction, and neurology and stroke care carry extra demands. The team analyzed one hundred forty-seven regulatory sources from fifty-two jurisdictions.

Every jurisdiction required certain core documentation, yet they diverged substantially on consent forms, data retention, electronic prescribing, and platform rules. The authors scored each system's regulatory intensity to compare them. Their conclusion is that telemedicine is now permanent, regulated care, and harmonization should aim at interoperability and mutual recognition between systems rather than identical rules everywhere.
pmc-13247520:
Meirelles and co-authors report two sisters whose chromosomes and bodies tell different stories, in this 2026 JCEM Case Reports article. Both women carry a 46,XY chromosome pattern, yet developed as females and came to care as adults because periods never started and puberty never arrived. Born to related parents, they were tall, had female external anatomy, very low testosterone, and undescended testes where ovaries would be expected.

Genetic testing found the cause: a new, homozygous splice-site change in LHCGR, the receptor that lets the body answer luteinizing hormone and build male hormones before birth. Without it, the hormone-producing Leydig cells never developed properly, confirmed when the removed gonads were examined. The case widens the known mutation list for this rare cause of sex-development differences.
pmc-13248520:
Insuan and colleagues built a slow-release carrier for eucalyptus oil, reported in 2026. The oil kills bacteria and fungi, but it evaporates within a day, wasting its effect. The team loaded it into a porous silica block whose surface chemistry grips oily molecules, then tracked how the oil escaped and worked.

Free oil vanished within twenty-four hours, while the loaded block released its active parts, including eucalyptol, over days. Treated surfaces kept bacteria such as E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus in check for up to seven days, and a garlic fungus stayed suppressed too. The authors propose such carriers for healthcare and food storage settings.
pmc-13249120:
Licht-Handler and colleagues set out a plan for building grief support apps in two cultures, in a 2026 protocol. Grief help is scarce, and most research comes from wealthy Western countries. The team is developing phone-based momentary interventions, brief support delivered in daily life, one for China and one for Switzerland, for bereaved people without a formal grief disorder diagnosis.

Content will be drafted with grief experts and bereaved users, then revised after a second round of feedback. Interviews in China have already begun with seventeen participants. The authors expect finished designs by the end of 2026 and discuss openly how the two versions may need to differ.
pmc-13250020:
Kreutzberg and colleagues mapped depression care across Germany's regions, in a 2026 health services study. Claims data covered more than a million adults with diagnosed depression in one large sickness fund, and the team measured 2023 costs, sick days, specialist contact, and psychotherapy use. A grouping tool adjusted for each patient's other illnesses, and regions were scored for deprivation and urbanization.

People in the most deprived regions took about six more sick days per year than those in the least deprived, and slightly fewer received psychotherapy. Urban patients cost a little more and saw specialists more often. Most regional differences stayed unexplained by deprivation, city size, or illness burden, which the authors flag as the real puzzle for planners.
pmc-13250220:
Memon and co-authors explain how they picked standout countries for a family planning research project. Their 2026 BMJ Global Health methods paper looks for poorer countries whose contraceptive use grew far beyond what development levels predict. The search used data from after 2000, when global attention returned to family planning.

The team compared modern contraceptive use and satisfied demand against predictions based on the Human Development Index for each country. Senegal, Malawi, and Kenya cleared the strictest cutoff, all of them in Africa. Loosening the cutoff added Sierra Leone, Laos, and Bolivia so that other regions had comparators. The authors argue that studying such outliers, with a time lag built in, can reveal practical drivers that other countries might copy.
pmc-13250720:
Melanie Penner and co-authors review what helps autistic children and youth in this 2026 article. Autism shapes how a person communicates and experiences the world, and each child's path through childhood differs in strengths and needs.

Long-term studies show early skill building matters, while new needs and chances for independence appear with age. Support programs show real benefits, though the review insists on counting harms from therapies too, and on outcomes autistic people themselves value. Programs are slowly including more diverse communities and adapting to them. Above all, autistic voices name acceptance and true inclusion as core parts of a good life.
pmc-13251820:
Mengchun Wu and co-authors uncover a single-letter edit switch in a crop fungus in this 2026 study. The fungus causes head blight in cereals, and a protein called Spo11, which cuts DNA to start sexual shuffling, turned out to have a second job holding back the first division.

A stop signal inside the Spo11 message is corrected to a working code only during sexual reproduction, through RNA editing. Without the protein, division speeds up and spores fail. A version born already corrected keeps spores fine but harms growth and division timing. The edit acts as a dial for protein dose, and family history shows it has been gained and lost over time.
pmc-13253720:
Delcio Almeida Magalhães and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a wild maned wolf with grave injuries. The free-ranging adult male had a broken, infected back leg bone with dead tissue and maggots. Scans also showed one kidney destroyed by large worms, Dioctophyma renale, a parasite of the kidney.

Surgeons removed the leg to save his life, then removed the harmed kidney once he was stable. He got dog donor red blood cells during surgery, a cross-species transfusion, with no bad reaction. Over one year of checks, he walked well on three legs and showed no kidney failure.
pmc-13254120:
Ulrich Krispel and co-authors test a scan method to spot liver cancer in a 2026 study. Optical coherence tomography, a light-based scan, was paired with anomaly detection, a method trained only on normal tissue. The data set held 173 images from 69 patients having liver surgery, covering three cancer types and healthy liver.

A pre-trained Vision Transformer model reached 80 percent sensitivity and 78 percent specificity, with 79 percent accuracy overall. The aim is faster checks during surgery than frozen section tests now used. The authors note the data set was small and noisy, but call the approach promising.
pmc-13254220:
Xingguang Liu and colleagues study a gene pair that helps stomach cancer grow in a 2026 paper. Gastric cancer has high rates of illness and death worldwide. The team combined database analyses, cell tests, mouse tumor models, and single-cell data to probe SRSF1, a splicing factor, and Mcl-1, a protein that blocks cell death.

SRSF1 was overproduced in tumor tissue and tied to poor outlook. It boosted cancer cell invasion and movement while blocking a death-linked form of Mcl-1, shutting down a cell death pathway. Cells with high SRSF1 also interacted more with fibroblasts, reshaping the tumor surroundings.
pmc-13254420:
Thang Minh Le and colleagues report emergent stenting for tandem stroke blockages in a 2026 study. Tandem occlusions block two vessel territories at once. At their stroke center, 145 patients got emergency stenting outside the skull, paired with clot removal, between December 2020 and June 2025.

At three months, 108 patients, or 74.5 percent, had favorable outcomes, and 97, or 66.9 percent, had good outcomes. Smoking, lipid disorder, higher stroke severity scores, worse early scan scores, and procedure complications all tied to poor outcomes. The authors call stenting an essential way to reopen vessels in these cases. All patients were treated at one comprehensive stroke center, and outcomes were judged three months after the procedure with standard measures of daily function and recovery.
pmc-13257320:
Piejko and colleagues make the case for intercepting circulating tumor cells in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a cancer that relapses early even after surgery. Their hypothesis-driven review weighs evidence on staging, cell detection in portal versus peripheral blood, and blood-based minimal residual disease testing. It then examines one proposed weapon: engineered T cells aimed at the surface protein CEACAM6.

Portal blood yields more tumor cells and predicts relapse better, while tumor-informed DNA positivity forecasts shorter disease-free survival. CEACAM6 is overexpressed on these tumors, but the authors caution that expression alone does not prove a safe target. They propose biomarker-selected trials using combined cell and DNA clearance as endpoints.
pmc-13258520:
Jorge Bonhomme and Victoria Mollón compare two ways of computing how layered composites split apart. Engineers use the virtual crack-closure technique to split crack energy into opening and sliding parts. The standard version can return impossible negative values for sharply asymmetric test pieces, a flaw this 2026 paper probes.

They modeled two lopsided beam tests with finite elements and ran standard and revised calculation orders. The revised methods shuffle energy between the opening and sliding modes, while the standard result lands between them. Total crack energy came out identical under all three. Contact between specimen arms, they warn, can also fake negative readings.
pmc-13259620:
Cristina Di Giorgio and co-authors finger a cytokine that helps stomach tumors hide from the immune system. Leukemia inhibitory factor, or LIF, was unexplored in gastric cancer's use of the PD-L1 shield. Their 2026 study measures both molecules in removed tumors and tests a LIF-blocking drug candidate.

Tumor LIF ran high and tracked with more PD-L1 and worse survival. Through a JAK and STAT3 relay, LIF ordered cells to make more PD-L1 and turn invasive. The antagonist LRI-305 cut that signal, lowered PD-L1, and partly woke immune activity back up. Pairing LIF blockade with checkpoint immunotherapy is their proposed next step.
pmc-13262220:
Saleh Mohamed and co-authors profile the chemistry hiding in desert date peel. Balanites aegyptiaca fruit is eaten and used across arid Africa, as it has been for ages, and its peel concentrates plant phenolics. Their 2026 lab study names those compounds and tests what they can do.

Lab work found gallic acid, rutin, quercetin, catechin, and a flavonoid glucoside leading a rich phenolic roster. The extract mopped up free radicals across five antioxidant assays. Against five human disease bacteria, tiny doses stopped growth, and every strain died within ten hours. Peel, usually thrown out, could help keep foods fresh the natural way.
pmc-13263020:
Ejura Yetunde Salihu, Apoorva Reddy, and Amy Price map peer support in online antidepressant discussions in a 2026 journal article. People often discuss drug side effects and withdrawal on Reddit, where they can speak freely about stigmatized topics. The team scraped ten busy threads from a depression forum and coded mentions of symptoms, withdrawal, and support, then analyzed how topics connect.

Posts most often discussed emotional flattening, sleep problems, and memory or thinking issues. Mentions of dizziness tended to appear alongside withdrawal talk and offers of empathy. Dream-related side effects and requests for personal experiences also clustered together. Brain zaps, a withdrawal sensation, appeared with offers of teaching support. The authors say clinicians can learn patient language and needs from such forums.
pmc-13263320:
Mathis Stetzuhn and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on tuning tiny magnetic waves in a layered crystal called CrSBr. The waves are magnons, ripples that travel through ordered magnetic material. The crystal is an antiferromagnet, where neighboring atomic magnets point in opposite directions. Two electrical gates let the team add electrons and apply an electric field.

Both magnon frequencies rose as electron density increased, and the response to a perpendicular electric field was uneven between the two modes. A layer-by-layer spin model reproduced the behavior. In a three-layer device the team tuned the waves by up to two gigahertz directly on the chip, a step toward adjustable magnetic electronics.
pmc-13263720:
Fang-Shuo Hu and Alexey Solodovnikov name a new genus of rove beetles, Luffy, with two new species inside it. One comes from Yunnan in China and the other from northern Laos. Their 2026 taxonomic paper illustrates the beetles and argues their place in the Staphylinina subtribe.

Luffy joins the Ocypus group and appears to be the closest relative of the Eucibdelus lineage. Pinning that relationship down required re-examining which shared traits truly define the lineage. The authors update its diagnosis accordingly. A small genus thus sharpens the map of a whole beetle branch, showing how new finds reorganize old classifications.
pmc-13263920:
Susanne Simon and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how often a first diagnosis of pneumonia holds up by discharge. Pneumonia is a lung infection, here caught outside hospital. The team compared first and final diagnoses in 1,385 adults treated in Hannover, Germany.

The first diagnosis was confirmed in only about half the cases. The most common replacements were other lung conditions, then heart conditions, then kidney problems. Confirmed cases had clearly higher CRP, a blood marker of inflammation, and slightly higher body temperature. Even so, single tests split the groups poorly. The authors urge a careful second look after admission to cut wrong diagnoses and needless antibiotics.
pmc-13264020:
Tomohiko Makiyama and colleagues find a cell-cycle kinase moonlighting as a fat-droplet regulator in liver cells. The droplet-coating protein PLIN2 is tightly controlled, and NEK2A emerged as its suppressor in their 2026 experiments on human hepatoma cells. Removing the kinase raised PLIN2; adding it lowered the protein.

pmc-13264620:
Zeinab F Elsharkawy and co-authors present a 2026 paper on using the human ear to identify people. Ears keep a stable, personal shape, but photos vary with angle, light, and size, which hurts matching. Their system joins two deep learning tools and then protects the stored template so it can be cancelled if leaked.

One tool reads broad features and the other reads fine detail, and their outputs are merged. A search method then keeps only the most telling features. A filter step turns those features into a template that cannot be reversed into the raw ear data. On five public ear data sets, accuracy ranged from about 93 to nearly 100 percent. The authors say the system beat prior methods.
pmc-13264820:

pmc-13264920:
Ana Paula da Cunha, Jurema Corrêa da Mota, and Francisco Inacio Bastos wrote a 2026 survey study on felt barriers to primary care in Manguinhos. The area is a poor and violence-hit part of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. About 1,000 residents were interviewed face to face in 2024. Younger residents saw more barriers in stories about socially marginalised behavior, hinting at low trust in services. pmc-13266420:
Juliana Alvares Duarte Bonini Campos leads a 2026 study of mental health among pharmacy students in southeast Brazil. The team ran 11 survey waves from 2018 to 2025 at one public university. Students filled in scales for low mood, anxiety, stress, distress, loneliness, and general mood state.

Anxiety stayed high throughout. Women and students with a past mental health diagnosis had higher odds of symptoms. Stress, tension, and over-arousal sat at the center of the symptom network.
pmc-13267520:
Edgar López-López, José L Medina-Franco, and Filip Miljković present a 2026 computer method for breaking molecules into useful pieces. Tested on five data sets, from drugs to natural products and food compounds, it produced more pieces than known methods. Its pieces also reached parts of chemical space the other tools missed, and they were smaller and simpler. The code is free online.
pmc-13267620:
Qianwei Tang and colleagues present a 2026 study of a sticky gel that delivers a healing drug to mouth ulcers. Dexamethasone calms inflammation well, but the wet, moving mouth washes treatments away fast. The team packed the drug into tiny plastic particles, then set those into a gelatin gel. In lab tests the particles did not harm gum cells and helped them grow. In animals, one application healed mouth ulcers quickly. The authors offer the system as a step toward longer-lasting mouth treatments.
pmc-13267820:
Jing Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 multi-center study of satisfaction among disabled older inpatients in China. The team surveyed 1,157 residents at seven institutions. They asked whether men and women judge nursing home style care differently, and how illness type changes that judgment.

Men were clearly less likely than women to report satisfaction. The gap held for heart and vessel disease wards and for chronic geriatric disease groups. For nerve disease groups the gap was smaller and less certain. Most residents carried nerve or heart conditions, often both. The authors argue that one-size care misses real differences in what men and women need. They urge care plans shaped by gender, covering social and emotional support as well as medical needs.
pmc-13267920:
Shenglu Xu and Hong Gao wrote a 2026 letter raising doubts about a study of vibration for injection pain. The study gave each person a control shot, then a shot with vibration meant to dull pain. The letter writers say the fixed order is a problem: everyone got the control first, so learning, expectation, and leftover soreness could skew self-reported pain.

Claims that vibration works better with thicker needles rested on two groups of ten, without a proper interaction test. They found small mismatches in the reported effect sizes and an impossible height value in a data table. The writers ask for clearer reporting so others can check the work.
pmc-13269620:
Arthur C K Chu and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a radioactive form of an antibody drug for breast cancer. The antibody targets a growth receptor found in large amounts on some cancer cells. Two mercury forms attached to it emit short-range electrons that damage DNA up close.

The labeled drug bound strongly, at 87 to 91 percent, to receptor-rich cancer cells and moved into their nuclei. Nuclear dose rose with the number of receptors on each cell line. Tumors in mice took up the drug on scans.
pmc-13270220:
Ali Keshavarz and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on whole-grain bread eating among university students in southwest Iran. A validated questionnaire was given face-to-face to 567 students at a medical sciences university in the 2024 to 2025 academic year. Knowledge, perceived barriers, and wider diet habits were scored.

Rarely eating whole-grain bread was reported by 42.15 percent of students, while 32.45 percent ate it at least one to three times weekly. Mean knowledge scored 13.88 and barriers 18.53 on the scales used. Eating rose with knowledge and fell as barriers rose, with correlations of 0.196 and minus 0.422. Barriers also tracked with less fruit, vegetable, and dairy intake and more sweet and salty snacks.
pmc-13270820:
Zobaer Akond is lead author of a 2026 genome-wide study of RNA interference gene families in Brassica rapa, an oilseed crop grown for vegetable oil and food. These genes help switch other genes off and defend plants against viruses and stress, but they had not been mapped in detail in this species.

The team found four DCL genes, 13 AGO genes, and six RDR genes spread across the plant's ten chromosomes. Their structures closely matched those of a well-studied relative, Arabidopsis. Analysis linked the genes to virus defence and gene silencing, and traced shared segments that suggest some genes arose by duplication. The authors frame the catalogue as a base for crop improvement.
pmc-13271420:
Xiaoliang Li and Qi Feng report a 2026 case of pneumonia in which lung wash fluid revealed two hard-to-grow bacteria at once. One was Tropheryma whipplei, the cause of Whipple's disease. The other was Chlamydia psittaci, a bird-linked germ that causes psittacosis. Finding both together in a lung infection is rare, and standard cultures often miss such organisms.

The patient was a 69-year-old male farmer with five days of high fever. Flu treatment and then a first antibiotic failed, and chest scans showed patchy shadows with thickened lining. A targeted gene sequencing test on lung fluid identified both bacteria. Treatment switched to two suitable antibiotics, fever fell fast, and scans cleared steadily over six months.
pmc-13271520:
Loema Moshi Buyi is lead author of a 2026 interview study of why intensive care nurses at Tanzania's Muhimbili National Hospital struggle to follow guidelines for suctioning breathing tubes. Suctioning keeps the airways of ventilated patients clear. Guidelines exist for doing it safely, yet adherence is weak in resource-limited settings.

Seventeen experienced nurses were interviewed. Three barrier groups emerged. The first was scarce resources, including too few staff, equipment, and supplies. The second was human and behavioural challenges, such as knowledge gaps and resistance to changing routine practice. The third was guidelines that were hard to access and felt untailored to local conditions. The authors conclude the problem is mainly systemic, not individual neglect.
pmc-13272220:
Lindsay A. Scans and fluid tests already showed such antibodies clear amyloid from the brain; this study checked the tissue itself.

The team compared a key memory region from six treated participants, who died between seven weeks and five years after their last dose, with nine matched untreated patients. Treated brains showed a strong reduction in amyloid burden, with some amyloid redistributed around small vessels. A tau-related measure near plaques fell, but established tangles did not change, and immune cell reactivity matched untreated patients. Plaques appeared to rebuild with time since the last dose.
pmc-13273520:
Muhammad Hassan Saeed leads a 2026 meta-analysis of colchicine, an anti-inflammatory drug, for preventing atrial fibrillation after heart and chest surgery. This irregular heartbeat is the most common rhythm problem after such surgery and links to heart failure, stroke, and death. The team pooled randomised trials published up to September 2025.

Twelve trials with 5,637 participants were included. Colchicine cut the incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation, with a risk ratio of 0.73, and both short and long courses worked. Gut side effects rose, including diarrhea, but bleeding, sepsis, and in-hospital death did not increase clearly. The authors support colchicine as a safe, inexpensive add-on, with short courses offering the best tolerability.
pmc-13273820:
Meng and colleagues write a 2026 letter to the editor about deep learning in gum disease diagnosis. The letter responds to a study by Valente and colleagues. That study used a YOLOv8l model to read dental images.

The writers praise the model's promise for periodontal diagnosis. Periodontal disease affects the gums and bone around teeth. They also raise concerns about class imbalance in training data. Rare disease stages may be underrepresented, skewing results. The letter points to Vision Transformers as another approach. It also urges combining images with other data types. Three-dimensional scans could add useful detail. The authors close with directions for stronger future studies.
pmc-13274420:
Ali Arshad and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on plastic beads designed to pull PFAS 'forever chemicals' out of water. PFAS persist in the environment and harm health, and ion exchange is a standard cleanup route. The team built their beads by a method that forms microscopic channels as the plastic hardens.

The beads swapped ions at a capacity of about one millimole per gram. For two short-chain PFAS, they soaked up the chemicals more than twice as fast at first as a leading commercial resin. Their grip on all tested PFAS was stronger, suiting them to dilute pollution, though the commercial resin held more overall. A salt and methanol wash stripped the beads completely clean for reuse.
pmc-13274620:
Kateryna Murlanova and a large team present a 2026 journal article showing that a gene in star-shaped brain support cells is required for normal thinking in mice. NPAS3 is a gene switch tied to cognitive problems in several psychiatric conditions, and it is strongly active in astrocytes, the brain's support cells. The team deleted it only in mature astrocytes.

The deletion lowered a mitochondrial glutamate carrier, cutting the cells' energy output and their lactate production. Neighboring neurons in the prefrontal cortex then fired less, grew fewer connection spines, and signaled more weakly. The mice performed poorly on a trace fear learning test. Giving lactate, the missing fuel, rescued their learning, tying astrocyte energy directly to cognition.
pmc-13275320:
Sammy H S Chan and colleagues report a 2026 journal article capturing the shapes of proteins caught mid-fold on the ribosome, the cell's protein factory. Proteins often start folding while still being built, pausing in stable halfway forms that vanish once free. Those intermediate shapes could not be predicted by current AI tools and had never been seen in detail.

Using fluorine-based magnetic resonance tricks engineered into the protein, plus computer simulations, the team solved two intermediate structures of an antibody-like domain still attached to the ribosome. Each had a native-like folded core but loose, nonnative ends, letting them grip a helper chaperone in distinct ways. The shapes suggest parallel folding routes and are conserved across the protein family.
pmc-13275920:
Mohamed Abdelhamed and co-authors report a 2026 materials article on putting a sugar industry waste to work in plastic. Making sugar from beets leaves behind piles of precipitated calcium carbonate, a chalky powder that can blow into water and air. The team mixed this waste into PVC, a common plastic, at several loadings.

Adding the powder made the plastic resist heat better, losing far less weight when heated. A small loading, about one part in twenty, raised bending strength by roughly a third. Heavier loadings hurt stretch, pulling strength, and impact resistance, though. Microscope images showed the powder spread evenly at low loadings but clumped at high ones, which explains the pattern. Density and water uptake rose slightly as more powder was added.
pmc-13276120:
Sebastian Riemann and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on how obesity and asthma feed each other. More than six hundred fifty million adults worldwide live with obesity. People with obesity develop asthma more often, and most asthma patients in trials and registries carry excess weight.

The authors explain that extra fat harms asthma through many routes, not just one inflammation type. Fat tissue sends faulty chemical signals, stirs low-grade inflammation, upsets metabolism, and physically squeezes the lungs. Asthma control is poorer and flare-ups are more common. Losing weight, by lifestyle change, drugs, or surgery, improves symptoms and lung function across asthma types. Modern gut-hormone drugs used for weight loss still need dedicated asthma trials, the authors argue.
pmc-13276320:
Latifa Ou-Skou and co-authors report a 2026 case report on a gallstone that blocked the small intestine. Gallstone ileus is an uncommon cause of bowel blockage, mostly in older patients. A stone escapes the gallbladder through an abnormal channel into the gut, then lodges and obstructs it.

The patient was a sixty-nine-year-old woman with diabetes and heart disease, ill for five days with belly pain, vomiting, and no bowel movements. A plain X-ray hinted at the problem but could not confirm it. A CT scan showed the blockage, air inside the bile ducts, and a layered stone stuck in the lower small intestine. Special reconstructions even showed the channel from gallbladder to duodenum. Surgeons removed the stone through the bowel and deferred gallbladder surgery given her risks. She recovered without complications.
pmc-13276520:
Xue Tian and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on using tobacco straw char to grow safer, better pak choi. Heavy metals like lead and cadmium pollute much Chinese farmland and slip into vegetables. Turning waste tobacco straw into biochar could lock metals in soil while using up farm residue.

The char loosened the soil, raised its organic matter and key nutrients, and shifted soil bacteria toward greater diversity. Metal levels in the edible shoots fell by about a third for cadmium and nearly two fifths for lead. A middle rate, three percent of soil weight, scored best overall in the authors' combined evaluation.
pmc-13276720:
Matteo Aloi and co-authors present a 2026 journal article mapping how features of narcissistic personality disorder connect to each other. Modern views hold that grandiosity hides a vulnerable core of shame and rejection sensitivity. Reading one's own and others' minds, called metacognition, may hold the system together.

In the resulting web, that vulnerability sat at the center as the most connected feature. Sensitivity to others and mind-reading integration ranked next. It tied strongly to negative emotions and detachment, while grandiosity tied to antagonism. That integration linked harmful traits with distress between people, acting as a bridge. The authors say the pattern fits a therapy model that targets this integrative capacity.
pmc-13276820:
Paul Schulan leads a 2026 laboratory study of how gas plasma changes a model protein. The protein is ovalbumin, the main protein in egg white, and plasma is a charged gas that makes reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. The team made twelve plasma mixes and mapped chemical changes on the protein.

Using precise mass measurement, they found more than eighty kinds of oxidative change, located amino acid by amino acid. Atomic oxygen and hydrogen peroxide played a large role in the damage pattern. Each gas mix left its own fingerprint, with different hot spots on the protein. Knowing those patterns may help link protein oxidation to disease and to plasma use in medicine.
pmc-13277020:

Twenty-seven academics from seven fields took part. Reasons to review included helping science, learning, career growth, personal satisfaction, and pay. Barriers included heavy workload, weak recognition, doubts about skill, worries about honesty, and poor journal handling. Weighing the two sides shaped each choice. Better recognition and journal support could keep reviewers willing, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278620:
Christina Sauer leads a 2026 mixed methods study of a cancer care app called SOFIA, tested with patients including those in palliative care. The app combines symptom self-reports that patients enter electronically with a coaching component. Interviews at two points in a twelve-week period were paired with app usage data from active users.
