pmc-13471320:
Li and colleagues engineer a protective coating for healing vesicles aimed at slowing intervertebral disc degeneration, the breakdown of spinal discs that causes chronic back pain, in 2026 regenerative medicine research. The vesicles, called exosomes, come from human embryonic stem cells and carry repair signals. But the degenerated disc is hostile: reactive oxygen molecules and inflammation destroy them quickly, pushing disc cells toward inflammatory death and aging.

The team armored the exosomes with nanoplates of manganese dioxide, creating a system named hESC-Exos@MnO2 in the study. The armor breaks down in the acidic, peroxide-rich disc environment, soaking up reactive oxygen species as it dissolves. Released manganese ions then work alongside the exosomes to rebuild matrix material between disc cells. Treated cells showed less oxidative injury, partly preserved mitochondrial function, and reduced cell-cycle arrest. Li argues the combined shield-and-repair design outperforms naked exosomes in this setting.
pmc-13471520:
Byagamy and colleagues measured how well the deworming drug praziquantel works, and how fast children get reinfected, in a high-transmission corner of northern Uganda. Their 2026 cohort study screened 802 primary school children aged 5 to 16 for Schistosoma mansoni, the blood fluke behind intestinal schistosomiasis, and followed them for 24 weeks.

Baseline infection stood at 34.8% of the children tested, and the 279 infected children received a single standard dose. That dose cured 82.1% of infections at four weeks but cut egg output by only 32.9% overall, while a second dose for non-responders cured 93.9% of them. By 24 weeks, 7.7% of cured children were reinfected and true new infections ran at 5.0% of the uninfected group, prompting a call for twice-yearly dosing.
pmc-13471620:
Papadopoulou and Feldman review how doctors measure disease in juvenile dermatomyositis, a childhood autoimmune disease attacking muscle and skin, and where the toolbox still falls short. Their 2026 update walks through strength scales, skin scores, composite indices, imaging, and patient-reported outcomes built over decades of international work.

Single lab values mislead: more than 20% of children show normal muscle enzyme levels at diagnosis, and enzymes can normalize on steroids while disease stays active. Skin scores carry real meaning, since roughly 40% improvement in the CDASI activity score tracks meaningful quality-of-life gains for patients. The authors' stated goal is one simple unified tool capturing every important health domain, built with strong patient input.
pmc-13473020:
Jääskeläinen and colleagues present a 2026 review of opioid-blocking drugs, such as naltrexone, for alcohol use disorder. These drugs are among the best-supported treatments, yet their benefit is modest and varies widely between patients. The review asks how brief receptor blockade could produce lasting change, and whether timing of the dose is the missing piece.

The classic account says the drugs blunt alcohol's reward and craving. An extinction account adds that drinking while blocked weakens the learned drinking habit itself, which fits trials where patients take the drug only before drinking occasions. Animal work, though, shows timing relative to drinking sessions can decide the effect, in ways extinction alone does not explain. The review argues trials should treat timing as a variable, not an afterthought, to find who benefits and when.
pmc-13473320:
Shen-Hao Liu and co-authors review new care options in 2026 for an aggressive form of B-cell leukemia in adults. In this subtype, a gene called KMT2A is broken and rejoined in a harmful way. Standard chemo plus stem cell transplant still leaves high relapse rates. The review gathers proof for antibody drugs, cell therapy, and a new class of pills called menin blockers.

Antibody drugs that link immune cells to cancer cells now help in first care and after relapse. Cell therapy made from a patient own T cells can work, though cancer may hide the target or switch type. Menin blockers attack the gene fault at its root and show early promise. The authors map where each option fits and what blocks wider use.
pmc-13473420:
Akdoğan and colleagues present a 2026 study of pathways into anhedonia, the loss of pleasure that marks major depression. The team tested whether insecure attachment, a pattern of uneasy close relationships, connects to depression severity through trouble managing emotions and through anhedonia itself. They studied 102 unmedicated patients with major depression and 102 matched controls, using clinician-rated scales for depression and pleasure.

Medication-free patients matter here because drugs can blur the very pathways under study. The model traces a chain: shaky attachment limits access to emotion regulation strategies, and that limit deepens anhedonia and overall severity.  If the chain holds, therapy gains a target order: rebuild emotion strategies and the pleasure system may recover with mood, instead of treating anhedonia as a leftover symptom.
pmc-13473620:
Orlando and colleagues in South Australia tested in 2026 a side road for low back pain that steers folk away from the emergency ward. Most back pain there is not grave, yet ward care is slow and dear. Their path sent such folk to a team clinic, with phone app checks to track the mend. The team read the charts of 143 patients from the first ten months, and heard from a score in talks.

Most patients signed up for the app checks. At two weeks, pain and daily task scores had both gained by a clear mark, while mood scores had not. Nine in ten kept clear of the ward for three months. In talks, folk prized fast slots, care that fit their hopes, and the app as a spur to move. The authors pitch the path as a sound swap for ward care.
pmc-13473920:
Ragab Farouk and colleagues developed a family of compounds that block a human fat-splitting enzyme to fight coronaviruses of many kinds. Coronaviruses need host fats to copy themselves, so blocking the enzyme, called ATGL, starves them of building material.

Six blockers were tested against stand-in viruses from all four coronavirus genera using protein, gene, and imaging checks. One compound, DABPU-DE, showed the strongest antiviral action and the best safety margin of the six. Its small chemical group grips the enzyme tightly, while a bulkier cousin bound poorly and worked worst. Paired with remdesivir, a drug that jams the virus's copying machine, DABPU-DE suppressed SARS-CoV-2 strongly in lab-grown cells, Farouk reports.
pmc-13474520:
Huang and co-authors recount saving two lives in sequence. A 31-year-old woman at 38 weeks of pregnancy arrived with tearing chest pain from a type A aortic dissection, a rip in the body's main artery. Their 2026 case report describes imaging that confirmed the tear from the ascending aorta into the arch, with the right coronary artery involved and the aortic root stretched to 40 millimeters.

The team delivered a healthy baby girl by emergency cesarean first, with strong Apgar scores of 9, 9, and 10. They then embolized the uterine arteries to guard against bleeding before replacing the torn aorta in a Bentall operation with a coronary bypass. The mother went home on day 14 after surgery and showed sound aortic remodeling at two months. Published mortality for this emergency runs near 12% for mothers and 28% for babies.
pmc-13474720:
Xiaoli Zhou and co-authors improve a bone cement in 2026 that can be injected through a needle to fill bone gaps. Six food- or drug-grade additives were screened for easier injection without weak or slow setting. One additive, a cellulose-based thickener at two percent, gave the best balance. Injection ease rose to about ninety-five percent with little change in set time or strength.

The tuned cement was tested in human cadaver wrist fractures with three fix plans: pins alone, cement alone, or both. Cement groups resisted twisting and heavy pressing better than pins alone. Under normal loads all plans held alike. The cement could serve as a filler that also adds real support.
pmc-13474820:
Jie Ma and co-authors follow heart risk after epilepsy in 2026 using United Kingdom Biobank data on nearly half a million adults. Just over seven thousand had epilepsy at the start. Heart outcomes covered blocked arteries, heart failure, rhythm faults, stroke, and heart-related death. Follow-up ran a median of more than thirteen years.

About twenty-nine percent of the epilepsy group developed heart disease, double the share in peers. Raised risk held for every single outcome, with stroke showing the steepest climb. Adjusting for shared gene risk barely moved the numbers. Heart checks may belong in long-term epilepsy care plans.
pmc-13476720:
R. Bernardon and co-authors report in 2026 on machine-supported resuscitation for children in cardiac arrest across the French pediatric network. Records covered 164 children treated from 2019 to 2023 at network centers. Most arrests struck inside hospitals, and most children had prior heart disease. Survival was checked at intensive care exit, hospital exit, and one year.

Survival sat near thirty percent at hospital exit and a touch lower at one year. Male sex and higher lactate a day after arrest marked poorer odds. Leg vessel access for the machine marked better odds in the model. Finding candidates before arrest is urged, since post-arrest rescue stays grim.
pmc-13476920:
Katelyn A Russell and co-authors deliver a repeat DNA stretch in 2026 into mice lacking a gene tied to Lou Gehrig disease and dementia. The repeat in C9orf72 is the most common gene cause of both diseases. A virus carrier injected at birth spread the repeat widely, with strong reach into the spinal cord. Mice carried graded loss of their own gene copy to test combined effects.

Repeat carriers grew mildly weaker over time, while coordination faults tracked gene loss more than repeats. Spinal zones showed repeat protein buildup, motor cell loss, and immune cell activation. Sparse marks of the hallmark protein fault also appeared, plus faulty message splicing. The mild model suits early-stage drug tests.
pmc-13477320:
Yang Yue and colleagues published a 2026 review on how coxsackievirus B3, a leading cause of viral heart inflammation, damages the heart through its surrounding cell environment. About one in five cases progress to a weakened, enlarged heart. The review pulls together research on the many cell types living in heart muscle and how each one responds during infection.

Fibroblasts, blood vessel lining cells, mast cells, and several immune cell types each play a part in how the illness develops. The authors then survey treatment ideas aimed at this environment, including drugs that tune cell behavior and smarter ways to deliver them. They also discuss organoid models, computer tools, and blood markers that could support more precise diagnosis and care.
pmc-13478020:
Wantong Zhao and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study of chromosome problems in miscarriage tissue using SNP arrays, a high-throughput DNA scanning method. Chromosome errors are a leading cause of pregnancy loss, and careful typing can guide advice for couples trying again. The team collected 564 miscarriage samples for analysis.

About 60 percent of samples carried such a flaw. Extra chromosome copies, called trisomy, appeared in 225 cases and involved nearly every one, while a missing X chromosome appeared in 39 cases. Twenty-three cases had three full chromosome sets, and 32 had pieces of chromosomes missing or doubled. About 40 percent of losses showed no such variant, which the authors credit to possible single-gene causes that need gene-reading methods instead.
pmc-13479820:
Lili Xu and coauthors published a 2026 review and meta-analysis of anxiety and depression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease that worsens over time. Low mood and worry are common in this group, yet reported rates vary wildly between studies. Four data banks were searched from their start to late October 2025 under standard reporting guidelines.

Two screeners worked on their own, pulled out rate figures, and rated study quality. Pooled numbers give a world average for each illness, while checks of study gaps hunt for what drives the spread, such as region, test tool, or how sick patients were. The authors mean the pooled numbers to support routine mental health screening in fibrosis clinics and to size future treatment trials.
pmc-13483120:
Christine Sevilla-Dedieu and co-authors present a 2026 phone survey on whether a taste for risk predicts healthy habits among French adults. The random sample held 2,666 people insured by the national health system. Each gave social and health details plus a thirty-item score of risk appetite across life domains, and the team modelled three habits: regular sport, not smoking, and a normal weight range.

Just under three in five played sport often, near seven in ten did not smoke, and about three in five sat in the normal weight band. Risk scores linked firmly to each habit, yet the direction flipped by habit. A bold streak may feed sport while fighting weight control, for instance. Health-minded people thus show no single pattern; each habit trades risk off in its own way, which prevention drives should respect.
pmc-13483420:
Pan Jiang and co-authors share a 2026 case report on a jaw joint problem where scans and motion told different parts of the story. A 22-year-old woman arrived with three months of clicking in both jaw joints and pain on the left. Standard criteria and MRI both pointed to discs slipping forward, then snapping back on opening.

Her first splint, built to hold the jaw forward, made the left side worse, so the team stopped it. A computerised jaw tracker then mapped her motion, drawing a figure-eight path with poor overlap between repeats. Forward travel on the left ran near three to four millimetres against ten to eleven on the right. A pivot splint followed; short checks showed easier motion, lighter symptoms, and a better disc position on repeat scan. One case proves little, the authors note, yet motion data sharpens judgement when still images mislead.
pmc-13483620:
Julia Michelin and co-authors train deep learning models to spot dental problems from video rather than still photographs. Their 2026 validation study recorded 708 videos with a toothbrush fitted with a tiny mouth camera. Thousands of extracted frames were labeled by two dental experts for findings such as decay, fillings, plaque, and staining, plus tooth type.

The findings model reached strong overall precision, performing best on amalgam fillings and decay. A separate tooth-type model scored even higher, with molars and premolars identified most reliably. Performance held up despite no fixed filming routine for users. Embedding such checks into a daily brushing device could support remote monitoring and earlier care, especially where dentists are scarce.
pmc-13483720:
Stephani Edwina Lucia builds a live imaging window into the pancreas to watch pancreatic cancer blood vessels change over time. Published in 2026, the study implants tumor cells and a viewing window in mice, labels vessel walls with a fluorescent marker, and tracks glowing red blood cells for flow. Repeated viewing of the same regions follows growth of this highly lethal cancer.

Time-lapse viewing caught vessels sprouting, being pruned away, widening, and collapsing as tumors progressed. Flow varied sharply from vessel to vessel, with some channels losing flow abruptly while neighbors flickered or partly recovered. Vessel-targeting drugs have repeatedly failed in this cancer despite strong growth signals. Watching supply lines evolve at cell level may reveal when and where such drugs could actually help.
pmc-13484320: Walid Nabgan and co-authors are named on a 2026 journal notice concerning a catalysis article about reforming and cracking microplastic waste dissolved in phenol. The notice is an expression of concern only, recording that the editor flagged unresolved questions about accountability for the work on July 23, 2026. Related publications show a broader pattern that casts doubt on reliability. The authors offered an explanation that neither settled nor confirmed the concerns. Readers should treat the flagged findings as unverified while the journal process continues.
pmc-13486120:
Cong Chen connects a little-known antibody-factory protein to how severe pancreatic inflammation becomes. Published in 2026, the study profiles blood immune cells from mild and severe pancreatitis patients across disease stages with single-cell sequencing. B cell programs tied to antibody production grow more prominent late in severe disease, with the protein MZB1 standing out.

Mouse experiments test cause directly, since animals lacking MZB1 suffer worse pancreatic inflammation. Missing MZB1 also cuts IgA antibody output and weakens the intestinal barrier, letting gut-driven inflammation feed back into the crisis. Supporting the MZB1 to IgA to barrier chain may therefore calm severe pancreatitis from an unexpected direction, beyond the innate immune targets that dominate current thinking. Humoral immunity earns a seat at the severity table.
pmc-13486420:
Nevin Belder builds a gene signature that flags which ulcerative colitis patients are sliding toward colon cancer. Published in 2026, the single-author analysis mines transcript data from colitis and cancer cohorts separately, hunting changes that repeat across both. A cell-state program called epithelial-mesenchymal transition keeps surfacing among switched-up genes.

Twenty-four shared candidate genes narrowed to fourteen that run high in colitis-linked precancer compared with quiet colitis, each separating the states strongly. Machine learning distilled a seven-gene panel whose combined score climbs stepwise from quiet disease through precancer to cancer. Long-standing colitis carries real cancer risk, yet colonoscopy alone cannot see molecular momentum. A tissue score that rises along the danger path could focus surveillance on the patients who need it most.
pmc-13487920:
Asal Kamani Fard and Mohammad Paydar study women's walking and well-being in six middle-income neighborhoods of Santiago, Chile, in a 2026 survey. Walking is a main way women get around, yet fear and poor street conditions can discourage it. The team used questionnaires with both closed and open questions, plus maps and street audits to record the built setting.

Women named insecurity as the chief barrier, tied to crime, weak lighting, and unsafe streets. Walking habits were linked with how well women felt, though the design cannot show cause. Income, work, social ties, and street quality all played a part. The authors urge safer, better lit, and more welcoming streets.
pmc-13488120:
Bochu Liu and co-authors map online fresh food ordering across Shanghai neighborhoods in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Delivery apps may ease shopping where stores are scarce, yet use may still favor richer areas. Citywide order records for green groceries, supermarkets, and fruit were linked to over eleven thousand small areas, with local income, age mix, car ownership, and nearby food shops recorded for each area.

Orders clustered in better-off neighborhoods, and rates ran lower where shares of older, younger, or low-income residents were higher. Areas with more nearby supermarkets and grocery stores ordered less online across all food types. Car-free areas ordered more, which hints delivery helps when travel is hard, though gaps remain.
pmc-13488220:
Heng Xiao and Yanbin Ren survey human papillomavirus infection among women in southern Hebei, China, in a 2026 study from Handan Central Hospital. Cervical samples from more than forty-one thousand patients and health-check visitors between 2022 and 2025 were typed for twenty-three virus strains, split into high-risk types tied to cancer and low-risk types. Rates were compared across age groups and cervical disease levels.

About twenty-four percent of samples tested positive overall. Types 52, 16, and 58 were the most common, and high-risk types dominated the findings. Infection peaked in women under twenty and rose again after sixty. Rates ran much higher in women with precancerous changes or cervical cancer than in the general group. The authors offer the data for screening and vaccine planning.
pmc-13488720:
Ösken and team screened nutritional health in 113 patients with Sjögren disease, an autoimmune condition best known for dry eyes and mouth but able to attack organs throughout the body. Their 2026 study split patients into 26 with such organ involvement and 87 without, scoring nutrition with two blood-based indexes that combine albumin, cholesterol, and immune cell counts.

Patients with organ involvement showed worse nutrition on both indexes, with higher risk scores and lower protective values than the comparison group. They also carried certain autoantibodies, anti-Ro and anti-Ro-52, more often in this sample. The nutrition scores correlated with a standard disease activity index the clinicians recorded. Average age was about fifty-six, and nearly ninety-five percent of patients were women. Ösken recommends both cheap, routine-lab scores for flagging malnutrition risk in rheumatology clinics.
pmc-13490420:
Yeh and team scanned the brains of 24 younger and 27 older adults while they judged picture sequences showing sports actions in sensible or scrambled order. Following motion sequences underpins daily skills like driving, and aging may change the strategy used. Their 2026 imaging study varied sequence order across three conditions and recorded both coherence ratings and brain activity for each quartet of pictures.

Younger adults' ratings tracked the true ordering faithfully across the conditions presented in the scanner. Older adults were less sensitive to ordered sequences yet still rated them above randomized ones. Their brains leaned harder on left frontal regions and on default-mode areas, the network tied to internal knowledge, especially for scrambled sequences. Yeh reads this as a shift from bottom-up watching toward top-down guessing, not simple sensory decline.
pmc-13491720:
Xiangyu Guo and four colleagues ask in 2026 whether blood chemistry profiles can sharpen genetic predictions of feed efficiency in pigs. Feed conversion ratio, the feed needed per unit of growth, is costly to measure head-on, so breeders predict breeding values from DNA. The team tested whether adding metabolite profiles from magnetic resonance spectroscopy sharpened those predictions in Duroc pigs.

The herd held 8,174 pigs, with males at a test station providing feed records and females checked through their offspring. Adding the chemistry data lifted prediction accuracy by only about two percent. Pairing the trait with daily gain added a gain of the same small size. Neither gain reached statistical significance. The authors blame one-time sampling and suggest better sampling designs could let chemistry data contribute more.
pmc-13491820:
Hui Jiang and four colleagues test in 2026 whether music tempo can sharpen self-control in men recovering from drug addiction, and whether psychological resilience changes the answer. Forty-four men, split into high and low resilience groups by questionnaire, performed a reaction task where drug pictures meant withholding a response. Brain waves were recorded under fast, medium, and slow music plus silence.

High-resilience men responded faster overall. Brain signals showed low-resilience men spending more effort on early conflict detection, while high-resilience men allocated resources more efficiently at a later stage. Under slow music the high-resilience group showed a clear boost in conflict monitoring that vanished at fast tempo. The authors argue that music-based rehabilitation should be tuned to each patient's psychological profile rather than applied uniformly.
pmc-13492020:
Huiling Zhou and six colleagues build in 2026 a deep learning system that flags likely cyberbullying perpetrators among Chinese university students, a group that is hard to spot because offenders are rare. Only fifty-four of 660 surveyed students admitted perpetrating, so ordinary algorithms drowned in the majority class. The team answered with two-stage training plus a weighted penalty that forces attention onto the rare offenders.

The model recovered ninety-two percent of true perpetrators, far ahead of standard methods such as random forests. Explanation analysis ranked screen time, negative emotions, weak school connectedness, online disinhibition, violent media exposure, and deviant friends as the strongest predictors. School connectedness appeared to buffer several risks at once, which the authors say gives prevention programs a concrete lever.
pmc-13495220:
Congcong Liu and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 study from China, a leadership course for intensive care nurses. Nurse leadership shapes care quality, yet courses aimed at bedside nurses, rather than managers, are rare in China. Thirty-five nurses from two teaching hospitals took part, with about half given the course and half serving as the comparison group.

The course ran eight sessions on team building, planning, emotional skill, communication, and leading change. Afterward the trained group scored higher on leadership scales covering organization, planning, and people skills, and also on confidence and intensive care competence. Interviews with nine nurses added three themes: a wider grasp of what leadership means, shifts in their own thinking and habits, and hurdles plus hopes for future rounds. The authors urge nurse managers to spread such training more widely.
pmc-13495420:
Diego F Wyszynski reviews, in a 2026 article, pregnancy in systemic lupus erythematosus, a long-term autoimmune disease that mostly strikes women in their childbearing years. Lupus and pregnancy strain each other: the disease raises the odds of baby loss, early birth, blood pressure crisis, clots, and small babies, above all when kidneys are involved. Pregnancy can also stir the disease back to life.

Better watching and care have cut complications, yet risk stays above that of other mothers, and foreseeing flares or bad outcomes remains hard. Placental failure and immune attack are the suspected engines. Some lupus drugs can harm a fetus, which forces careful drug choice. The best odds come when conception waits for a quiet stretch of disease, with close joint care by several specialties and pregnancy-safe treatment holding the disease down.
pmc-13495520:
Lucas M Seuren and colleagues ask, in a 2026 interview study, why family doctors in Ontario take up, keep using, or drop a virtual team support line called SCOPE. The phone service links primary care doctors with hospital and community help for complex patients. The team interviewed twenty primary care doctors, three internists, and six project staff over video calls.

Seven themes shaped use. Doctors weighed a health system they saw as broken, plain awareness that the line existed, and whether its services matched their needs. A tool that felt useful and easy won a first try; habit and the effort of change then decided whether use stuck. Feeling heard by the service kept doctors coming back. The authors say such lines help only when doctors feel backed, grasp the gains, and get time to learn the new way of working.
pmc-13499920:
Divya Deodhar and colleagues compare in 2026 bloodstream infections caused by Candida auris, a hardy drug-resistant yeast, with infections from other Candida species at a university hospital in Muscat, Oman. Yeast in the blood is life-threatening and increasingly healthcare-linked. Their retrospective review covered all adults with such infections over five years, from January 2018 to December 2022, comparing risk links, outcomes, and drug susceptibility between groups.

Of 160 patients, 58 carried the resistant species while 102 carried other Candida types. Prior colonisation with Candida species was the strongest link to the resistant infection, raising odds several-fold in the reported ratios, and recent healthcare contact within ninety days also linked strongly. The authors suggest one drug family, echinocandins, as an early empirical choice when these warning links are present, while local susceptibility patterns are confirmed.
pmc-13500420:
Abigail Hui En Chan and colleagues assess in 2026 drug resistance in a gut worm of livestock that can also infect people, sampled in Thailand. Benzimidazole dewormers are heavily used, and resistant worms had been found at high levels locally. Working with 60 adult Trichostrongylus colubriformis worms from Sukhothai and Satun provinces, the team read resistance directly from a tubulin gene, a standard marker. A mitochondrial gene mapped diversity and population structure.

Strong resistance was present, with the mixed genotype carrying one resistant and one sensitive copy forming most worms. Genetic diversity ran high, while Thai worms differed sharply from those in other countries, hinting at limited gene flow across borders. That isolation cuts both ways, since local control measures could likely contain resistance spread, provided watching of this zoonotic worm continues.
pmc-13500720:
Zhiheng Tai and four co-authors report a 2026 study of a titanium composite made by laser directed energy deposition, a form of metal 3D printing. They built samples from the alloy Ti6Al4V, which is strong and light but wears poorly, and tried to grow hard titanium nitride particles inside it during printing. One route deposited the metal under a nitrogen-argon mix, while a second route remelted the surface under pure nitrogen. Dry sliding wear tests ran at room temperature and at 300 degrees Celsius.

The remelted samples grew larger, more densely spread nitride particles. Their friction was somewhat higher, yet wear volume fell by about 44.8 percent at room temperature and 78.8 percent at the higher temperature compared with the plain alloy. The directly deposited samples, with sparser and smaller particles, improved much less.
pmc-13500820:
Lilla Otrokocsi leads a five-author team with a 2026 mouse study of whether vaccines given in pregnancy affect how the offspring act. Pregnant mice received the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine BNT162b2, a flu vaccine, or a control, and pups were tested at four and eight weeks of age. Blood and fetal brain tissue were checked for immune markers: cytokines, the P2X7 receptor, BDNF, and fat oxidation damage. A comparison group received poly(I:C), which mimics viral infection.

The COVID vaccine raised two maternal cytokines modestly without inflaming the fetal brain. Some mild, age- and sex-linked changes in how pups acted appeared, but no consistent autism-like pattern emerged at either age. The flu vaccine caused smaller, passing effects, while poly(I:C) triggered strong inflammation and lasting changes. The authors conclude that prenatal COVID vaccination showed no widespread harm to brain development in this model.
pmc-13501620:
Derya Demirtaş Esmer leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 study of whether low muscle mass blunts chemotherapy response in advanced ovarian cancer. The retrospective study covered 52 overweight or obese women with stage III to IV epithelial ovarian cancer treated between 2019 and 2022 with platinum and taxane chemotherapy before interval surgery. Muscle mass was measured on baseline CT scans at the third lumbar vertebra. Women were split into low and high muscle mass groups at the cohort median, and those combining obesity with low muscle were flagged.

That combined group responded worst: response rates were 46.7 percent against 62.2 percent for the others, and disease control rates were 80 percent against 100 percent. Body mass index alone and low muscle mass alone showed no significant effect. Median disease-free survival after surgery was 19.3 months. The authors propose muscle assessment as a risk marker, while noting overall survival data were immature.
pmc-13501820:
Ming Zhou leads a five-author team with a 2026 study of whether the choice of anti-seizure drug changes survival in low-grade glioma, where epilepsy strikes most patients. The team combined lenses: machine learning over 105 targets of ten anti-seizure drugs, molecular docking, a past-records patient cohort, and cell experiments. A thirteen-gene signature predicted prognosis. One sodium channel gene, SCN9A, emerged as a hazard factor, while two glutamate receptor genes, GRIN2C and GRIN3A, acted as protectors.

Three drugs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and lacosamide, were predicted to extend survival by blocking the hazard gene's product. Phenobarbital pointed the other way, shortening survival by suppressing the two protective genes. The cohort check supported those directions, and bench tests agreed: blocking SCN9A curbed malignant cell behaviour, while suppressing the protective pair enhanced it. The authors offer the work as guidance for drug choice.
pmc-13503820:
Xiaoyu Xue leads a team showing how a genome-guard complex tags proteins with SUMO, a small modifier, in a 2026 study. Most tagging enzymes work alone, but the Nse2 enzyme only works as part of the larger Smc5/6 complex. How the other parts of the complex help was unclear.

Tests in yeast showed that DNA boosts the complex's tagging action by pulling enzyme and target close. Four partner parts use their grip on DNA to support that boost. Parts that bind ATP, the cell fuel, help the complex latch onto DNA and change shape for the task. The findings frame Smc5/6 as a joint tagging machine switched on by DNA and fuel together.
pmc-13503920:
Alejandro Santos-Mayo leads a team that built an AI model which predicts brain wave responses to words and pictures, in a 2026 paper. Brain waves read from the scalp, called EEG, show how the brain reacts to meaning and feeling. Most AI work decodes those waves; far less work runs the other way.

Their model, Concept2Brain, turns a picture or text into a rich trait vector with a public vision-language tool, then maps that vector into a brain wave space. The fake responses it makes closely match real ones recorded from people. The model is offered as a free web service, so labs can build open EEG data sets for any concept or image. The authors see it as a step toward modeling brain activity with AI.
pmc-13505420:
Yi He and colleagues built a structural model of apolipoprotein A-II, the second most common protein carried on HDL, the particles that move cholesterol out of tissues. The protein grips lipids more tightly than its better-known partner APOA1, yet its shape on the particle was unsettled. The team combined computer modelling with targeted mutations to test how the chain folds.

Their model wraps the protein's paired chains as a double hairpin belt around disc-shaped HDL. Most charged building blocks sit in the hairpin loop, and internal bridges plus ring stacking hold the fold steady. Two strong lipid-binding stretches appear in each half of the pair, and the hairpin seems built to meet partner proteins. Chemical crosslinking found sixteen links between parts of the chain, and fifteen of them fit the belt model. The result gives lipid researchers a picture for explaining how APOA2 shapes HDL behaviour.
pmc-13506120:
Tony Tannoury and co-authors report outcomes for the longest front-of-neck fusions in their series, spanning four or five levels, drawn from 1,428 cervical fusion patients treated between 2009 and 2021. Twenty-seven patients met the study rules and had at least two years of follow-up. The graft material was the patient's own hip bone, fixed with a front plate and screws.

Function and pain improved markedly: average disability grade dropped by more than half, and neck and arm pain scores fell with clear statistical strength. Neck alignment also improved on imaging, and every patient achieved solid fusion. Swallowing trouble was the commonest early problem, affecting about thirty percent, but it faded to a small share by late follow-up. Three patients developed wear at a neighbouring segment. The authors conclude the extended operation gives excellent results for multi-level cord compression when patients are chosen well.
pmc-13507020:
Anna Piotrowska and colleagues report 2026 mouse tests of cenicriviroc, a drug that blocks two chemokine receptors tied to nerve pain. Mice had a chronic squeeze injury to the sciatic nerve, a standard model of nerve pain. Twice-daily doses were compared with morphine over sixteen days, and spinal tissue was checked for pain-related signals.

On day three, pain relief matched morphine, and on days eight and sixteen the new drug worked better. Mice given cenicriviroc before morphine also lost less response to morphine over time. Spinal readings showed lower pain-driving signals and higher calming ones at key points. Dual blockade may offer a fresh route for nerve pain care.
pmc-13508220:
Yuanyuan Yin and four co-authors pilot a seminar-case teaching model for postgraduate students in orthodontics, the field of teeth straightening, in 2026 work. Chinese training in this field leans on lectures and apprenticeships, which can leave reasoning skills underbuilt. Their model mixes seminar debate with real case work. Sixty-four students from 27 dental schools joined a summer program and were split into six small groups. Each group, led by a seasoned teacher, worked through three complex cases.

Surveys before and after showed strong approval of the model. More than four fifths of students rated it better than traditional teaching. Large majorities reported gains in diagnosis, treatment planning, and clinical reasoning. Most felt ready to apply what they learned in clinic. Gains varied oddly with experience, dipping for the middle group. The authors present the model as a workable upgrade for specialist training.
pmc-13508520:
Li Ye, Maoting Chen, Qianling Wei, and Yue Wang study whether starting tube feeding within a day of heart surgery helps young children recover, in 2026 work. Feeding timing after congenital heart repair is disputed. Records covered 246 children aged one month to three years operated between 2021 and 2023. The early group, 128 children, began feeding within twenty-four hours. Infection rates, nutrition blood levels, and time in intensive care and hospital were compared.

Early feeding came with far fewer hospital infections, about fifteen percent against twenty-seven percent. Surgical wound infections also ran lower in the early group. Blood nutrition markers a week after surgery were higher with early feeding. Those children left intensive care sooner and went home days earlier on average. Adjusted models named delayed feeding an independent risk factor for hospital infection. The authors back starting feeds within a day when the child's state allows.
pmc-13509320:
Walid Atiki, Najia Ameur, Atika Zidouh, Abdelmoula Elouardi, and Latifa Tahri present a 2026 field survey of drug resistance in bacteria taken from broiler farms in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra region of Morocco. The group sampled manure, drinking troughs, farm soil, more distant fields, and well water across 13 farms. In total they collected 543 samples between late 2023 and spring 2025.

Escherichia coli turned up in about a third of samples and Salmonella in about a quarter. Roughly six in ten isolates of each kind resisted drugs from three or more classes. Resistance was most common in manure, troughs, and farm soil. Resistant bacteria also appeared in nearby soil and well water. The authors say the pattern calls for tighter farm hygiene and joint human and animal health monitoring.
pmc-13510020:
Jiang and co-authors optimise the finger bones of a biomimetic robot hand. Their 2026 paper tackles a design tension: compact hands lose versatility. With total finger length fixed, the team asks how to split it among the phalanges. Designs were scored three ways. The criteria were grasp capability in a shared workspace, kinematic dexterity from the Jacobian matrix, and key-press range for typing-like strikes.

A full grid search produced distinct optima per criterion, and Pareto analysis found 117 non-dominated designs balancing the three. Key-press range proved the most sensitive objective, varying by about a quarter across designs. A hierarchical strategy that privileged key-pressing while balancing the rest yielded a recommended compromise. Built and tested, it achieved a 98.8 percent keystroke success rate over 1,000 cross-row strikes without wrist movement. Grasp and dexterity validation remains future work.
pmc-13510820:
Nakao and colleagues tested in 2026 a body composition measure, intracellular water scaled by height squared, as a partner to the standard skeletal muscle index. Both come from bioelectrical impedance analysis, a method that sends a weak current through the body. The standard index can mislead when fluid balance is off, since extra water outside cells inflates it. The team studied 477 hospital patients and split results by sex, weight class, and hydration level.

Nakao found the water-based measure tracked body mass index more strongly than the muscle index in both men and women. The two measures agreed closely in men but only weakly in women. In men, their agreement grew sharply as body mass rose, while hydration status shifted the pattern further. The authors argue the water measure reflects true cell volume and adds useful context beside the standard index in sick patients.
pmc-13511720:
Hazal Su Bıçakcı Yeşilkaya and five co-authors design a system that reads emotion and stress from wearable brain and heart sensors, in 2026 work. Results travel over future 6G health networks. A deep learning model with an attention step sorts brain wave recordings into three emotion classes, while an image-style network sorts heart signal traces into three stress states. Radio performance was simulated inside a virtual hospital at two frequency bands.

On standard datasets, the brain wave model sorted emotions with accuracy above ninety percent. The heart model scored lower, with a clear drop from validation to held-out testing. Simulated radio links showed short signal smearing and wide usable bandwidth at both bands, better at the higher one. The authors present the frame as a workable base for personal health monitoring over next-generation networks.
pmc-13512820:
Togzhan Serbatyrova, Gulnar Shalgumbayeva, Assel Tukinova, Gulnara Sarsebayeva, and Laura Danyarova run a case-control study of gestational diabetes in Kazakhstan, where evidence from Central Asia remains thin, in 2026 work. The condition, diabetes first appearing in pregnancy, is rising worldwide and harms mothers and babies. The team compared women with the condition against women with normal glucose tolerance to find tied factors and outcomes.

Obesity before pregnancy and schooling level each held an independent link to gestational diabetes after other factors were counted. Women with the condition faced more high blood pressure problems, more cesarean deliveries, and more oversized babies than the comparison group. The authors say tackling obesity before pregnancy could cut both the condition and its fallout. They call for larger multi-center studies to guide maternal health policy in the region.
pmc-13514320:
Canonico and co-authors looked to kombucha, a fermented tea, as a source of yeasts for new plant-based drinks. Their 2026 study pulled yeast strains from the tea and named each type by its genes. They found fifty-two distinct strains in all. One type, Brettanomyces anomalus, was by far the most common in the mix. The team then put the yeasts through lab tests that mimic the gut.

More than eight in ten yeasts lived through the fake gut tests. Many also stuck to each other and held back two germs that can cause illness. Two strains of one yeast and one strain of a third stood out as the best picks. Mixed pools of these yeasts made drinks with good lab scores and good taste marks. A strain from a wild source also helped brew a kombucha with no bacteria at all.
pmc-13514820:
Lule and colleagues studied in 2026 whether chronotype, a person's natural tilt toward morning or evening activity, links to hidden belly fat and blood fat risk. They enrolled 282 adults with no known chronic disease and no regular medicines at one centre. Each person filled in standard questionnaires on morningness and sleep quality, and the team computed combined risk indices from body measures and blood tests.

Lule found that greater morningness went with lower scores on both a visceral fat index and a blood fat risk index, even after accounting for sleep quality and other factors. Sleep quality itself showed no independent link to either index. Hints that the link ran stronger in women did not survive stricter statistical correction. The link also faded in the subgroup with strictly normal blood sugar. The authors say late chronotype may flag early risk even when sleep feels fine.
pmc-13517320:
Mark Godley and five colleagues review how chronic energy shortage reshapes athletes' bodies in a 2026 article. When training burns more than food replaces, the leftover energy for basic body functions falls short, a state called relative energy deficiency in sport. The authors gathered eighty-five studies since 2000 and sorted the effects across four compartments: bone density, muscle mass, fat stores, and body water.

The patterns differ by sport and sex. Endurance and leanness-focused disciplines carry the highest risk, with up to three-fifths of athletes affected in some estimates. Bone thins, hormones falter, and fat and muscle shift in ways that screening tools can misread. Godley's team appraises what current nutrition and screening advice rests on and where it wobbles. Their synthesis aims at care teams who must spot underfueling early, before performance problems become lasting damage.
pmc-13517420:
Qiaobo Lei and five colleagues feed laying hens a prickly-ash leaf extract in a 2026 trial. Plant additives are sought as antibiotic-free ways to keep layers productive, and the leaves of Zanthoxylum armatum 'Jiuyeqing', a green prickly ash from southwest China, carry antioxidant compounds. Diets with several extract levels ran for eight weeks, and the team tracked laying, egg quality, antioxidant defences, gut structure, and liver chemistry.

Six grams per kilogram of feed gave the best overall response. Hens laid more eggs with deeper-coloured yolks, and their antioxidant protection strengthened. Immune-linked measures shifted as well. Gut structure responded unevenly along its length, a reminder that plant extracts rarely act uniformly. Liver metabolite profiles moved in step with the dose. Lei's team proposes the leaves, often an underused farm by-product, as a feed resource that lifts both output and the value of the crop itself.
pmc-13518820:
Jiejun Luo and six colleagues pin down in 2026 a sea-level rise rate beyond which tidal wetlands worldwide start vanishing fast. Salt marshes and mangroves drown as seas climb, yet proving the link at global scale had been difficult. The team merged several remote sensing sources covering two decades.

Loss sped up in a nonlinear way as relative sea-level rise increased. Past about 9 millimeters per year, the chance of accelerated loss topped 92 percent and the loss rate rose eightfold. Marshes shrank gradually before that point, while mangroves held steady until the threshold, then fell quickly. Edge erosion showed a slightly lower threshold, giving managers a concrete warning benchmark.
pmc-13519020:
Ipsita Kumar Sen and seven colleagues synthesize glowing carbon dots capped with heparin in 2026 and test how they mingle with human blood proteins. Carbon dots are tiny, low-toxicity light emitters suited to cell imaging, and heparin, a blood-thinning sugar chain, served as both cap and stabilizer. Glucose supplied the carbon.

The dots averaged 2.5 nanometers across with a strong negative surface charge. Fluorescence tests showed firm binding to both serum albumin and methemoglobin. Against lung cancer cells in culture the capped dots were slightly more toxic than bare dots, with a half-kill dose near 176 micrograms per milliliter. Red blood cell damage was negligible at high dose, supporting blood compatibility.
pmc-13520220:
Jian Zhao leads a nine-author forensic study in 2026 using skin microbes and metabolites to tell apart two causes of death in decomposing mice: hemorrhagic shock and organophosphate poisoning. Both leave few marks after decay sets in, beating standard autopsy and toxicology. Facial skin was sampled at three decay stages spanning 2 to 16 days.

Shock cases carried lower microbial variety throughout, with other bacteria dominating each cause and stage. Some 237 telltale microbe types emerged, while chemical profiles showed cause-linked molecules that shifted with time since death. Histidine and phosphate pathways split the causes best. Zhao's team argues paired skin signatures could estimate time of death and name its cause at once.
pmc-13520320:
Rui Xie and colleagues describe in 2026 five years of denture care for a boy born without teeth due to a rare inherited condition affecting skin, hair and teeth. A fully digital plan was used so new dentures could keep pace with rapid facial growth.

Care began at age four with scans and three-dimensional planning for a complete denture. Visits every six months checked fit, with relining or full remaking guided by measured growth. Eating, speech and appearance all improved over the follow-up period. The report offers a repeatable, measured workflow for other children who need dentures while still growing.
pmc-13520520:
Jiaqing Luo and Xiaobing Li propose in 2026 three new numbers for describing children's dental arch shape between ages four and twelve, aiming for measures that are repeatable and easy to interpret. Standard alignment scores miss large-scale shape and upper-lower jaw coordination.

Measures capture fine alignment wobble, overall shape departure from population templates, and mismatch between upper and lower arches. Applying them to 473 digital models, covering normal and faulty bites, showed wide individual variation. Fine wobble appeared most often and frequently alone, while jaw mismatch rarely appeared alone. Follow-up measures helped separate temporary wobble from lasting shape differences.
pmc-13520620:
Mike Westmeijer and nine colleagues, with the Dangle Research Group, published this 2026 study on recovery after lower limb salvage with free flap reconstruction. In that surgery, tissue is transplanted to cover leg wounds. Patients from four Dutch academic centres, enrolled in the Dangle study, completed questionnaires on ability, quality of life and discomfort after surgery. The authors modelled which factors tracked with outcomes over time.

Fifty-one participants returned 113 questionnaires between them. Male sex and the absence of diabetes were each tied to greater physical capability, though neither changed the recovery path. Only time since surgery predicted improving quality of life. Foot reconstructions brought more discomfort than lower leg reconstructions. Scores for individual tasks stayed largely flat over time. Most factors cannot be changed, the authors note, but they set expectations and flag patients who may need rehab, mental health and pain support.
pmc-13521920:
Naomi Azulay and colleagues test in 2026 whether heartbeat dynamics recorded during a cold-pressor pain test can sharpen ten-year heart disease prediction in Norway beyond the national NORRISK2 model. Recordings came from a population study wave in 2007 to 2008, totalling 6,694 traces.

Pulse variability and baroreflex measures were added to the standard model, while a separate machine learning model used only the time-series signals. Test accuracy hovered near 0.80 for standard variants and reached 0.73 for signals alone. Merging both model outputs brought no gain. Added physiology therefore offered little beyond recalibrated standard risk factors in this dataset.
pmc-13523420:
Hakimi Kassim and colleagues test whether data from a dating app track area HIV patterns in Malaysia in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Publicly visible profiles on a place-based dating app were sampled on a grid across all states and federal lands. Per-person user rates and profile traits were compared with area rates of people living with HIV using rank methods.

User density tracked area HIV rates closely. Several profile traits showed initial positive links, yet none survived checks for multiple testing. The authors attribute the weaker result to the small number of regions and widespread non-disclosure on profiles. Grid sampling can therefore map user density in a set pattern, but profile traits cannot reliably show true local rates where omissions are common.
pmc-13523520:
Wenxuan Liu and colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, whether impacted wisdom teeth are linked with root damage on the neighboring second molar. External root resorption, where root tissue is eaten away, is hard to spot on ordinary X-rays and may be found only after lasting harm. Cone-beam computed tomography gives a clearer three-dimensional view.

Six databases were searched for human studies using that imaging method, through June 2025. Twenty-six articles entered the synthesis, most judged at low risk of bias. Pooled prevalence of resorption on second molars next to impacted third molars was 31 percent. Risk rose when the impacted tooth leaned forward, lay horizontally, or crossed sideways, and when it touched the deepest third of the neighbor's root. The findings inform decisions about symptom-free impacted teeth.
pmc-13525620:
Ramzy and co-authors review the reviews in this 2026 umbrella analysis of GLP-1 receptor agonists, the diabetes and obesity drug class that includes semaglutide, and atrial fibrillation, the common irregular heartbeat. Meta-analyses claiming these drugs prevent fibrillation have multiplied quickly. They often recycle the same trials. So the team appraised all of them for quality and overlap. Two questions were covered: new-onset fibrillation and recurrence after ablation.

Ten meta-analyses qualified. Their estimates pointed protective, with odds ratios for new fibrillation spanning 0.54 to 0.83 across reviews, yet confidence ratings were low in five reviews and very low in four, and none scored moderate or high. Overlap was heavy: shared primary studies reached a corrected covered area of 43.8 percent among recurrence reviews, and two reviews using an identical six-study base produced different estimates. The authors conclude the seeming consensus partly reflects repetition, and call for proper randomized trials.
pmc-13526120:
Lauren Geary leads a large group of medical writing leaders in a 2026 review backing lean authoring for medical study reports in the drug industry. Lean authoring means clear, concise, plain content that gives regulatory reviewers fast paths to decision-critical facts and a clean trail from design to results. Industry adoption, the authors argue, lags behind what reviewers want.

Noted benefits include easier reading, content reuse, cheaper drafting, and smoother regulatory review with fewer questions caused by unclear wording. Pushback against change is the main obstacle named. The article lays out benefits plainly, then a step by step uptake path: reviewer needs analysis and change planning. The goal is to prepare reports for future machine drafting while cutting the burden of regulatory review today.
pmc-13527920:
Merve Yılmaz and three colleagues report a 2026 veterinary study of two small regulatory molecules, miR-21 and miR-93, in ovarian tissue from slaughtered cattle. Cystic ovarian follicles, fluid-filled structures that fail to release an egg, are a common cause of poor fertility in cows. The team compared 35 healthy ovaries with 35 cystic ones.

Microscopy confirmed the thinned, worn layers typical of cysts. Both microRNAs were more abundant in cystic tissue, while a related gene called BMPR2 did not differ between groups. As a test marker, miR-93 separated cystic from healthy tissue well, reaching an area under the curve of 0.899 in the authors' analysis, and it tracked with BMPR2 levels inside cysts.
pmc-13528920:
Stefanie L. Moye leads a large team linking dietary omega-6 fats to rogue bone growth after injury in obesity in a 2026 study. The condition, heterotopic ossification, grows bone inside soft tissue. It locks joints and causes pain after trauma or burns. Fat mice on high-fat food grew far more of it. The team traced the fuel to the injury site itself.

Injured tissue in obese mice was rich in linoleic and arachidonic acids. Immune cells turned those into a signal, PGE2, via the COX-2 enzyme. That signal reprogrammed repair cells to build bone and cartilage. A low-linoleic diet cut the rogue bone despite equal obesity. Patient data agreed: obesity raised risk, and COX-2 blockers cut it only in obese patients. Diet makeup, not weight alone, is the actionable lever.
pmc-13530120:
Jose Borreguero heads a large 2026 team showing that portable low-field MRI can image hard tissues such as bone, tendon, and cartilage. Cheap Halbach magnet scanners promise wider access to scanning, yet their uneven fields block methods that picture dense tissue. The group built a full workaround for that limit.

Calibrated radio pulses, a two-shot mapping method, and model-based image rebuilding formed the core fix. Scans of knees and ankles finished in under 15 minutes and revealed structures that standard sequences miss. Measurements of tissue relaxation in living subjects came first for this scanner class.
pmc-13530220:
Yang and colleagues report a light-driven chemical synthesis in 2026 built around a new high-entropy sulfide photocatalyst, a material that mixes many metals into one crystal. Their catalyst, with the composition NiSnCaZnInS, uses visible light to drive reactions that normally need harsher conditions. Under illumination, the catalyst converted benzyl alcohol with ammonia into the imine product at a yield of 1240 micromoles per gram over five hours, and the reaction reached 91.7 percent selectivity for the desired product. Mixing several metals into the sulfide tuned how the material absorbs light and moves charge, which the authors credit for the performance. They present the system as a greener route to imines that avoids high heat and harsh reagents.
pmc-13530820:
Caplan and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 59, a systematic review comparing autologous minced cartilage implantation against microfracture and cell implantation techniques for focal knee cartilage damage. Minced cartilage implantation is a one-stage procedure that dices the patient's own cartilage into the defect.

The review gathered 41 studies with 51 cohorts and 2,116 patients published between 2015 and 2025. Cell implantation cohorts dominated the count, with minced cartilage the smallest and shortest-followed group, averaging about twenty-nine months against roughly five years for the others. Across a battery of standard knee scores, no technique's patient-reported outcomes differed significantly from the others at follow-up. Failure and reoperation rates were generally lowest in the minced cartilage cohorts. The authors judge the newcomer at least non-inferior at short to mid-term, while noting its long-term data are thin.
pmc-13531620:
Priscilla Wessly and colleagues measure in 2026 the radiation reaching imaging doctors during catheter heart procedures. These echocardiographers stand close to the X-ray beam while guiding valve and closure work. Real-time badges at chest and pelvis tracked dose across 230 procedures at one center over a year.

Pelvis dose under lead was almost always zero, and a full pregnancy estimate sat far below safety limits, reassuring news for reproductive safety. Chest dose ran far higher and climbed from closure work to mitral to tricuspid procedures. Standing at the bed head and using only a half shield raised dose sharply.
pmc-13531820:
Peipei Zhang and co-authors probe in 2026 a stress sugar ratio as a death predictor after open heart surgery on a heart-lung machine. Records for 1,221 intensive care patients came from a large United States database. The ratio compares admission sugar against a long-term average derived from blood testing.

Sixty-three patients died within 180 days. Risk stayed flat at lower ratios, then climbed once the ratio passed about 0.97, forming a threshold pattern rather than a straight line. Missing sugar data excluded many patients, and key operating times were unavailable, so the authors label the threshold exploratory.
pmc-13534420:
Jun Wakabayashi, Seiichiro Higashi, and Masashi Morifuji compare in 2026 NMN taken under the tongue versus by mouth in healthy men. NMN feeds production of NAD+, a molecule that falls with age, and the under-tongue route may bypass liver breakdown. Fourteen men took both forms in a crossover trial with an eight-day gap.

Blood was sampled for 60 minutes after each dose. Two end breakdown products rose faster and higher after under-tongue dosing, while NMN and NAD+ levels showed no clear route gap. No side effects occurred, yet the source of the early rise could not be pinned down.
pmc-13535120:
Mohammad Ali Mahdiabadi, Asma Moghaddam, and Nafiseh Erfanian review how gut microbe products from tryptophan can restore the gut barrier in inflammatory bowel disease. These products switch on the AhR sensor, which sets off protective pathways in the gut lining. Several gut bacteria make the key indole compounds named in the review.

Sensor activation lifts barrier proteins, guards the mucus layer, and calms inflammation through energy, antioxidant, and immune pathways. Animal studies show benefit that vanishes when the sensor is blocked. Human trial proof is still lacking, and some related compounds may carry risks with lasting exposure.
pmc-13536720:
Emanuela Mari and co-authors review the normal prion protein and its fragments in brain disease in a 2026 synthesis. The protein sits on nerve cell surfaces and helps with signaling and protection, yet its altered form drives prion illness. The review covers how the protein is cut into smaller pieces, what those pieces do, and how the protein interacts with harmful clumps seen in Alzheimer and Parkinson disease.

Some fragments calm inflammation and limit harm from toxic protein clumps, while others may aid damage. New ultra-sensitive tests that detect tiny seeding activity have changed prion diagnosis and raise the chance that protein fragments in body fluids could track disease. The authors outline future options ranging from fragment-based treatments to fluid markers of onset and progression.
pmc-13538520:
Özlem Saraç Atagün and colleagues assess teeth grinding awareness before implant therapy in a 2026 survey of 150 healthy adults aged 18 to 65 years seeking implants. Grinding can overload implants and crowns, so spotting it early matters. Clinical exams hunted grinding signs, while questionnaires covered self-reported grinding, jaw symptoms, stress, and personal awareness before surgery. Device-based measures were not used.

About three in ten patients met clinical signs for grinding, while about one quarter reported grinding in sleep, waking hours, or both. Age alone linked clearly to grinding status among tested traits. Awareness stayed limited overall, with schooling showing little sway except for one tooth loss belief link. Stress scores tied to neither diagnosis nor type. The authors recommend routine screening plus awareness raising before implant work.
pmc-13539820:
Zuojun Liu and six colleagues report a 2026 engineering study of a probiotic bacterium, Limosilactobacillus reuteri, reworked to make a useful antimicrobial compound called 3-HPA from cheap glucose. Three tangled problems held output back: a missing vitamin, an unbalanced cell chemistry, and a brake on sugar use.

Comparing sugars with multi-omics tools, the team found that galactose switches on the needed genes and reroutes carbon flow, even though cells grow poorly on it. Copying that program into a glucose-fed strain, plus feeding four supplements, lifted output many times over the starting level. The authors claim the highest yield yet reported for this bacterial group in flask culture.
pmc-13539920:
Yung-Shu Lee and five colleagues examine, in a 2026 genetic study, whether inherited variants in a gene called NUCB2 relate to how prostate cancer behaves. The gene makes a precursor of nesfatin-1, a protein first found in brain cells that also circulates as a hormone-like signal.

Four variants were compared between patients and healthy men, alongside tumor stage and spread details. Carrying a G letter at one variant site went with lower odds of advanced stage and of cancer invading along nerves. Public tissue data showed that variant also tied to lower NUCB2 levels. The authors read the variant as possibly protective against progression, while noting lifestyle links remain untested.
pmc-13540920:
Han Ma and colleagues present a computer framework in a 2026 paper. The framework infers how cells talk to each other. It works on spatial transcriptomics data. Such data map gene activity across a tissue slice. Older graph models freeze their view of cell relations too early.

Their system is called CAGNet. It works in two stages. First, an attention-based graph network learns a rich profile for each spot. Then the system alternates two steps. It refines cell clusters, then rebuilds the spatial graph. Each step improves the other. Across three public datasets, CAGNet beat six rival methods. It won on every accuracy measure used.
pmc-13542220:
Ramezani and colleagues fix a measurement problem in a promising kidney monitor. Urine oxygen tension, read from a bladder catheter, could warn of kidney oxygen starvation hours before blood tests react. The reading at the catheter's far end, though, is corrupted: urine dawdles in transit and oxygen leaks through the catheter wall. The distortion is worst when urine flow is low and the patient sickest. Their 2026 physics-based algorithm models both distortions and works backwards to reconstruct the true bladder value.

On a bench rig the correction cut average error from nearly eleven units of pressure to under one. It tightened the agreement band dramatically, while correlation with truth jumped from mediocre to strong in the reported figures. In eight pigs driven through haemorrhagic shock and resuscitation, nearly sixty-nine thousand paired samples showed the same pattern. Bias and absolute error roughly halved, with the largest gains at low flow.
pmc-13543420:
Fahrettin Kaya published a 2026 methods paper making nonlinear survival modelling fast enough for large medical cohorts. The workhorse Cox model assumes risk rises in a straight line with each factor, yet real biomarker risks often bend into U shapes. Flexible kernel versions capture such curves but slow to a crawl as sample size grows, and most machine-learning alternatives cannot put error bars on individual predictions.

Kaya's approach, called RFF-Cox, projects the data through random Fourier features, a trick that imitates a kernel with a fixed set of computed features, so cost grows far more gently. A key smoothing parameter is chosen by an approximation to the marginal likelihood. Uncertainty comes from the Fisher information matrix, propagated to survival predictions, and a Taylor-based framework yields hazard ratios and significance tests per factor. The package aims to give big-cohort studies both flexibility and honest error bars.
pmc-13546520:
Marisa Siebel and co-authors asked in 2026 whether delays between a biopsy diagnosis and the start of treatment affect how soon localized pancreatic cancer returns. They reviewed 91 patients treated with curative intent at one academic center between 2016 and 2024. About two thirds saw their cancer recur or spread during follow-up, with a typical time to recurrence of roughly 22 months.

Each extra week between biopsy and treatment was tied to about a 9 percent higher risk of recurrence or spread, after accounting for age, sex, surgery, and radiation. Missing surgery carried an even larger risk. The authors caution that the group was small and drawn from a single hospital, so larger multi-center studies should test the finding before practice changes.
pmc-13546720:
Zulfi Nur Amrina Rosyada and co-authors looked in 2026 at whether age changes the DNA packaging inside Bali bull sperm, a factor in fertility at insemination centers. Eight bulls were split into younger and older groups around the ten-year mark. Sperm movement was tracked by computer, while staining tests measured cap integrity, DNA breakage, and protamine, the protein that tightly packs sperm DNA.

Older bulls surprised expectations with better forward movement and better protamine packaging than the younger group, while cap integrity and DNA breakage matched. Protamine status tracked movement closely across bulls. A protein band near 10 to 11 kilodaltons also ran stronger in older bulls. The authors suggest adding packaging checks to routine bull selection.
pmc-13546920:
Sarah Simko, Janet Cruz, and Mallory Stuparich argued in 2026 that painful periods in teenagers should be screened routinely so that endometriosis is caught early rather than years late. Their article opens with a composite case: a girl whose severe cramps begin at her first periods. She manages with painkillers and heat for years, and her pain worsens on birth control pills. Only at 18, during appendix surgery, is she found to have endometriosis.

By 21 she carries a stage IV diagnosis, and repeated operations follow, including removal of an ovary, alongside spreading chronic pain. The authors use the story to show how dismissal of cramps as normal delays referral and lets disease escalate. They set out how doctors should assess adolescent period pain and when to send patients to specialists.
pmc-13547420:
Viviam Sanabria and a Brazilian team tested in 2026 whether biperiden, a drug that blocks one acetylcholine receptor family, can protect the brain in the first day after a moderate head injury. Traumatic injury triggers a surge of that chemical messenger, which can overexcite cells. Thirty-nine marmosets received a controlled lateral fluid percussion injury, then repeated drug doses starting six hours later or a salt solution.

A day after injury, treated animals showed less dying tissue in the hippocampus, lower levels of a neuronal damage marker in blood and tissue, and calmer astrocyte activation than controls. The drug's exact receptor target inside the brain was not directly checked. The authors present biperiden as an early intervention candidate worth further primate work.
pmc-13548520:
Kousuke Matsumoto and colleagues ask whether video explanations satisfy dental patients as well as spoken ones, in a 2026 survey from a Japanese hospital dental department. Patients received explanations in three situations: consent before wisdom tooth removal, home care after an extraction, and oral care for inpatients facing surgery under general anesthesia. In total, 297 questionnaire responses were compared between the video and spoken groups.

Ratings of clarity, length, and changes in fear or anxiety showed no meaningful gap between the two formats in any of the three situations. Answers also did not differ between men and women, and age showed only a weak link with fear scores. The authors conclude that video works best as an added option beside conversation, not as a replacement for it.
pmc-13548620:
A. A. Janakiram and colleagues develop a website to support parents of teenagers with anorexia nervosa and test whether families will use it, in a 2026 mixed methods study. Parents carry much of family-based therapy, the leading treatment, yet they often feel unprepared. Nineteen families at a specialist outpatient center were offered six months of access to the educational site alongside their usual therapy.

Eleven parents actually used the site and rated it satisfying and easy to navigate, typically visiting about once a month. Their general well-being and mental health scores did not shift over three months, though confidence in handling the illness rose with a large effect that just missed statistical significance. Parents praised ready access, thorough content, and a calmer approach to their child. The authors judge the add-on acceptable and worth a larger trial.
pmc-13548720:
Mickael Naassila and colleagues mine data from a smartphone app that supported France's national Dry January campaign in 2024, in a 2026 observational study. Temporary abstinence challenges cut drinking for many, yet how people actually behave day by day inside such campaigns was little known. The analysis covered 2,032 adult users, sorting them by age, sex, and the drinking risk level they reported for a reference week before January.

Heavier baseline drinkers and younger users dropped out sooner, while sex and pre-campaign binge drinking did not predict leaving. Users who stayed showed a stable weekly rhythm, with drinking peaking on Fridays and Saturdays even during the challenge. Average daily drinking still declined through the month in every risk group, most steeply among the heaviest drinkers. The authors see room to design apps that hold onto young and heavy-drinking users better.
pmc-13550020:
Salar Bakhtiyari and Iraj Alipourfard reframe cell therapy for ischemic stroke as a metabolic rescue mission, in a 2026 review. When a blocked vessel starves brain tissue, energy failure cascades into ion chaos, toxic glutamate release, and calcium-flooded mitochondria, while the surrounding support cells keep rewriting their fuel use for weeks. The authors argue transplanted cells help less by replacing dead neurons than by retuning this chemistry.

Mesenchymal stromal cells, neural and blood vessel progenitors, cord blood cells, and even cell-free vesicles deliver growth signals, antioxidant cues, tiny regulatory RNAs, and mitochondrial support. In the framework proposed, these inputs steady energy production, calm inflammatory sugar burning, and reseal the vessel and neuron partnership. The review matches cell types to stroke phases and calls for potency tests and engagement biomarkers before clinical routine.
pmc-13550420:
Khaldoun J Al-Hadid and colleagues wrap garlic's active compound, allicin, into tiny polymer bubbles to steady it and pair it with a chemotherapy drug, in a 2026 laboratory study. Allicin shows useful cell effects but breaks down easily and absorbs poorly. The Soluplus micelles formed uniform spheres about seventy-four nanometers wide, trapped nearly all the allicin, and released it far more slowly than the free compound while staying intact under heat.

Pretreating cells with the loaded micelles changed how doxorubicin acted, in opposite directions depending on the cell type. Heart muscle cells and colon cancer cells showed a protective metabolic shift, while prostate cancer cells became more sensitive to the drug. The authors call the carrier a promising way to stabilize allicin and tune chemotherapy, stressing that the findings are early dish-level evidence.
pmc-13550620:
Thamali Ayagama, with six colleagues, published a 2026 reanalysis of protein data from goats with atrial fibrillation, a common irregular heartbeat. The condition raises energy demand in heart muscle cells, and mitochondria supply that energy. Working from published left atrial tissue data, the team focused on the mitochondrial fraction and ran pathway and network analyses.

Proteins for oxidative phosphorylation, the main energy-making chain, were consistently enriched. A heat shock protein called HSPA9 emerged as a possible hub coordinating changes in two respiratory chain complexes, with most of its regulatory links agreeing across pathways. The authors read the pattern as a coordinated, system-wide mitochondrial adjustment rather than isolated protein changes.
pmc-13550720:
Nima Mohammadi, Amalia GM Scannell, and Marilú Andrea Silva-Espinoza published a 2026 review of avenanthramides, antioxidant compounds found almost only in oats. Human studies show less than two percent of an eaten dose reaches the bloodstream, yet laboratory work finds strong effects, creating a puzzle. The review follows the compounds stage by stage through digestion instead of treating absorption as the whole story.

Food structure, processing, and enzymes shape how much is released in the gut, where the compounds may slow starch breakdown and glucose transport. In the colon, microbes convert them into related forms whose activity varies by a person's microbial type. The authors conclude that local gut effects likely matter most, while calling for well-designed human trials to confirm the pathways.
pmc-13550920:
Indra Prasetia, with a team of co-authors, published a 2026 study of a flexible study scheme in Indonesia. The scheme lets students learn off campus and outside their degree. The team asked how it empowers students and what skills it builds. They interviewed 17 people chosen for their roles. They grouped the answers by theme.

Empowerment came through six routes. Staff eased the way, cut red tape, and gave advice. They also teamed up with, guided, and backed the students. Graduates gained skills in leading, teaching, and talking with others. They also gained problem solving, clear thinking, and tech skills. Real work placements drove much of the gain, the team says.
pmc-13551520:
In 2026, Teresa R. Schwendler and eight colleagues studied how Guinea's programs and policies could better support nutrition for mothers, infants, and young children. Nutrition in the first thousand days shapes lifelong health, and relevant efforts span health, water and sanitation, food, and social protection systems. The team reviewed policy documents from 2019 to 2022 and interviewed twenty stakeholders across those systems.

Policies proved strongly multisectoral, and most evidence-based program types were both written into policy and actually running in Guinea. Stakeholders named implementation, not policy design, as the main barrier. The authors suggest better financial planning and coordination between national and local levels would turn a strong framework into stronger results.
pmc-13551820:
Silla Mescouto-Conrado, Maryuri Abigail Perez-Coaquira, Cristian Edwin Adriano-Rengifo, and Cesar Augusto Galvez published a 2026 study of lifestyle and burnout in Peru. The sample held 205 religious leaders. The design was cross-sectional, with one survey wave. A modeling method tested links among the measures at once.

Lifestyle showed a strong negative link to burnout. The model explained nearly two thirds of the spread in burnout scores. One part of burnout did not link to lifestyle. That part was a sense of reduced personal achievement. Habits such as social support, activity, and sleep looked protective. The team suggests churches can cut leader burnout by backing healthy daily routines.
pmc-13554220:
Indrakshi Banerjee and three colleagues review how mitochondria, the cell's power plants, talk to the nucleus through small chemicals in a 2026 paper. Those chemicals do more than carry energy; they also steer enzymes that tag genes on or off. Signals flow both ways, since the nucleus directs how mitochondria are built and kept in repair. Messengers in the blood even let organs coordinate through the same chemicals.
