When this two-way traffic breaks down, metabolism and gene control clash and disease follows. The review names such clashes epimetabopathies, a frame for disorders where both systems fail together. Readers get a map of the signalling routes plus ideas for tests and treatments. The authors stress how much of cell fate rides on this chemical dialogue.
pmc-13554320:
Ma and co-authors ask whether the path of inflammation over time, not just its level, predicts heart events in statin users. Their 2026 Beijing cohort study followed 210 patients on statins for at least a year, each with three or more measurements of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, an inflammation marker. Latent class modelling sorted patients into trajectory groups, and events were tracked over a median of about twelve months.

Three patterns emerged: persistently low inflammation in about 45 percent of patients, a moderately fluctuating band in 40 percent, and persistently high levels in about 15 percent. Thirty-eight patients, about 18 percent, suffered a major cardiovascular event. Survival curves separated significantly across the trajectory groups, with the persistently high group faring worst. Adjusted models tied trajectory membership to event risk beyond standard factors. The authors argue repeated inflammation readings refine risk checks in treated patients.
pmc-13555920:
Jie Wu leads a ten-author team training learning models to sort lung nodules by routine blood tests in a 2026 study. Scans and biopsies remain the standard route, yet both are invasive or hard to repeat. Their Nanjing hospital cohort held 1,238 patients with lung nodules, plus 250 healthy controls. Five algorithms competed across six sorting tasks, from healthy versus benign to early versus late cancer.

A boosted-tree model won overall and became the final tool. Feature counts differed by task, with the widest set used to separate healthy people from benign cases. Accuracy soared for some contrasts and stayed modest for benign versus early cancer, the hardest call. An explanation method ranked which lab values drove each judgement for clinicians.
pmc-13558420:
Nihal Babiker and nine colleagues pooled in 2026 the trial evidence for luspatercept, a drug that helps red blood cells mature in people with beta-thalassaemia. The inherited disorder leaves patients anaemic and dependent on lifelong transfusions. Their systematic review searched five databases to May 2025 for randomised trials in adults and assessed bias with a standard Cochrane tool.

Three trials and one single-arm study, 608 patients in all, qualified. About six in ten treated patients cut their transfusion burden by at least a third, four in ten halved it, and over a third stopped transfusions entirely for a period. Headache, bone pain, and joint pain were the common side effects, and serious events touched about a fifth of patients. The authors judge the drug effective while urging longer safety follow-up.
pmc-13558720:
Yitao Wu and eight colleagues rebuilt in 2026 a compact object detection network to perform fine-grained lung cancer reading on scans, sorting seven classes at once. Existing aids mostly answer cancer or not, leaving subtype and stage as separate chores. Their unified model must find each lesion. It names the tissue class among normal lung and the three main non-small cell subtypes. It also places anatomical location with staging detail. Tumours vary wildly in size and look nearly alike, which makes the task hard.

Three upgrades carry the design. A dilated block widens the view without slowing inference. A positional gating attention spotlights telling textures and mutes background. A dynamic upsampler preserves lesion borders during fusion. On a set of 1,886 images the model posted precision near ninety-eight percent with very strong detection scores, all at a small parameter count suited to clinical hardware.
pmc-13559220:
Shao and colleagues review in 2026 advances in Fourier ptychographic microscopy, a label-free imaging method that watches living cells without dyes or fluorescent tags. Tags bleach and poison cells over time, which limits how long biologists can observe them.

The technique stitches together many low-resolution images taken under angled LED lighting to reconstruct one sharp, wide picture. It reaches resolution near 150 nanometers while keeping a broad field of view. Since its introduction in 2013 it has spread quickly, but speed remains its weakness, because hundreds of LEDs must fire in sequence. The review gathers the field's collective fixes: two-dimensional super-resolution schemes that beat the diffraction limit by iterative reconstruction, faster illumination patterns, and smarter algorithms. The authors chart how these advances turned a slow novelty into a practical tool for dynamic live-cell imaging.
pmc-13559620:
Xuran Zhang and Runfang Gao mine single-cell and bulk gene data to characterize an exhausted-looking T cell state in breast cancer and turn its genes into a survival predictor. Their 2026 study centers on CD8 T cells carrying both TIM3 and CD101 markers. Single-cell data came from a public repository, while bulk data came from cancer atlas and GEO cohorts.

Clustering resolved seventeen cell groups across seven types, and T cells split further into four subtypes. Trajectory analysis hinted that one TIM3-positive state can transition into the CD101-positive state. From 121 genes differing around this population, the team built an eleven-gene prognostic model using penalized regression. The signature predicted survival strongly across the cohorts tested. The authors frame the work as a map of breast tumor immune diversity, with the gene model offered for sorting patients by risk.
pmc-13559920:
Sekar and colleagues studied in 2026 twenty years of hospital admissions in England for miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy, a pregnancy growing outside the womb. Using national NHS admissions data from 2004 to 2024, the team tracked yearly counts by age group and by deprivation level. That level measures the poverty of a patient's home area. Trend software then found turning points in the curves.

Sekar found miscarriage admissions fell clearly between 2018 and 2021, then rose slightly afterward. Ectopic pregnancy admissions rose until 2012, dipped as gentler treatment guidelines spread, and rose again after 2021. A steady deprivation gap ran through the whole period: the poorest tenth of areas had about twice the admissions of the richest. The share of admissions among women aged 25 to 34 also grew, reaching roughly half. The authors urge fairer access and targeted prevention.
pmc-13560320:
Xin Guo and colleagues review a proposed outside-in pathway for aortic dissection, in which fat wrapped around the aorta turns from protector to aggressor. Their 2026 article focuses on perivascular adipose tissue, sometimes called the vessel wall's fourth layer. Under inflammation or metabolic stress, this fat releases mediators, most notably TGF-β1, that cross into the wall's middle layer.

Sustained TGF-β1 stimulation may push smooth muscle cells into a cooperative gene-control network built around the transcription factors RUNX1 and NF-κB. That network would silence the cells' contractile program while switching on inflammation and matrix breakdown, destabilizing the wall. The authors evaluate the findings for this fat-to-muscle axis and mark its limitations honestly. They suggest future drugs against the axis will need local delivery, since systemic blockade risks bleeding and immune suppression.
pmc-13560720:
Adrian S. Turner and colleagues assemble the genome of Yamadazyma mexicana, an industrial yeast, to near-chromosome completeness. Their 2026 genome announcement covers strain NCYC 1483, the species' type strain, first isolated from rot pockets of organ-pipe cacti during surveys in the 1970s. Long-read Nanopore sequencing generated nearly ten million reads at very deep coverage.

The final assembly holds eight contigs, seven of them chromosome-sized, improving on an earlier short-read version scattered across fifty-five pieces totaling 11.8 million bases. The yeast earns its keep several ways: it suppresses post-harvest anthracnose in avocados, lives across cacti, soil, and insect debris, and has lately appeared as a rare cause of human eye infection. A complete reference genome for the type strain supports all those research threads, from biocontrol breeding to clinical identification.
pmc-13562620:
Chuandong Wu and eight colleagues test whether a giant linked renewable base could untangle the Yellow River Basin's clash of energy, water, and ecology. The basin mines over half of China's coal yet holds little of its fresh water. Their 2026 proposal combines hydropower, solar, wind, and pumped storage into one coordinated system, leaning on basin-wide cooperation and grid expansion. Modelling asked what a full build-out would replace, and what it would cost or save the environment.

Each year the base could displace 23.8 percent of coal-fired generation, some 249.4 terawatt-hours. Energy emissions would fall by 28.0 percent, electricity-sector water use by 31.5 percent, and ecosystem carbon storage would recover by 9.0 percent. All the parts rely on established technology rather than breakthroughs. The authors offer the scheme as a worked example of how one region can chase several sustainability goals at once instead of trading them off.
pmc-13562720:
Tatiana Iakovleva and two colleagues stress-test a shortcut for measuring how much information a quantum system holds about a quantity worth estimating. Quantum Fisher information sets the ultimate precision limit for quantum sensors, but real systems leak into their surroundings, which makes it hard to compute. A reformulation in Liouville space, where states become vectors, promised an easier dissipative version. Their 2026 paper derives exact relations between the two quantities for a qubit, for qudit systems, and for a harmonic oscillator.

For a qubit, the true value can be recovered from the dissipative one by a mapping that depends on purity. In higher dimensions the conversion tangles beyond any compact form. The dissipative quantity sometimes sits above and sometimes below the true one, so it bounds nothing reliably. The authors conclude its numbers cannot be read at face value, and map where the Liouville approach helps or misleads.
pmc-13563820:
Zhirong Li and five colleagues ask what biology might connect sugary drinks to later depression. The link has appeared in population data, but the middle steps are guesswork. Their 2026 study followed 192,045 UK Biobank participants, relating sweetened drink intake to new depression diagnoses over time. Three datasets, from American surveys and a Chinese school health study, checked the direction of the result. Blood proteins, metabolites, inflammation markers, and brain scan features were screened as statistical go-betweens.

Heavy drinkers faced an 18 percent higher risk of developing depression than non-drinkers, and the datasets leaned the same way. A signature of 229 blood proteins tied both to the drinks and to the risk. Mediation screening nominated 72 proteins, 36 metabolites, and 5 inflammatory markers, with an interleukin-related protein showing the strongest share at 9.6 percent. The authors label all of it exploratory: candidate pathways for experiments, not proof that soda works through them.
pmc-13566420:
Elahe Zare Borzeshi and colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic analysis, whether body chemistry measured in blood or urine can predict who will respond to blood pressure drugs. From more than two thousand papers between 2013 and 2023, only five studies qualified, covering water pills, beta-blockers, and two other common drug families.

Forty-six chemical markers linked to drug response, touching fat processing, energy cycles, and amino acid pathways. A few markers stood out across studies, yet the base is tiny and narrow. The authors call for testing in larger, more varied groups and in combined drug treatment before chemical profiling can guide prescribing.
pmc-13569520:
Li-Chao-Yue Sun and colleagues map, in a 2026 bibliometric analysis, global research on monitoring antifungal drug levels in patients. Such monitoring matters because these drugs vary widely between people and have narrow safe ranges. Publications from 2014 to late 2024 in a major citation database totaled 569 from thirty-four countries.

The United States, China, and Germany published most, output rose steadily, and two journals led the field. Hot topics included monitoring one widely used drug, drug interactions, a newer agent, severe fungal lung infection, life-support circuits, and immune-weakened children. Machine learning for dose prediction emerged most recently. Clinicians and funders can see where the field is heading.
pmc-13573420:
Wenzhe Chen, with 13 colleagues, presents a 2026 design for hybrid nano bubbles that treat sudden kidney injury. Such injury often follows a flood of reactive oxygen that burns kidney tubules and fires up inflammation. Single drugs rarely calm both fronts, so the team fused two helpers into one carrier.

The bubbles join vesicles shed by umbilical cord stem cells with particles of a green tea compound and a selenium amino acid. In cell tests, the hybrids cut oxidative stress, shielded cell powerhouses, and steered immune cells toward a calm state. In animals, kidney function improved and damaged tissue repaired better than with either part alone. Gene reads showed less DNA damage stress as well. The authors lay the work as a base for clinical translation.
pmc-13575120:
Seyed Mostafa Jafari, Saeed Masoum, and Elahe Seyed Hosseini test glowing carbon dots as carriers for hard-to-dissolve cancer drugs in a 2026 study. Carbon dots are tiny carbon particles that dissolve well in water and are gentle on living tissue. The team doped their dots with boron and nitrogen to tune their properties.

Two drugs, curcumin and paclitaxel, were loaded onto the dots. Tests measured how much drug the carriers could hold and how much stuck successfully. Release was then tracked for 72 hours in fluids matching two acidity levels, one like healthy tissue and one more acidic like a tumour. Several mathematical models were fitted to describe how the drugs came off the carriers over time.
pmc-13575220:
Xingzheng Zhou leads a 2026 model test study of suction caisson foundations under repeated sideways loading. Caissons are large hollow foundations sucked into the seabed, used for offshore wind turbines. Wind and waves push them sideways for years, so long-term movement matters for turbine safety.

Tests varied how fast the loading cycled and how much downward load sat on the lid. Sideways drift grew with faster cycling, while the caisson also tended to rise over time. Water pressure inside and outside built up as cycles mounted. Heavier lids cut sideways movement, stiffened the whole setup, and reduced tilt. Past 2,000 cycles the tilt angle began rising fast. Under staged loading, stiffness faded as cycles accumulated. The findings guide design of modified caissons for offshore wind.
pmc-13576320:
Fundagül Bilgiç Zortuk, Eyüp Burak Küçük, and Çağrı Yeşildağ compare root shortening across three ways of fixing a Class II bite problem in a 2026 study. Moving teeth with braces can erode root tips, a side effect called apical root resorption. The methods were a Forsus spring device, headgear, and fixed braces after removing the upper first premolars.

Sixty patients, twenty per group, had 480 teeth scored on panoramic X-rays after active treatment and during retention. Differences were scattered across single teeth and time points. The spring group showed more shortening in one lower side tooth than the headgear group. The extraction group showed more in two upper teeth than the spring group. Scores barely shifted between the two checks in most teeth. The authors conclude each route carries its own pattern of modest root loss.
pmc-13578320:
Qian Wang and a large outbreak team trace a stomach illness cluster at a primary school in Nanchang, China, in a 2026 report. Ten swab samples came from sick students and teachers during the November 2024 event. Lab screening for the usual gut viruses found sapovirus, a less watched cause of vomiting and diarrhea, in five of them.

Gene reads from those five matched each other fully, and the type was pinned as GI.6, a form rarely reported in that province. Its shell gene sat closest to a 2023 strain from a nearby province, with only a few amino acid changes. Whole genome reads filled out the match. Spread ran through contact, the team found, and they urge closer tracking of this virus type in the region.
pmc-13578720:
Xiaonian Chen and colleagues simulate how concrete crushes under load when its stones are jagged polygons, in a 2026 study. Real concrete stones are angular, not round, and their shape steers where cracks start and how the block fails. The team wrote a program that scatters random polygons through a virtual block and sorts each particle by role, stone, mortar, or seam.

A smooth particle method then squeezed the blocks in a press simulation. More stones, or a wider size spread, turned single shear cracks into diffuse damage and made the block more brittle. More edges per stone did the reverse, spreading fine cracks and adding give. Failure shapes matched published results well, backing the tool for studying mix design before casting real blocks.
pmc-13591820:
Soheila Majidi and Amin Rouhi study, in 2026, whether obsessive compulsive symptoms dent the job performance of front line health workers in Hamadan, Iran. Such symptoms mix unwanted thoughts with repeated acts, and health staff face heavy mental strain at work. Their survey drew 403 workers from 50 urban health centers and posts, using standard scales for symptoms and performance.

About half the workers showed symptoms below the clinical line, while nearly all rated their job performance as good. Total symptom scores showed no firm link to performance. Symptoms ran higher in women and in staff with less schooling. Sex and contract type, not symptoms, predicted performance scores. Majidi and Rouhi advise mental health support and training for staff.
pmc-13592320:
Lawson and colleagues published a 2026 study on forcing a dye molecule to twist one way. Perylene diimide dyes can form helices that bend light in useful ways. Most twisted versions flip between hands and lose their special glow. The team used a rotaxane, a ring threaded on an axle, as the guide.

Their rotaxane's built-in twist is stable and cannot flip over time. It pushed the dye into a single-handed helix that stayed put. The dye then showed steady light-bending and glowing effects in tests. The flat dye face also let rotaxanes stack together, a rare trick. Control reached from single molecules up to grouped assemblies alike. Lasting single-handed glow suits sensing, imaging, and catalyst design work.
pmc-13592620:
Jian Zhang and four colleagues ask what drives strong learning when professional training and entrepreneurship teaching merge. Their framework runs from resource input through mental construction to active engagement, drawing on three theories. A survey of 584 university students measured teaching content, teacher skill, student engagement, campus company resources, and policy support against combined learning outcomes. Statistical paths traced how each factor connected, directly or through teaching practice quality.

Content, teacher skill, engagement, and company resources each linked positively to outcomes, mostly by lifting how well teaching worked in practice. Policy support showed no direct link, only an indirect one through the same practice channel. Zhang and the team advise course redesign, stronger practice based teaching, and deeper campus company collaboration.
pmc-13595520:
Romain Hollard and co-authors surveyed 118 pig vets across 25 countries about how they treat mycoplasma infections in pigs, then set practice against published rules and guidance. Mycoplasmas are hard to diagnose and treat, antibiotics are often the only option, and resistance is a growing worry in their 2026 report.

Practice matched the guidance on the main choices: macrolides dominated prescriptions, followed by tetracyclines and pleuromutilins, and nearly all vets used lab tests at least sometimes. Testing for drug response lagged, with only about a third requesting it in most cases. A small minority at times prescribed antibiotics that cannot work against mycoplasmas or that are key for human health, and doses sometimes drifted from the label. The authors urge wider drug-response testing and wider sharing of treatment guidelines.
pmc-13595720:
Jiayin Du and colleagues used a long-running Chinese aging cohort to untangle how childhood adversity, uric acid, and digestive disease in later life connect. Their 2026 longitudinal study followed 3,666 middle-aged and older adults, of whom 617 developed digestive disorders, modeling risks with survival analysis and testing uric acid as a go-between.

Growing up around household mental illness, or in an unsafe neighborhood, each predicted later digestive disease, and uric acid levels were themselves tied to digestive disorders. The mediation result was subtle: the unsafe neighborhood effect ran partly through uric acid in a negative direction, complicating any simple story that more uric acid means more harm. The pattern held across demographic subgroups. The authors call for work on mechanisms and on preventing childhood adversity whose health shadow reaches into old age.
pmc-13596720:
Yuqing Hu and colleagues traced how pressure overload in the right side of a child's heart stalls the maturation of heart muscle cells. In samples from children with tetralogy of Fallot and in newborn rats with a banded lung artery, the tiny tunnels called T-tubules, which synchronize each heartbeat's contraction, failed to develop normally.

Gene activity scans showed tubule-related genes switched down, with Bin1, a builder of those tunnels, among the most suppressed. Restoring Bin1 in the banded rats rescued tubule maturation. The chain ran through chromatin. Pressure closed access to the Bin1 gene. A transcription factor, Mef2d, proved to be the brake. Silencing it freed Bin1, and mutating its binding sites erased its effect. The authors present the pathway as a therapeutic direction for children's heart diseases driven by right-sided pressure.
pmc-13602820:
Ireneusz Sobolewski and four colleagues present an integrated lab system for engineering a heat-loving bacteriophage. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria, and TP-84 attacks Geobacillus stearothermophilus, a bacterium that thrives at high temperatures. Delivering a full phage genome into wall-stripped host cells, called protoplasts, had worked for plasmids but never for rebooting a whole phage. The team tuned cell density, enzyme levels, polymer type, and DNA dose until uptake became reliable.

With the tuned method, natural and fully synthetic TP-84 genomes entered protoplasts and restarted, producing infectious phage. A simplified single-layer agar step then yielded high-titer stocks and enough DNA for sequencing from one Petri dish. Recombinant variants also proved more stable grown this solid way than in liquid culture. The authors offer the combined workflow as a platform for rapidly building and testing engineered thermophilic phages.
pmc-13612620:
Zhao Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of how liver problems affect the way the body handles viloxazine. Viloxazine is a non-stimulant drug used for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adults. Adults with mild, moderate, or severe liver impairment each took one dose of the extended-release capsule form, sold as Qelbree, and were compared with matched adults whose livers worked normally.

Blood tests over 72 hours showed that drug exposure stayed within about a quarter of the level seen in the control group at every level of liver damage. The drug did leave the body more slowly when liver damage was moderate or severe. Side effects were few, mostly headache and sleepiness, and the authors conclude that liver impairment alone does not call for a blanket change in dose.
pmc-13612720:
Karine Aouchiche and a large team describe the genes behind a rare hormone condition found in babies, in a study of infants tested between 2019 and 2025. The condition, congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, means the body makes too little of the hormones that drive puberty and fertility. The team looked at babies diagnosed before age two, drawn from a much larger group who had gene testing for the condition.

Thirteen boys were included, and all had a very small penis at birth, while four also had undescended testes. Gene panel testing found new variants that widen the known picture of the condition. Early gene results can guide hormone treatment in infancy and help families understand what to expect, so mapping these variants in the youngest patients fills a real gap.
pmc-13616120:
Qi Chen and colleagues present in 2026 a case series of four patients with two lung diseases at once. One is pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, a rare disease where protein-rich material fills the air sacs. The other is a lung infection by Nocardia bacteria. Each condition is uncommon alone, and together they form a risky pairing, since the infection can kill without the right antibiotic. The cases differed in the Nocardia species involved and in how the illness ran.

Infection lasted from three months to over two years across the four patients. All were treated with antibiotics chosen by lab sensitivity testing, and outcomes ranged from cure and stable health to death. The authors warn that fever plus new shadows on lung scans in such patients should trigger a fast hunt for Nocardia, and they review what past reports add to the picture.
pmc-13616520:
Geraldine Rodríguez-Nieto, Mark Mikkelsen, and Stephan P. Swinnen study how the balance between the brain's main go and stop chemical messengers tracks with brain network activity while people switch mental gears. Forty young adults aged 18 to 35 took part, plus forty older adults aged 60 to 85. Each group performed a cognitive flexibility task inside a scanner. A spectroscopy method measured the glutamate and GABA balance at rest and during the task.

Task-driven shifts in that balance linked with how strongly two hub regions, in the frontal and parietal lobes, connected with the rest of the brain. The link played out differently in the young group, fitting known age changes in both chemistry and flexibility. Chemistry measured live during thinking, the study shows, helps explain why some brains reroute activity smoothly and others strain.
pmc-13617220:
Georgia Lloyd and four colleagues report a 2026 Australian study of partnered pharmacist medication charting for children arriving at a hospital emergency department. Under this model, pharmacists help write medication charts with doctors instead of only checking them later. The retrospective study at a tertiary children's hospital compared three periods in sequence: usual care, an early medication history service, and full partnered charting.

Medication errors fell steeply across the three models. About seven in ten children had at least one error under usual care, about half under the history service, and under six percent under partnered charting. That works out to roughly one error prevented for every two children seen. Stays were also about a day shorter under partnered charting, and documentation of dosing weight and allergies improved. The authors support the model as a scalable safety approach for children's hospitals.
pmc-13617820:
Xiaokang Luo and Xinjian Yan write a reply defending their anticoagulation strategy for a patient with congenital factor VII deficiency who received a mechanical heart valve. Readers had questioned monitoring blood thinning by factors II and X instead of the standard INR test. The authors explain why warfarin is unavoidable here: direct oral anticoagulants failed in mechanical valve trials and remain contraindicated, leaving warfarin as the only endorsed option.

Their core argument: INR misleads in this condition. The test weights factors II, VII, and X equally, yet warfarin's protection comes mainly from suppressing the long-lived factors II and X. The patient's inborn factor VII shortage inflates INR on its own. In their case, a falsely high INR delayed anticoagulation until day six after surgery and the patient suffered a brain clot. Monitoring factors II and X directly, they argue, reflects true anticoagulation intensity and avoids dangerous misjudgments.
pmc-13619120:
Nathaly Bianka Moraes Fróes and six colleagues wrote a scoping review mapping how nurses have used the Neuman Systems Model in women's health. That model treats each person as a system protected by lines of defense against stress. The reviewers searched ten databases and thesis collections between April and June 2024 for studies, reviews, opinion pieces, and grey literature.

Uses they found include judging stress around medical procedures and motherhood, understanding breast cancer experiences, studying violence, giving contraception advice, and teaching about the female athlete triad. Most studies borrowed only parts of the model rather than applying all five of its variables together. The authors still see promise in the framework, because its defense lines give nurses a shared way to plan prevention and support for women.
pmc-13619620:
Lan Li and Qianqian Fan studied why university students stay engaged in Tai Chi courses, which demand body coordination and steady practice over a whole term. They interviewed eight teachers and sixteen students and coded the conversations in stages, checking their reading against cases that did not fit. Their question was how support from teachers and classmates keeps students practicing.

Three linked pathways emerged from the interviews. Teachers gave layered demonstrations, protective feedback, and cultural meaning, which built students' sense of mastery. Classmates supplied company, examples to copy, and shared duties, slowly turning outside pressure into inner commitment. Teacher and peer support also reinforced each other across the course. Cases where support failed marked the limits of the pattern. The authors call their result a dual-support model for embodied, skill-based learning.
pmc-13620020:
Elisabeth Tamayo and five colleagues review what science still does not know about the fungi that rot wood. Wood evolved to resist decay, yet these fungi cracked that defense hundreds of millions of years ago and now drive nutrient cycling in forests. The review covers how colonization starts, through spore germination at wounds or spread from soil, and how fast strength loss can follow.

Threats run one way: the same fungi attack living trees, timber, and buildings, and some harm health. Value runs the other way, since their enzymes, transporters, and byproducts could feed a greener bioeconomy. The authors blend the literature with their own genomic and database analyses to join the macroscopic and microscopic views. Their aim is an honest map of open questions, not just settled knowledge.
pmc-13624420:
Saiyan Bian and colleagues hunt for drivers of liver cancer growth in hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common form of the disease. Combining gene data, tissue maps, patient samples, and cell models, they single out a chromatin protein called CHAF1B. Turning CHAF1B up or down changed how fast cancer cells grew, moved, and formed tumors.

The protein also pushed fat building inside the cells, with more lipid droplets and active fat-making genes. Its effects ran through a partner protein, SETDB1, whose fate depends on which type of ubiquitin tag it carries. A screen then found USP4, an enzyme that protects CHAF1B from breakdown, and blocking that protection weakened the cancer traits, marking a possible drug target.
pmc-13624820:
Yu Jeong Bang and colleagues present a consensus statement, published in 2026. It comes from the Korean Society of Anesthesiologists. It covers stomach checks before anaesthesia in patients taking GLP-1 drugs. These are weight-loss and diabetes drugs. They slow stomach emptying. Even fasting patients may carry stomach contents. Contents could enter the lungs during anaesthesia. This is a rare but dangerous event.

The statement recommends bedside stomach ultrasound for selected patients. Contents and volume can be judged directly. It sets out anaesthetic precautions for people on GLP-1 based therapy. Evidence for scan-guided practice is still thin, the authors note. The recommendations standardise expert practice while further studies are gathered.
pmc-13625220:
Ute Habel leads a large German consortium setting out to find the biological roots of aggression across mental disorders. Aggression appears in many diagnoses, follows varied courses through life, and stays poorly understood at the level of brain and body. Their plan follows a shared cohort at three sites, with nine hundred adults and two hundred children and teenagers, plus forensic patients, and compares them with matched healthy controls.

Each person receives layered measures of behavior and biology, framed by two research domains covering threat response and thinking systems. Repeated measures over time should let the team define aggression biosignatures, patterns that cut across diagnoses rather than sitting inside one label. The protocol, already registered, aims to ground future care in those shared mechanisms.
pmc-13628520:
Amal Lakhal and three colleagues report a light-driven way to make the cyclopropyl radical. This three-carbon ring fragment is famously hard to produce cleanly. Their 2026 method starts from a silicon-based starting material that is easy to make. Light-driven oxidation frees the radical. Older routes leaned on metal-heavy reduction instead.

The team put the radical to work in two kinds of bond-forming reactions. One paired nickel with light to yield arylcyclopropanes. Those are prized building blocks in drug chemistry. Tests showed the method tolerates many chemical groups. Careful checks also exposed a side reaction with the solvent that limits capture. The work gives rare direct proof of how this shy radical behaves.
pmc-13630220:
Yingzhe Wang and six colleagues joined chemical profiling with gene activity mapping to solve a puzzle. The herb Eupatorium lindleyanum packs its active compounds in flowers and leaves. Its roots hold few. The plant is the source of a classic remedy for coughs and bronchitis. No molecular account existed of how it builds these compounds.

The team catalogued 321 compounds of the target family across root, stem, leaf, and flower. Clear tissue clusters appeared. They also sequenced the active genes of each tissue. Matching the two datasets surfaced twenty building genes. They span both known production paths. Network hub genes appeared too, plus five regulator families likely to steer output. The authors offer the candidate list as a base. Breeding or engineering higher-yielding plants can build on it.
pmc-13631120:
Jason Miguel Bean published this short reflective essay in 2026, drawn from his work in an exercise physiology laboratory. He writes about calibrating a breathing mask used to measure oxygen uptake while a young athlete runs on a treadmill to exhaustion.

Bean treats the moment of collapse not as a ruined test but as the cleanest point in the data. The runner pushes until breath turns harsh and focus slips, then folds toward the rails. For Bean, that drop marks a real threshold where muscle stops obeying the mind. The essay lingers on the salt, noise, and effort of the lab, and on what a tester learns by watching someone reach a true limit.
pmc-13643720:
Noé Herbel and twenty-four colleagues present a validation study of the Gustave Roussy Immune Score in patients receiving bispecific T-cell engager drugs in early phase I trials. The score, built from a blood cell ratio, albumin, and an enzyme level, already forecasts outcomes with checkpoint immunotherapy.

The team reviewed 150 patients across eleven trials run at their institute between 2016 and 2025. Patients classed low risk by the score lived far longer, with median survival near eighteen months against five, and also progressed more slowly. The advantage was strongest in blood cancers. The authors propose the score for trial patient selection.
pmc-13645220:
Yasmin Schmitz and eight colleagues present a study of PfATG18, a protein governing the digestive vacuole of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. The parasite eats hemoglobin inside red blood cells, and its vacuole must balance incoming food vesicles against membrane strain.

Removing the protein fragmented the vacuole, piled up undigested vesicles, and killed the parasites. Before that, the vacuole's proton pump fell apart architecturally, and blocking the pump copied the damage. The protein acts through pump-assembly partners rather than touching the pump itself. A resistance-linked variant instead made young parasites extra sensitive to a frontline drug.
pmc-13645520:
Maximilian Römer and eight colleagues present a case report of treating forty-four brain metastases at once with focused radiation after whole-brain treatment had already been used. Their patient, a sixty-two-year-old man with extensive small-cell lung cancer, first responded almost completely to whole-brain radiation.

About ten months later, scans showed forty-one new lesions plus growth in three older ones. Using a single-isocenter HyperArc technique, the team treated all forty-four in three fractions. Thinking tests showed only selective dips, later scans showed strong shrinkage, and no treated lesion had recurred at last follow-up. Two later courses handled new lesions the same way.
pmc-13646120:
Yulin Geng and Hong Zhang run a randomized trial on leg swelling that follows gynecological cancer surgery, testing a care plan shaped by body weight and traditional meridian theory. Sixty patients were split evenly between the new plan and standard care for six months. The new plan combined weight-tailored meridian massage with diet and health guidance. Standard care used compression stockings, education, and aerobic exercise, with outcome judges kept unaware of group assignment.

Leg volume fell by about a third in the treated group, against about a seventh under standard care. Quality of life scores also improved more than twice as much. Patients with the highest body weight seemed to gain the most, though that split was exploratory. Three treated patients had brief skin redness, and no serious harms appeared. The pair present weight-aware, integrated care as a stronger option for this chronic swelling problem.
pmc-13647120:
Liming Huo and six colleagues review seventy-nine hospital-acquired infections in a Chinese psychiatric hospital from March 2022 to June 2025. Psychiatric inpatients catch infections easily because thinking problems, weak self-care, and closed wards all raise exposure. The team profiled infection types and germs, tracked depression and anxiety scores from admission to discharge, and priced the extra cost. Risk factors for infections outside the lungs got special attention.

Lung infections made up about three quarters of cases. Women and patients with companion caregivers had notably higher rates of non-lung infections, a pattern the authors flag for ward practice. Mood and anxiety scores improved during the stay, though symptoms remained at discharge. Each extra infection day added a clear block of cost, and over half of cases never had a germ identified. The authors call the findings preliminary and urge tighter infection control in psychiatric wards.
pmc-13648820:
Kelsey M. Sumner and colleagues ran a trial of two flu shots that skip egg growth, for the 2024-2025 US season. One shot is built from pure virus protein made in cells. The other grows the virus in cell culture. Past proof on which shields best was thin.

The trial gave 591 adults, aged 18 to 64, one shot or the other by chance. Teams then watched for flu-like illness for six months and tested the sick. Flu A struck about 2 in 100 of the protein shot group and about 6 in 100 of the cell shot group. Blood tests in a subset showed stronger blocks on the virus coat for the protein shot. The authors say it shielded better that season.
pmc-13649420:
Shunrong Luo and three colleagues studied eye surface wounds that fail to heal because of the very drops used to treat the eyes. They reviewed 60 cases seen from 2020 to 2024 and tracked which drops were used, how often, and for how long.

Damage grew worse with more drugs used at once, more doses per day, and longer use. Most cases were judged probable drug reactions, and many were severe. Once harmful drops were stopped and replaced with gentler, preservative-free ones, most wounds healed within a month. The worst cases also got soft bandage lenses or membrane grafts. Total cure reached over four in five cases with this step-by-step care.
pmc-13649720:
Hollie Adams and two colleagues asked people with Parkinson's disease and their carers which daily aids help most. The disease slowly erodes independence in washing, dressing, and eating, and most past work stared at walking aids. Their web survey drew 293 replies and rated 40 devices from not useful to very useful.

Shower grab bars topped the list, rated very useful by four in five people. Plain grab bars came next, then electric toothbrushes, jar openers, and reacher tools. The authors say these patient-ranked results can help clinicians put simple, cheap aids first when they advise families. The aim is more independence in daily life for people with the disease.
pmc-13650120:
Donghao Li and nine colleagues, publishing in 2026, test what would happen to China's environmental footprint if residents actually ate according to the national healthy diet guidelines. Work on other countries often finds healthier diets lighter on the planet, so the team checked whether that holds across Chinese provinces.

Using a multi-regional input-output table and eleven food categories, the authors traced carbon and water footprints from 2017 to 2023 and modeled a full switch to the guideline diet. Footprints already rose over the study years, heavier in the southeast than the northwest. The guideline pattern raised both footprints further, with dairy as the main driver, and it shifted large shares of the burden between provinces through trade. One coastal province acted as a hub, passing impact onward while receiving it from neighbors. The study names diet change as a lever that can backfire without regional planning.
pmc-13651520:
Daniele Benetti and eleven colleagues ask whether the current flowing through a hematite photoanode really means oxygen is being made. Water oxidation is usually assumed to yield oxygen gas, and these rust-based electrodes are workhorses of solar fuel research, yet oxygen output at low rates had rarely been measured directly.

By detecting oxygen live with mass spectrometry while separately tracking how rate depends on the density of oxidizing holes at the surface, the team found a stark split. When single holes acted alone under first-order kinetics, almost none of the current produced oxygen. As hole density climbed and the kinetics turned cooperative, oxygen efficiency rose sharply. The same switch appeared in the dark under plain electrochemistry, marking it as a property of the material rather than of light. The authors frame multi-hole chemistry as the gatekeeper of selective oxygen evolution on metal oxides.
pmc-2667420:
Guh, Zhang, Bansback, and co-authors estimate how often overweight and obesity lead to other diseases. People carrying excess weight face higher risk of many medical conditions, which can bring further illness and early death. Planners need numbers for how often each linked condition actually begins.

The team carried out a systematic review and pooled analysis of prior studies. Their estimates cover the incidence of each co-morbidity tied to excess weight. Solid rates help governments weigh prevention spending and help doctors explain to patients which risks rise first as weight climbs.
pmc-3928520:
Krämer, Green, Pollard, and co-authors describe causal analysis approaches in Ingenuity Pathway Analysis, a commercial tool for interpreting gene-expression data. Prior biological knowledge greatly helps researchers make sense of such data. Causal networks built from relationships curated out of the literature are especially suited to the task.

Those networks let the software propose mechanistic hypotheses: which upstream regulators could explain an observed pattern of gene changes. Such hypotheses guide follow-up experiments instead of leaving teams with raw lists. The paper explains the reasoning behind a widely used commercial analysis platform.
pmc-4424520:
Agarwal, Mulgund, Hamada, and their co-authors gave a global view of male infertility in 2015. Infertility affects a large share of couples worldwide. Men are the sole cause in a notable fraction of cases and contribute to about half of all cases overall.

The authors stress that global figures hide wide differences between regions. Causes, access to testing, and cultural attitudes vary a great deal around the world. Male factors have often been under-studied compared with female factors. A clear worldwide picture helps clinics and policy makers give male infertility the attention and services it has lacked.
pmc-6084020:
Arnold Mitnitski, Alexander Mogilner, and Kenneth Rockwood developed a frailty index approach in this 2001 paper. Judging health in older people needs more than a list of diseases. The authors define an index as the share of health deficits a person has gathered.

Deficits include symptoms, signs, limits in daily tasks, and abnormal test results. The index behaves like a state measure, rising with age and predicting death and care needs. It works even when the exact deficit list changes between studies. The idea became a foundation of frailty research and is still widely used in geriatric medicine.
pmc-8262720:
Melissa Adasme and co-authors reported in 2021 an expanded version of PLIP, a tool that profiles the interactions between a small molecule and its target. As protein structure data pile up, understanding exactly how a drug-like molecule grips its target grows more important for design. PLIP automatically detects those contacts and draws them in clear visualizations.

The 2021 update widened the profiler beyond proteins, so it can also analyze molecules binding to DNA and RNA. The authors describe the new scope and the formats the tool produces for further work. Interaction profiles help medicinal chemists see which contacts hold a drug in place, and which changes might make it grip harder.
pound-hugh-selwyn-mauberley-1920:
Ezra Pound published Hugh Selwyn Mauberley in 1920, just after the First World War wrecked the London literary world he had conquered. The work is a sequence of eighteen short poems. Pound later treated it as a farewell to that world before he left England for Paris and Italy.

The sequence sketches Mauberley, a fastidious minor poet out of step with his age, and the age itself. War dead, profiteers, and faded aesthetes pass in cool, ironic quatrains. Pound mourns a civilization that chose commerce over art, in verse of lapidary control. Mauberley is his masterpiece of the postwar reckoning and one of the central poems of modernism.
pound-instigations-1920:
Instigations, published in 1920, gathers Pound's essays and provocations from the years when he was modernism's loudest advocate in London. The critic here is a provocateur: praising, attacking, and clearing space for new work.

The volume includes his long appreciation of Henry James, pieces on the French critic Remy de Gourmont, and his 'Art' manifestoes. Pound argues that criticism should test work against the best that exists, anywhere, in any age. His judgments are swift, learned, and often unfair, but never dull. The book shows how modern taste was fought into being, one essay at a time.
russell-bolshevism-1920:
In 1920 Russell traveled to Soviet Russia with a Labour delegation and came home to write this report. The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism, published that year, is a rare thing: a sympathetic visitor's clear-eyed refusal to convert.

Russell admired the revolution's energy and its leaders' ability, and he met Lenin. But he found the regime's methods appalling: secret police, crushed dissent, and a dogma that licensed any cruelty. He predicted much of what followed with grim accuracy. The book split him from the British left and still reads as a model of honest political travel writing.
sandburg-smoke-and-steel-1920:
Carl Sandburg published Smoke and Steel in 1920, his third book of poems. Sandburg, the son of Swedish immigrants, had worked as a laborer, soldier, and Chicago newspaper reporter. He wrote about the industrial Midwest from inside knowledge of its mills and rail yards.

The poems honor furnaces, freight trains, and the workers who tend them. Sandburg's long free-verse lines stack images of smoke, pig iron, and prairie wheat. He also remembers war dead and praises ordinary people's endurance. The book carries forward the work of his Chicago Poems with a wider national sweep. It remains the great book of American industry in verse.
sanger-woman-and-new-race-1920: Woman and the New Race, Margaret Sanger's 1920 birth-control classic. The new womanhood. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
santayana-character-opinion-us-1920:
Character and Opinion in the United States, published in 1920, gathers lectures the Spanish-born Santayana gave on the American mind. No outsider has written about America with this mixture of affection, amusement, and cool distance.

He describes the genteel tradition, the inherited idealism of American culture, beset by the skyscraper world of business and sport. Emerson, James, and Harvard itself pass under his gaze. His image of the American as a man divided, his will in the present and his intellect in a colonial mansion, is still quoted. The book remains a penetrating portrait by a resident alien.
schlick-space-time-physics-1920:
Space and Time in Contemporary Physics, published in English in 1920 in Henry L. Brose's translation, is Moritz Schlick's introduction to relativity for philosophers. Schlick, founder of the Vienna Circle, was the thinker best placed to explain what Einstein meant.

He leads readers from Newton through special relativity to the general theory's curved geometry, always asking what the physics assumes and what it proves. The treatment is lucid, brief, and philosophically exact. The book became the Vienna Circle's founding statement on physics. It still serves as a model of how philosophy should receive a scientific revolution.
schrenck-notzing-phenomena-materialisati:
Albert von Schrenck-Notzing put seers in a lab in Phenomena of Materialisation, his report of 1920. Schrenck-Notzing was a healer in Munich with a zeal for strict tests. His seers wore sewn suits, sat in lit cages, and were held by the hands. Yet, he claims, a strange stuff crept from them and took shapes like limbs and veils.

He calls the stuff ectoplasm and prints plates by the score. Peers cried fraud in case past case. His book is the high mark of that strange line of tests. Its claims still row.
seaborn-symzonia-1820:
Captain Adam Seaborn is the pen name on this sea tale of 1820, the first novel of the hollow earth. No one knows for sure who wrote it, though Symmes and his kin are oft named. The tale takes Symmes's polar holes as its map and sails straight in.

The ship's crew pass through the north hole and find a mild inner world, named Symzonia. Its folk are fair, wise, and strange, with crafts and laws of their own. The book set the form for a long line of tales of worlds hid inside our own.
shelley-prometheus-unbound-1820:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Prometheus Unbound in Italy and published it in 1820. He took the Greek Titan Prometheus, chained by Zeus for giving fire to mankind, as his hero. Greek legend left Prometheus bound forever; Shelley set out to free him.

In Shelley's lyrical drama, Prometheus endures centuries of torture without cursing his enemy. When hatred finally leaves his heart, the tyrant Jupiter falls and a new age of love begins. Spirits, Earth, and the Moon sing the change in soaring choruses. The play is less a stage work than a vision of human liberation. It stands as the purest statement of Romantic optimism.
splendor-solis-alchemical-treatises-of-s: Splendor Solis, alchemical treatises of Solomon Trismosin, 1920, with 22 allegorical paintings. The sun's splendor. This book preserves that alchemy. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The historical record keeps it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
spr-proceedings-vol30-1919-1920:
Volume thirty binds parts seventy five through seventy eight and an appendix, for 1919 and 1920. Peace returns, and the Society for Psychical Research counts its losses and its files. The postwar sittings with mediums draw crowds of the bereaved. Cross references and proxy sitters guard the reports as before.

Telepathy experiments resume their peacetime forms and scoring. Apparition cases from the war years receive their checked write ups. The volume bridges the archive from war into a new decade. Its records fed the famous postwar books on survival. Volume thirty closes the society's first forty years in print. The debate it serves ran on to 1930.
stoddard-rising-tide-color-1920:
Lothrop Stoddard published The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy in 1920. Stoddard, a Harvard-trained writer, surveyed the world after the First World War and warned his white readers that their global rule was ending. The book's title gave its whole argument in one image.

Stoddard treated the growth and revolt of colonized peoples in Asia and Africa as a single threat to white supremacy. He urged unity among white nations and strict immigration bars at home. The book sold widely and shaped restrictionist debate in the United States. Scholars cite it as a key primary source on white-supremacist ideology and the fears behind immigration restriction.
suppressed-gospels-vol-2-1820:
Volume 2 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in this edition in 1820. The volume centers on the Protevangelion, an early account of the birth and youth of Mary. Wake, an archbishop of Canterbury, had translated early Christian writings outside the New Testament.

The Protevangelion tells of Mary's parents, her childhood in the Temple, and the birth of Jesus with added wonders. Such texts shaped art and folk belief for centuries, though churches left them out of scripture. Reading them shows what early Christians wanted to know about the holy family's hidden years. The volume belongs to a nine-volume set of these disputed writings.
suppressed-gospels-vol-3-1820:
Volume 3 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in 1820. Its main text is the Infancy of Jesus Christ, an early gospel about the childhood of Jesus. The canonical gospels say almost nothing about those years, and this text filled the gap with wonders.

Stories show the child Jesus giving life to clay birds, striking playmates, and working miracles in Egypt. Medieval readers loved these tales, and they fed plays, poems, and paintings. Church leaders judged the book unreliable and left it outside scripture. The volume preserves a vivid record of how popular faith pictured the young Jesus.
suppressed-gospels-vol-4-1820:
Volume 4 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820. Its named text is the Gospel of Nicodemus, an early account of the trial, death, and descent of Christ. Nicodemus appears in John's gospel as a secret follower who came to Jesus by night.

The text expands Pilate's court, the wonders at the crucifixion, and Christ's descent to free the dead. A second part tells of Joseph of Arimathea and his imprisonment and release. Medieval drama drew heavily on these scenes. The volume shows how early and medieval Christians enlarged the Passion story far beyond the four gospels in their Bible.
suppressed-gospels-vol-5-1820:
Volume 5 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in this edition in 1820. The set gathered early Christian writings that stood outside the New Testament. Wake, archbishop of Canterbury, had made these translations to let readers judge the texts for themselves.

Writings in this middle volume continue the set's mix of gospels, acts, and letters linked to apostles and early teachers. Some claim missing details of Christ's life, while others teach or warn the young churches. Scholars value the set for showing the wide range of early Christian writing. General readers get stories and teachings that nearly entered scripture but did not.
suppressed-gospels-vol-6-1820:
Volume 6 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820. Its named figure is Clement, an early leader of the church in Rome. Writings linked to Clement were among the most respected texts outside the New Testament.

Letters and teachings in the volume deal with order in the church, good conduct, and the duties of bishops and members. Clement's name carried weight because tradition placed him close to the apostles themselves. Readers can see how the early church settled questions of authority and morals. The volume helps explain why some texts were treasured for centuries even though they never became part of the Bible.
suppressed-gospels-vol-7-1820:
Volume 7 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in this edition in 1820. The nine-volume set reprinted Wake's translations of early Christian writings left outside the New Testament. By this volume the set has moved deep into letters and acts linked to the first generations of the church.

Texts here preserve teachings, travels, and trials ascribed to apostles and their followers, with much added legend. Some passages agree with scripture, while others add marvels the churches rejected. The set lets readers compare accepted and disputed writings side by side. That contrast is the value of the volume: it shows the border of the Bible being drawn in real time.
suppressed-gospels-vol-8-1820:
Volume 8 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820, near the end of the nine-volume set. Wake's project gave English readers the early Christian writings that churches had read, debated, and finally set aside. Volume 8 continues that disputed library.

Gospels, acts, and letters in the volume claim apostolic roots, yet carry stories and teachings found nowhere in scripture. Some fed medieval devotion, art, and feast days for a thousand years. Others survive only in fragments and old lists. Together they show how much early Christian writing the canon left behind, and why scholars still mine these texts for the beliefs of the first churches.
tawney-acquisitive-society-1920:
R. H. Tawney published The Acquisitive Society in 1920, a classic of ethical socialism. Tawney argues that modern society honors acquisition over function. Property that serves no work, he claims, has weak moral title. Rights should attach to service rendered, not to mere ownership.

He calls for industry organized as a profession, with standards and public purpose. The book grew from his wartime and postwar lectures and essays. Its prose is lucid, grave, and quietly angry. Tawney influenced the Labour Party's moral outlook for a generation. Later editions kept it in print for students. It remains a model of social criticism grounded in ethics rather than envy.

Legends of Jesus as a child fill the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, a work the early church never took into its canon. The boy forms sparrows from river clay and breathes them alive before startled playmates. His powers amaze the village, and sometimes they frighten it.

The child's temper proves as miraculous as his gifts: those who cross him wither or fall. Teachers fare no better against his strange knowledge. The stories are vivid, unruly, and very human in their curiosity about a holy childhood. The evidence notes no public-domain text is attached to this entry yet. The tales survive because believers loved them.

Few forgeries have done more harm than the Protocols of the Learned Elders of Zion. The text claims to record a Jewish plan for world domination. In fact it was fabricated in the orbit of the Tsar's secret police, the Okhrana, stitched together from older satire and fiction.

Newspapers and courts exposed the fraud within two decades of its spread, yet the lie kept traveling. It fed pogroms, Nazi propaganda, and hate movements that still quote it. This library keeps the text as evidence: a case study in how a fake document can poison a century. It is presented as a debunked forgery, never as fact.

William Walker Atkinson, a New Thought writer, published under the pen name Yogi Ramacharaka for books on Eastern-style spiritual teaching. In Mystic Christianity he turns that lens on Jesus, reading the Master's life and sayings as an inner teaching rather than mainly a matter of church doctrine. The work first appeared in the early 1900s.

Miracles and parables become lessons about the growth of the soul. Atkinson blends ideas from Eastern and Western religion into one system, arguing that hidden meaning lies beneath familiar Gospel stories. Readers get an early American attempt to join Christian devotion to a wider, comparative spirituality popular in his period.
tob-10220:
Bertrand Russell published The Problems of Philosophy in 1912 as a short introduction for general readers. He begins with a familiar object: the table in front of us. How do we know it is real, and what exactly do we know when we look at it or touch it?

From appearance and reality, Russell moves through matter, knowledge by acquaintance and description, universals, and truth and falsehood. He is candid that philosophy often raises questions it cannot finally settle. Readers get a clear demonstration of why the big questions matter anyway, and a model of thinking slowly and precisely about things common sense takes for granted.

Albert Pike published Morals and Dogma in 1871 as lectures on the thirty-two degrees of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry. Each degree receives a chapter drawing morals from ancient symbols, comparative religion, and philosophy. The volume is massive, dense, and endlessly digressive by design.

Pike ranges from Egyptian and Greek mysteries to Kabbalah and medieval chivalry, reading Masonic ritual as a school of ethics and toleration. Few members have read it whole, yet it remains the most famous and most misunderstood book in American Masonry, quoted and misquoted by admirers and conspiracy writers alike. Patient readers find a nineteenth-century moral philosophy in ritual dress.
